    (Dmax b : ℝ) ≤ C * b * log b * log (log b) ^ 3 * log (log (log b)) ^ K

problems.title: Erdős Problem 306
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/306](https://www.erdosproblems.com/306)
- [Li26] S. Li, *Unit fractions with semiprime denominators: an elementary proof of Erdős
  Problem 306*. arXiv:2609.32140 (2026).
- [Ta26] [Tang, Yuren, *A Lean 4 formalisation of Erdős Problem
  306*](https://github.com/Yuren-Tang/erdos-306), a proof modulo two Rosser–Schoenfeld axioms.

statements.name: Erdos306.erdos_306
statements.doc:
Let $\frac a b\in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ with $b$ squarefree. Are there integers $1 < n_1 < \dots < n_k$,
each the product of two distinct primes, such that $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$?

The answer is yes [Li26].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_306 : ∀ (q : ℚ), 0 < q → Squarefree q.den →
    ∃ k : ℕ, ∃ (n : Fin (k + 1) → ℕ), n 0 = 1 ∧ StrictMono n ∧
    (∀ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k), ω (n i) = 2 ∧ Ω (n i) = 2) ∧
    q = ∑ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k), (1 : ℚ) / (n i)

statements.name: Erdos306.erdos_306.variants.integer_three_primes
statements.doc:
Every positive integer can be expressed as an Egyptian fraction where each denominator is the
product of three distinct primes.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_306.variants.integer_three_primes (m : ℕ) (h : 0 < m) :
    ∃ k > (0 : ℕ), ∃ (n : Fin (k + 1) → ℕ), n 0 = 1 ∧
    ∀ i, (hik : i < k) → n ⟨i, by omega⟩ < n ⟨(i + 1), by omega⟩ ∧
    (∀ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k), ω (n i) = 3 ∧ Ω (n i) = 3) ∧
    m = ∑ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 (Fin.last k), (1 : ℚ) / (n i)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 307
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)

statements.name: Erdos307.erdos_307
statements.doc:
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$
1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right)
$$
?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., _Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program._
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_307 : ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)

statements.name: Erdos307.erdos_307.variants.coprime
statements.doc:
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)
$$
and
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime : ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧
    Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)

statements.name: Erdos307.erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_notMem
statements.doc: There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_notMem : ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 ∉ P ∪ Q ∧
    1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧ Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)

statements.name: Erdos307.erdos_307.barrier
statements.doc:
A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at
least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by
symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full
`sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean`): the left conjunct is `card_ge_59`,
the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. Both depend on `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` and
nothing further: the evaluation of the first 59 primes is kernel-checked by `decide`, so no
`native_decide` enters this statement.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_307.barrier {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) (hQne : Q.Nonempty)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    59 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) ∧ (4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2

statements.name: Erdos307.erdos_307.barrier_sixty
statements.doc:
A stronger machine-checked **barrier** (Bonfioli, 2026), closing the 59-prime level: any solution of
Erdős 307 in fact uses at least `60` primes in total. The full `sorry`-free proof is `erdos307_sixty`
in the linked repository (`Sixty.lean` at tag `v1.1.1`); its only non-logical input is a `native_decide`
depth-first search establishing that no admissible 59-prime support survives the Pythagorean
`plus`-value square test, with axioms `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` together with that
`native_decide`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_307.barrier_sixty {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    60 ≤ #(P ∪ Q)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 308
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/308](https://www.erdosproblems.com/308)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., _Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory_. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Cr99] Croot, III, Ernest S., _On some questions of Erdős and Graham about Egyptian
  fractions_. Mathematika (1999), 359-372.

statements.name: Erdos308.erdos_308.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $N\geq 1$. What is the smallest integer not representable as the sum of distinct unit
fractions with denominators from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$?

This was essentially solved by Croot [Cr99] (see `erdos_308.variants.croot`); in particular,
for all sufficiently large $N$, the smallest such integer is either $m_N$ or $m_N+1$, where
$m_N=\lfloor \sum_{n\leq N}\frac{1}{n}\rfloor$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_308.parts.i : ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, f N = m N ∨ f N = m N + 1

statements.name: Erdos308.erdos_308.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $N\geq 1$. Is it true that the set of integers representable as the sum of distinct unit
fractions with denominators from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has the shape $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $m$?

It follows from Croot's bounds [Cr99] that this holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_308.parts.ii :
    ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, ∃ m, representable N = Set.Icc 1 m

statements.name: Erdos308.erdos_308.variants.shape
statements.doc:
If $m_N=\lfloor \sum_{n\leq N}\frac{1}{n}\rfloor$, then the set of integers representable is, for
all $N$ sufficiently large, either $\{1,\ldots,m_N-1\}$ or $\{1,\ldots,m_N\}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_308.variants.shape : ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop,
    representable N = Set.Icc 1 (m N - 1) ∨ representable N = Set.Icc 1 (m N)

statements.name: Erdos308.erdos_308.variants.croot
statements.doc:
Croot [Cr99] bounded $\eta(N)$, the largest integer such that every integer in
$\{1,\ldots,\eta(N)\}$ is representable; this is $f(N)-1$, so his bounds read
$$\left\lfloor\sum_{n\leq N}\frac{1}{n}-\frac{9}{2}(1+o(1))\frac{(\log\log N)^2}{\log N}
\right\rfloor + 1 \leq f(N)$$
and
$$f(N)\leq \left\lfloor\sum_{n\leq N}\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{2}(1+o(1))
\frac{(\log\log N)^2}{\log N}\right\rfloor + 1.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_308.variants.croot :
    ∃ o₁ o₂ : ℕ → ℝ, Tendsto o₁ atTop (nhds 0) ∧ Tendsto o₂ atTop (nhds 0) ∧
      ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop,
        ⌊(harmonic N : ℝ) - 9 / 2 * (1 + o₁ N) * (log (log N)) ^ 2 / log N⌋₊ + 1 ≤ f N ∧
        f N ≤ ⌊(harmonic N : ℝ) - 1 / 2 * (1 + o₂ N) * (log (log N)) ^ 2 / log N⌋₊ + 1

statements.name: Erdos308.erdos_308.variants.all_N
statements.doc:
Is it true that, for every $N\geq 1$, the set of integers representable as the sum of distinct
unit fractions with denominators from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has the shape $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some
$m$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_308.variants.all_N :
    ∀ N ≥ 1, ∃ m, representable N = Set.Icc 1 m

problems.title: Erdős Problem 309
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/309](https://www.erdosproblems.com/309)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Yo97] Yokota, Hisashi, *On number of integers representable as a sum of unit fractions. II*.
  J. Number Theory (1997), 162--169.
- [Cr99] Croot, III, Ernest S., *On some questions of Erdős and Graham about Egyptian fractions*.
  Mathematika (1999), 359-372.
- [Yo02] Yokota, Hisashi, *On the number of integers representable as sums of unit fractions.
  III*. J. Number Theory (2002), 351--372.

statements.name: Erdos309.erdos_309
statements.doc:
Let $N\geq 1$. How many integers can be written as the sum of distinct unit fractions with
denominators from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$? Are there $o(\log N)$ such integers?

If the number of such integers is $N(n)$ then it is trivial that $N(n)\leq \log n+O(1)$. Yokota
[Yo97] proved that $N(n)\geq \log n-O(\log\log n)$.

Croot [Cr99] proved that every integer at most
$$\leq \sum_{n\leq N}\frac{1}{n}-(\tfrac{9}{2}+o(1))\frac{(\log\log N)^2}{\log N}$$
can be so represented.

If $F(N)$ counts the number of integers which can be represented in this fashion, then the
current best lower bound known is
$$F(N) \geq \log N+\gamma -\left(\frac{\pi^2}{3}+o(1)\right)\frac{(\log\log N)^2}{\log N}$$
due to Yokota [Yo02].

The answer to the question is no: $F(N) \sim \log N$. Here $0$ (the empty sum) is counted.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_309 :
    ¬ (fun N : ℕ => (F N : ℝ)) =o[atTop] fun N : ℕ => Real.log N

statements.name: Erdos309.erdos_309.variants.asymptotic
statements.doc: The number of representable integers satisfies $F(N) \sim \log N$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_309.variants.asymptotic :
    Tendsto (fun N : ℕ => (F N : ℝ) / Real.log N) atTop (𝓝 1)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 310
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/310](https://www.erdosproblems.com/310)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [LiSa24] Liu, Y. and Sawhney, M., *On further questions regarding unit fractions*.
  arXiv:2404.07113 (2024).
- [Bl21] Bloom, T. F., *On a density conjecture about unit fractions*. arXiv:2112.03726 (2021).

statements.name: Erdos310.erdos_310
statements.doc:
Let $\alpha >0$ and $N\geq 1$. Is it true that for any $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with
$\lvert A\rvert \geq \alpha N$ there exists some $S\subseteq A$ such that
$$\frac{a}{b}=\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}$$
with $a\leq b =O_\alpha(1)$?

Liu and Sawhney [LiSa24] observed that the main result of Bloom [Bl21] implies a positive
solution to this conjecture. They prove a more precise version, that if
$(\log N)^{-1/7+o(1)}\leq \alpha \leq 1/2$ then there is some $S\subseteq A$ such that
$\frac{a}{b}=\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}$ with $a\leq b \leq \exp(O(1/\alpha))$. They also observe
that the dependence $b\leq \exp(O(1/\alpha))$ is sharp.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_310 : ∀ α : ℝ, 0 < α → ∃ C : ℕ, ∀ N : ℕ, 1 ≤ N →
    ∀ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N, α * N ≤ A.card →
      ∃ S ⊆ A, ∃ a b : ℕ, 0 < a ∧ a ≤ b ∧ b ≤ C ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = a / b

statements.name: Erdos310.erdos_310.variants.liu_sawhney
statements.doc:
Liu and Sawhney [LiSa24] proved that if $(\log N)^{-1/7+o(1)}\leq \alpha \leq 1/2$ then there is
some $S\subseteq A$ such that $\frac{a}{b}=\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}$ with
$a\leq b \leq \exp(O(1/\alpha))$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_310.variants.liu_sawhney : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in Filter.atTop,
    ∀ α : ℝ, Real.log N ^ (-(1 / 7 : ℝ) + ε) ≤ α → α ≤ 1 / 2 →
      ∀ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N, α * N ≤ A.card →
        ∃ S ⊆ A, ∃ a b : ℕ, 0 < a ∧ a ≤ b ∧ (b : ℝ) ≤ Real.exp (C / α) ∧
          ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = a / b

problems.title: Erdős Problem 311
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/311](https://www.erdosproblems.com/311)
- [ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980), p. 40.

statements.name: Erdos311.erdos_311
statements.doc:
Let $\delta(N)$ be the minimal non-zero value of $\lvert 1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\rvert$ as $A$
ranges over all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Is it true that
$$\delta(N)=e^{-(c+o(1))N}$$
for some constant $c\in (0,1)$?

The formulation in [ErGr80] has the additional condition that $A$ contains no $S$ with
$\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$; Kovac (in the comments on the problem page) showed that the
formulation above is equivalent. We state $\delta(N)=e^{-(c+o(1))N}$ as
$-\log \delta(N) / N \to c$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_311 :
    ∃ c ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1,
      Tendsto (fun N : ℕ => -Real.log (delta N) / N) atTop (𝓝 c)

statements.name: Erdos311.delta_ge_inv_lcm
statements.doc:
The trivial lower bound: every non-zero value of $1 - \sum_{n \in A} 1/n$ is a non-zero rational
with denominator dividing $[1, \ldots, N]$, so $\delta(N) \geq 1/[1,\ldots,N]$.
statements.statement: theorem delta_ge_inv_lcm (N : ℕ) : 1 / (((Icc 1 N).lcm id : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ delta N

statements.name: Erdos311.delta_ge_exp
statements.doc: Since $[1, \ldots, N] = e^{(1+o(1))N}$, the trivial bound gives $\delta(N) \ge e^{-(1+o(1))N}$.
statements.statement: theorem delta_ge_exp : ∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, Real.exp (-(1 + ε) * N) ≤ delta N

problems.title: Erdős Problem 312
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/312](https://www.erdosproblems.com/312)

statements.name: Erdos312.erdos_312
statements.doc:
Does there exist a constant `c > 0` such that, for any `K > 1`, whenever `A` is a sufficiently large
finite multiset of integers with $\sum_{n \in A} 1/n > K$ there exists some $S \subseteq A$ such that
$1 - \exp(-(c*K)) < \sum_{n \in S} 1/n \le 1$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_312 :
    ∃ (c : ℝ), 0 < c ∧
      ∀ (K : ℝ), 1 < K →
        ∃ (N₀ : ℕ),
          ∀ (n : ℕ) (a : Fin n → ℕ),
            (n ≥ N₀ ∧ (∑ i : Fin n, (a i : ℝ)⁻¹) > K) →
              ∃ (S : Finset (Fin n)),
                1 - Real.exp (-(c * K)) < (∑ i ∈ S, (a i : ℝ)⁻¹) ∧
                ∑ i ∈ S, (a i : ℝ)⁻¹ ≤ 1

problems.title: Erdős Problem 313
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/313](https://www.erdosproblems.com/313)
- [A54377](https://oeis.org/A54377) (Primary pseudoperfect numbers)

statements.name: Erdos313.erdos_313
statements.doc:
Are there infinitely many pairs `(m, P)` where `m ≥ 2` is an integer
and `P` is a set of distinct primes such that the following equation holds:
$\sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} = 1 - \frac{1}{m}$?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_313 : erdos313Solutions.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos313.erdos_313.variants.primary_pseudoperfect_are_infinite
statements.doc: It is conjectured that the set of primary pseudoperfect numbers is infinite.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_313.variants.primary_pseudoperfect_are_infinite :
    Set.Infinite {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n}

statements.name: Erdos313.erdos_313.variants.exists_at_least_eight_primary_pseudoperfect
statements.doc:
There are at least 8 primary pseudoperfect numbers. The first eight terms of
[A54377](https://oeis.org/A54377) are exhibited together with their explicit
prime decompositions.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_313.variants.exists_at_least_eight_primary_pseudoperfect :
    8 ≤ (Set.encard {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n})

problems.title: Erdős Problem 314
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/314](https://www.erdosproblems.com/314)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [LiSt24] J. Lim and Steinerberger, S., *On differences of two harmonic numbers*.
  arXiv:2405.11354 (2024).

statements.name: Erdos314.erdos_314
statements.doc:
Let $n\geq 1$ and let $m$ be minimal such that $\sum_{n\leq k\leq m}\frac{1}{k}\geq 1$. We define
$$\epsilon(n) = \sum_{n\leq k\leq m}\frac{1}{k}-1.$$
How small can $\epsilon(n)$ be? Is it true that
$$\liminf n^2\epsilon(n)=0?$$

This is true, and shown by Lim and Steinerberger [LiSt24], who further proved that, for any
$\delta>0$, there exist infinitely many $n$ and $m$ such that
$$n^2\left\lvert \sum_{n\leq k\leq m}\frac{1}{k}-1\right\rvert\ll \frac{1}{(\log n)^{5/4-\delta}}.$$
Erdős and Graham (and also Lim and Steinerberger) believe that the exponent of $2$ is best
possible here, in that $\liminf \epsilon(n) n^{2+\delta}=\infty$ for all $\delta>0$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_314 :
    atTop.liminf (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) ^ 2 * epsilon n) = 0

problems.title: Erdős Problem 315
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/315](https://www.erdosproblems.com/315)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Ka25] Y. Kamio, *Asymptotic analysis of infinite decompositions of a unit fraction into unit
  fractions*. arXiv:2503.02317 (2025).
- [LiTa25] Z. Li and Q. Tang, *On a conjecture of Erdős and Graham about the Sylvester's
  sequence*. arXiv:2503.12277 (2025).

statements.name: Erdos315.erdos_315
statements.doc:
Let $u_1=1$ and $u_{n+1}=u_n(u_n+1)$, so that $\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{1}{u_k+1}$ and
$u_k=\lfloor c_0^{2^k}+1\rfloor$ for $k\geq 1$, where
$$c_0=\lim u_n^{1/2^n}=1.264085\cdots.$$
Let $a_1<a_2<\cdots $ be any other sequence with $\sum \frac{1}{a_k}=1$. Is it true that
$$\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}<c_0=1.264085\cdots?$$

This is true, and was proved independently by Kamio [Ka25] and Li and Tang [LiTa25].

An earlier interpretation of this question on this site defined $u_1=2$ and
$u_{n+1}=u_n^2-u_n+1$ (Sylvester's sequence), which is the same sequence shifted by $1$; we use
the phrasing above as more faithful to [ErGr80]. The constant $c_0$ is called the Vardi constant.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_315 :
    ∀ a : ℕ → ℕ, (∀ i, 0 < a i) → StrictMono a → (∃ i, a i ≠ u i + 1) →
      ∑' i, (1 : ℝ) / a i = 1 →
      atTop.liminf (fun i => (a i : ℝ) ^ ((1 / 2 : ℝ) ^ (i + 1))) < c₀

problems.title: Erdős Problem 316
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/316](https://www.erdosproblems.com/316)
- [Sa97] Sándor, Csaba, On a problem of Erdős. J. Number Theory (1997), 203-210.

statements.name: Erdos316.erdos_316
statements.doc:
Is it true that if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$ is a finite set with
$\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n} < 2$ then there is a partition $A=A_1 \sqcup A_2$
such that $\sum_{n \in A_i} \frac{1}{n} < 1$ for $i=1,2$?

This is not true in general, as shown by Sándor [Sa97].

The minimal counterexample is $\{2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15\}$, found by Tom Stobart.

This was formalized in Lean by Mehta.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_316 : ¬ ∀ A : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ A → 1 ∉ A →
    ∑ n ∈ A, (1 / n : ℚ) < 2 → ∃ (A₁ A₂ : Finset ℕ),
      Disjoint A₁ A₂ ∧ A = A₁ ∪ A₂ ∧
      ∑ n ∈ A₁, (1 / n : ℚ) < 1 ∧ ∑ n ∈ A₂, (1 / n : ℚ) <  1

statements.name: Erdos316.erdos_316.variants.multiset
statements.doc: This is not true if $A$ is a multiset, for example $2,3,3,5,5,5,5$.
statements.statement:
lemma erdos_316.variants.multiset : ∃ A : Multiset ℕ, 0 ∉ A ∧ 1 ∉ A ∧
    (A.map ((1 : ℚ) / ·)).sum < 2 ∧ ∀ (A₁ A₂ : Multiset ℕ),
      A = A₁ + A₂ →
        1 ≤ (A₁.map ((1 : ℚ) / ·)).sum ∨ 1 ≤ (A₂.map ((1 : ℚ) / ·)).sum

statements.name: Erdos316.erdos_316.variants.generalized
statements.doc:
This is not true in general, as shown by Sándor [Sa97], who observed that the proper divisors of
$120$ form a counterexample. More generally, Sándor shows that for any $n\geq 2$ there exists a
finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}\backslash\{1\}$ with $\sum_{k\in A}\frac{1}{k} < n$ and no
partition into $n$ parts each of which has $\sum_{k\in A_i}\frac{1}{k}<1$.

A `Finpartition` has no empty parts, so partitions into at most $n$ parts are tested. Testing
exactly $n$ parts would let the singleton $\{2\}$ satisfy the statement vacuously.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_316.variants.generalized (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) : ∃ A : Finset ℕ,
    A.Nonempty ∧ 0 ∉ A ∧ 1 ∉ A ∧ ∑ k ∈ A, (1 / k : ℚ) < n ∧ ∀ P : Finpartition A,
    P.parts.card ≤ n → ∃ p ∈ P.parts, 1 ≤ ∑ n ∈ p, (1 / n : ℚ)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 317
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/317](https://www.erdosproblems.com/317)

statements.name: Erdos317.erdos_317
statements.doc:
Is there some constant $c>0$ such that for every $n\geq 1$ there exists some $\delta_k\in \{-1,0,1\}$ for $1\leq k\leq n$ with
$$0< \left\lvert \sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right\rvert < \frac{c}{2^n}?$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_317 :
    ∃ c > 0, ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ δ : Fin n → ℚ,
      Set.range δ ⊆ {-1, 0, 1} ∧
      letI lhs : ℝ := |∑ k, (δ k) / (k + 1)|
      0 < lhs ∧ lhs < c / 2^n

statements.name: Erdos317.erdos_317.variants.claim2
statements.doc:
Is it true that for sufficiently large $n$, for any $\delta_k\in \{-1,0,1\}$,
$$\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right\rvert > \frac{1}{[1,\ldots,n]}$$
whenever the left-hand side is not zero?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_317.variants.claim2 :
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ δ : (Fin n) → ℚ, δ '' Set.univ ⊆ {-1,0,1} →
    letI lhs := |∑ k, ((δ k : ℚ) / (k + 1))|
    lhs ≠ 0 → lhs > 1 / (Icc 1 n).lcm id

statements.name: Erdos317.claim2_inequality
statements.doc: Inequality in `erdos_317.variants.claim2` is obvious, the problem is strict inequality.
statements.statement:
lemma claim2_inequality : ∀ᶠ n in atTop,
    ∀ δ : (Fin n) → ℚ, δ '' Set.univ ⊆ {-1,0,1} →
    letI lhs := |∑ k, ((δ k : ℚ) / (k + 1))|
    lhs ≠ 0 → lhs ≥ 1 / (Icc 1 n).lcm id

statements.name: Erdos317.erdos_317.variants.counterexample
statements.doc:
`erdos_317.variants.claim2` fails for small $n$, for example
$$\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}=-\frac{1}{12}.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_317.variants.counterexample : ¬ (∀  δ : (Fin 4) → ℚ, δ '' Set.univ ⊆ {-1,0,1} →
    letI lhs := |∑ k, ((δ k : ℚ) / (k + 1))|
    lhs ≠ 0 → lhs > (1 : ℚ) / ((Icc 1 4).lcm id : ℕ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 318
problems.doc:
*References:*
  - [erdosproblems.com/318](https://www.erdosproblems.com/318)
  - [ErSt75] Erdős, P. and Straus, E. G., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 183.
  - [Sa75] Sattler, R., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 184-189.
  - [Sa82b] Sattler, R., On Erdős property P₁ for the arithmetical sequence. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch.
    Indag. Math. (1982), 347--352.
  - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
    theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
  - [La26] D. Larsen, [Erdős problem 318](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/blob/main/318.pdf) (2026)

statements.name: Erdos318.erdos_318.variants.univ
statements.doc: `ℕ` has property `P₁`. This is proved in [ErSt75].
statements.statement: theorem erdos_318.variants.univ : P₁ univ

statements.name: Erdos318.erdos_318.variants.odd
statements.doc: Sattler proved in [Sa75] that the set of odd numbers has property `P₁`.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_318.variants.odd : P₁ {n | Odd n}

statements.name: Erdos318.erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even
statements.doc:
For any infinite set `A` containing exactly one positive even number, `A` does not have
property `P₁`. Sattler [Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős, who presumably found this after
[ErGr80]. The element `0` is not counted, since `P₁` ignores it, and the infinitude hypothesis
excludes degenerate sets such as `{2}`, on which `P₁` holds vacuously.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.Infinite)
    (hA' : {n | n ∈ A \ {0} ∧ Even n}.ncard = 1) : ¬ P₁ A

statements.name: Erdos318.erdos_318.parts.i
statements.doc:
There exists a set `A` with positive density that does not have property `P₁`.
#TODO: prove this lemma by assuming `erdos_318.contain_single_even`.

The density sits in an existential, so `HasPosDensity` is the *stronger* reading here and
weakening it to positive lower density would claim less, which is the opposite of the usual
situation for Erdős' "positive density". It also costs nothing: by
`erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even` a witness only needs exactly one even element, and the
odd numbers together with one even number have density `1 / 2` on the nose.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_318.parts.i : ∃ A : Set ℕ, HasPosDensity A ∧ ¬ P₁ A

statements.name: Erdos318.erdos_318.variants.infinite_AP
statements.doc: Every infinite arithmetic progression has property `P₁`. This is proved in [Sa82b].
statements.statement: theorem erdos_318.variants.infinite_AP {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.IsAPOfLength ⊤) : P₁ A

statements.name: Erdos318.erdos_318.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Does the set of squares excluding 1 have property `P₁`?

Larsen [La26] proved that this set does have property `P₁`.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_318.parts.ii : P₁ ({n | IsSquare n} \ {1})

problems.title: Erdős Problem 319
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/319](https://www.erdosproblems.com/319)

statements.name: Erdos319.erdos_319
statements.doc:
What is the size of the largest $A\subseteq\{1, \dots, N\}$ such that there is a function
$\delta : A \to \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
  \sum_{n\in A} \frac{\delta n}{n} = 0
$$
and
$$
  \sum_{n\in A'}\frac{\delta n}{n} \neq 0
$$
for all non-empty $A'\subsetneq A$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_319 (N : ℕ) : IsGreatest
    { #A | (A) (_ : A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N)
      (_ : ∃ δ : ℕ → ℤˣ, ∑ n ∈ A, (δ n : ℚ) / n = 0 ∧
        ∀ A' ⊂ A, A'.Nonempty → ∑ n ∈ A', (δ n : ℚ) / n ≠ 0) }
    erdos_319.answer

statements.name: Erdos319.erdos_319.variants.isTheta
statements.doc:
Let $c(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq\{1, \dots, N\}$ such that there is a function
$\delta : A \to \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
  \sum_{n\in A} \frac{\delta n}{n} = 0
$$
and
$$
  \sum_{n\in A'}\frac{\delta n}{n} \neq 0
$$
for all non-empty $A'\subsetneq A$. What is $\Theta(c(N))$?

Trivially $c(N) \leq N$, and `erdos_319.variants.lb` gives $c(N) \geq (1 - \frac{1}{e} + o(1))N$,
so $c(N) = \Theta(N)$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_319.variants.isTheta (N : ℕ) (c : ℕ → ℝ)
    (h : ∀ N, IsGreatest
    { (#A : ℝ) | (A) (_ : A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N)
      (_ : ∃ δ : ℕ → ℤˣ, ∑ n ∈ A, (δ n : ℚ) / n = 0 ∧
        ∀ A' ⊂ A, A'.Nonempty → ∑ n ∈ A', (δ n : ℚ) / n ≠ 0) } (c N)) :
    c =Θ[atTop] erdos_319.variants.isTheta.answer

statements.name: Erdos319.erdos_319.variants.lb
statements.doc:
Adenwalla has observed that a lower bound (on the maximum size of $A$) of
$$
  |A| \geq (1 - \frac{1}{e} + o(1))N
$$
follows from the main result of Croot [Cr01].

[Cr01] Croot, III, Ernest S., _On unit fractions with denominators in short intervals_.
Acta Arith. (2001), 99-114.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_319.variants.lb : ∃ (o : ℕ → ℝ), (o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)) ∧
    ∀ᶠ N in atTop, (1 - 1 / rexp 1 + o N) * N ≤ sSup { (#A : ℝ) | (A) (_ : A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N)
      (_ : ∃ δ : ℕ → ℤˣ, ∑ n ∈ A, (δ n : ℚ) / n = 0 ∧
        ∀ A' ⊂ A, A'.Nonempty → ∑ n ∈ A', (δ n : ℚ) / n ≠ 0) }

problems.title: Erdős Problem 321
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/321](https://www.erdosproblems.com/321)

statements.name: Erdos321.erdos_321
statements.doc:
Let $R(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq\{1, ..., N\}$ such that all sums
$\sum_{n\in S} \frac{1}{n}$ are distinct for $S\subseteq A$. What is $R(N)$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_321 (N : ℕ) :
    R N = erdos_321.answer

statements.name: Erdos321.erdos_321.variants.isTheta
statements.doc:
Let $R(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq\{1, ..., N\}$ such that all sums
$\sum_{n\in S} \frac{1}{n}$ are distinct for $S\subseteq A$. What is $\Theta(R(N))$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_321.variants.isTheta :
    (fun N ↦ (R N : ℝ)) =Θ[atTop] erdos_321.variants.isTheta.answer

statements.name: Erdos321.erdos_321.variants.isBigO
statements.doc: Let $R(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq\{1, ..., N\}$ such that all sums $\sum_{n\in S} \frac{1}{n}$ are distinct for $S\subseteq A$. Find the simplest $g(N)$ such that $R(N) = O(g(N))$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_321.variants.isBigO :
    (fun N ↦ (R N : ℝ)) =O[atTop] erdos_321.variants.isBigO.answer

statements.name: Erdos321.erdos_321.variants.isLittleO
statements.doc: Let $R(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq\{1, ..., N\}$ such that all sums $\sum_{n\in S} \frac{1}{n}$ are distinct for $S\subseteq A$. Find the simplest $g(N)$ such that $R(N) = o(g(N))$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_321.variants.isLittleO :
    (fun N ↦ (R N : ℝ)) =o[atTop] erdos_321.variants.isLittleO.answer

statements.name: Erdos321.erdos_321.variants.lower
statements.doc:
Let $R(N)$ be the maximal such size. Results of Bleicher and Erdős from [BlEr75] and [BlEr76b] imply that
$$
\frac{N}{\log N} \prod_{i=3}^{k} \log_i N \le R(N),
$$
valid for any $k \ge 4$ with $\log_k N \ge k$ and any $r \ge 1$ with $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$. (In these bounds $\log_i n$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.)

[BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erdős, P., _The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42.
[BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erdős, Paul, _Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II_. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_321.variants.lower (N k : ℕ) (hk : 4 ≤ k) (hkN : k ≤ log^[k] N) :
    N / log N * ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 3 k, (log^[i] N) ≤ R N

statements.name: Erdos321.erdos_321.variants.upper
statements.doc:
Let $R(N)$ be the maximal such size. Results of Bleicher and Erdős from [BlEr75] and [BlEr76b] imply that
$$
R(N) \le \frac{1}{\log 2} \log_r N \left( \frac{N}{\log N} \prod_{i=3}^{r} \log_i N \right),
$$
valid for any $k \ge 4$ with $\log_k N \ge k$ and any $r \ge 1$ with $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$. (In these bounds $\log_i n$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.)

Since `Real.log` is defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$, the condition $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$ is
formalised as $\log_i N \ge 1$ for all $i \le 2r$, which is equivalent to it for the
genuine iterated logarithm and ensures that every intermediate iterate is positive.

[BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erdős, P., _The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42.
[BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erdős, Paul, _Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II_. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_321.variants.upper (N r : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r) (hrN : ∀ i ≤ 2 * r, 1 ≤ log^[i] N) :
    R N ≤ 1 / log 2 * log^[r] N * N / log N * ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 3 r, (log^[i] N)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 322
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/322](https://www.erdosproblems.com/322)
- [Er36] Erdős, Paul, *On the Representation of an Integer as the Sum of k k-th Powers*. J. London
  Math. Soc. (1936), 133-136.
- [Er65b] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent advances and current problems in number theory*. Lectures on
  Modern Mathematics, Vol. III (1965), 196-244.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., *Unsolved problems in number theory*. (2004), xviii+437.
- [Ma36] Mahler, Kurt, *Note on Hypothesis K of Hardy and Littlewood*. J. London Math. Soc. (1936),
  136-138.

statements.name: Erdos322.erdos_322
statements.doc: Let $k\geq 3$ and $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be the set of $k$th powers. What is the order of growth of $1_A^{(k)}(n)$, i.e. the number of representations of $n$ as the sum of $k$ many $k$th powers? Does there exist some $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ such that $$1_A^{(k)}(n) >n^c?$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_322 :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k → ∃ c > (0 : ℝ),
      {n : ℕ | (n : ℝ) ^ c < representationCount k n}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 323
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/323](https://www.erdosproblems.com/323)

statements.name: Erdos323.erdos_323.parts.i
statements.doc:
Is it true that $f_{k,k}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{1-\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$?

This would have significant applications to Waring's problem. Erdős and Graham describe this as
'unattackable by the methods at our disposal'.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_323.parts.i :
    ∀ k ≥ 1, ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ),
      (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (x : ℝ) ^ (1 - ε)) =O[atTop] (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (f k k x : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos323.erdos_323.parts.ii
statements.doc: Is it true that if $m < k$ then $f_{k,m}(x) \gg x^{m/k}$ for sufficiently large $x$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_323.parts.ii :
    ∀ k m : ℕ, 1 ≤ m → m < k →
      (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (x : ℝ) ^ ((m : ℝ) / (k : ℝ))) =O[atTop] (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (f k m x : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos323.erdos_323.variants.k_eq_2
statements.doc:
The case $k=2$ was resolved by Landau, who showed $f_{2,2}(x) \sim \frac{cx}{\sqrt{\log x}}$ for
some constant $c>0$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_323.variants.k_eq_2 :
    ∃ c > 0, (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (f 2 2 x : ℝ)) ~[atTop]
      (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ c * (x : ℝ) / Real.sqrt (Real.log (x : ℝ)))

statements.name: Erdos323.erdos_323.variants.k_gt_2
statements.doc: For $k>2$ it is not known if $f_{k,k}(x)=o(x)$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_323.variants.k_gt_2 :
    ∀ k > 2, (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (f k k x : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun (x : ℕ) ↦ (x : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 324
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/324](https://www.erdosproblems.com/324)

statements.name: Erdos324.erdos_324
statements.doc:
Does there exist a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ such that all the sums $f(a)+f(b)$ with
$a < b$ nonnegative integers are distinct?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_324 :
    ∃ f : ℤ[X], {(a, b) : ℕ × ℕ | a < b}.InjOn fun (a, b) => f.eval (a : ℤ) + f.eval (b : ℤ)

statements.name: Erdos324.erdos_324.variants.quintic
statements.doc:
Probably $f(x) = x^5$ has the property that the sums $f(a)+f(b)$ with
$a < b$ nonnegative integers are distinct.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_324.variants.quintic : {(a, b) : ℕ × ℕ | a < b}.InjOn fun (a, b) => a ^ 5 + b ^ 5

problems.title: Erdős Problem 325
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/325](https://www.erdosproblems.com/325)

statements.name: Erdos325.erdos_325
statements.doc:
Writing $f_{k, 3}(x)$ for the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers,
is it true that $f_{k, 3}(x) \gg x ^ (3 / k)$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_325 :
     ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k → (fun x : ℕ => (x : ℝ) ^ (3 / k : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      (fun x : ℕ => (cardIsSumThreePowerBelow k x : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos325.erdos_325.variants.weaker
statements.doc:
Writing $f_{k, 3}(x)$ for the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers,
is it even true that $f_{k, 3}(x) \gg_{\epsilon} x ^ (3 / k - \epsilon)$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_325.variants.weaker :
    ∀ ε > 0, ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k → (fun x : ℕ => (x : ℝ) ^ ((3 / k : ℝ) - ε)) =O[atTop]
      (fun x => (cardIsSumThreePowerBelow k x : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos325.erdos_325.variants.wooley
statements.doc:
For $k = 3$, the best known is due to Wooley [Wo15], who proved
$f_{3, 3}(x) \gg x^{0.91709477}$.

[Wo15] Wooley, Trevor D., Sums of three cubes, II. Acta Arith. (2015), 73-100.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_325.variants.wooley :
    (fun x : ℕ => (x : ℝ) ^ (0.91709477 : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      (fun x => (cardIsSumThreePowerBelow 3 x : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 326
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/326](https://www.erdosproblems.com/326)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980), p. 47.
- [Ca57] Cassels, J. W. S., *Über Basen der natürlichen Zahlenreihe*.
  Abh. Math. Sem. Univ. Hamburg (1957), 247-257.

statements.name: Erdos326.erdos_326
statements.doc:
Does there exist $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots\} \subset \mathbb{N}$ which is a minimal basis of
order $2$ (i.e. every large integer is the sum of $2$ elements from $A$, and no proper subset of
$A$ has this property), such that
$$\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{a_k}{k^2} = c$$
for some $c \neq 0$?

Erdős and Graham conjectured a negative answer to this question [ErGr80].

"Minimal basis of order $2$" is formalised as `Minimal` for the predicate
`Set.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder · 2` on sets of naturals ordered by inclusion.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_326 : ∃ (a : ℕ → ℕ), StrictMono a ∧
    Minimal (fun A : Set ℕ ↦ A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2) (Set.range a) ∧
      ∃ (c : ℝ), c ≠ 0 ∧ Tendsto (fun n ↦ (a n : ℝ) / n ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 c)

statements.name: Erdos326.erdos_326.variants.eq
statements.doc:
Erdős originally asked this for any basis (not necessarily minimal); such a basis was constructed
by Cassels [Ca57].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_326.variants.eq :
    ∃ (a : ℕ → ℕ) (_ : StrictMono a) (_ : Set.range a |>.IsAddBasisOfOrder 2) (x : ℝ) (_ : 0 < x),
      Tendsto (fun n ↦ (a n : ℝ) / n ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 x)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 328
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/328](https://www.erdosproblems.com/328)
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul, *A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory*.
  Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
  number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
- [Er80e] Erdős, P., *Some applications of Ramsey's theorem to additive number theory*.
  European J. Combin. (1980), 43-46.
- [NeRo85] J. Nešetřil and V. Rödl, *Two proofs in combinatorial number theory*.
  Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1985), 185-188.

statements.name: Erdos328.erdos_328
statements.doc:
Suppose $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and $C>0$ is such that $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\leq C$ for all
$n\in\mathbb{N}$. Can $A$ be partitioned into $t$ many subsets $A_1,\ldots,A_t$ (where
$t=t(C)$ depends only on $C$) such that $1_{A_i}\ast 1_{A_i}(n)<C$ for all $1\leq i\leq t$
and $n\in \mathbb{N}$?

The answer is no. Asked by Erdős and Newman. Nešetřil and Rödl [NeRo85] have shown the
answer is no for all $C$ (even if $t$ is also allowed to depend on $A$).

Erdős [Er80e] had previously shown the answer is no for $C=3,4$ and infinitely many other
values of $C$.

See also [774].

The linked proof writes the representation function as
`Set.ncard {p : ℕ × ℕ | p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ A ∧ p.1 + p.2 = n}`, which counts the same ordered
pairs as `sumRep`, and states the partition condition as a named definition with the same two
conjuncts used below. Its `∃ t` additionally carries `1 ≤ t`, which costs nothing: `t = 0`
forces `A = ∅`, and `A = {1}` has all representation counts at most `C` for `C ≥ 1`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_328 :
    ¬ ∀ C : ℕ, 0 < C →
      ∃ t : ℕ, ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∀ n, sumRep A n ≤ C) →
        ∃ P : Fin t → Set ℕ, (⋃ i, P i) = A ∧
          Set.univ.PairwiseDisjoint P ∧
          ∀ i, ∀ n, sumRep (P i) n < C

problems.title: Erdős Problem 329: Maximum Density of Sidon Sets
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
- [AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
- [Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.

statements.name: Erdos329.erdos_329
statements.doc:
**Erdős Problem 329.**
Let `A ⊆ ℕ` be a Sidon set. How large can
`lim sup_{N → ∞} |A ∩ {1,…,N}| / N^{1/2}`
be?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_329 : sSup {sidonUpperDensity A | (A : Set ℕ) (_ : IsSidon A)} =
    erdos_329.answer

statements.name: Erdos329.erdos_329.variants.lower_bound
statements.doc:
Erdős proved that upper density `1 / 2` can be attained; in particular,
there exists a Sidon set whose upper density is *at least* `1 / 2`.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_329.variants.lower_bound : ∃ (A : Set ℕ), IsSidon A ∧ sidonUpperDensity A ≥ 1/2

statements.name: Erdos329.erdos_329.variants.kruckeberg_1961
statements.doc:
Krückeberg ([Kr61]) exhibited an infinite Sidon set `A` with
`sidonUpperDensity A = 1 / Real.sqrt 2`, improving Erdős’ earlier
`1 / 2` lower bound.

[Kr61] Krückeberg, Fritz, $B\sb{2}$-Folgen und verwandte Zahlenfolgen. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1961), 53-60.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_329.variants.kruckeberg_1961 : ∃ (A : Set ℕ), IsSidon A ∧
    sidonUpperDensity A = 1 / Real.sqrt 2

statements.name: Erdos329.erdos_329.variants.turan_1941
statements.doc:
Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved the upper bound of 1.

[ErTu41] Erdős, P. and Turán, P., On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems. J. London Math. Soc. (1941), 212-215.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_329.variants.turan_1941 : ∀ (A : Set ℕ), IsSidon A → sidonUpperDensity A ≤ 1

statements.name: Erdos329.erdos_329.variants.converse_implication
statements.doc:
The converse: if the maximum density is 1, then any finite Sidon set
can be embedded in a perfect difference set modulo $n > 0$.

Since the consequent is false (due to the counterexamples in [Ha47] and [AlMi25]),
this implication is logically equivalent to the statement that the maximum upper
density of Sidon sets is NOT 1.
Because the maximum upper density problem is still open, the truth value of this
implication is also an open research problem.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_329.variants.converse_implication :
    (sSup {sidonUpperDensity A | (A : Set ℕ) (_ : IsSidon A)} = 1) →
    (∀ (A : Finset ℕ), IsSidon (A : Set ℕ) → ∃ (D : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) (_ : n > 0),
      ↑A ⊆ D ∧ IsPerfectDifferenceSet D n)

statements.name: Erdos329.exists_sidon_pos_density
statements.doc: It is possible to construct a Sidon set with positive density.
statements.statement: theorem exists_sidon_pos_density : ∃ (A : Set ℕ), IsSidon A ∧ 0 < sidonUpperDensity A

problems.title: Erdős Problem 330
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/330](https://www.erdosproblems.com/330)

statements.name: Erdos330.erdos_330_statement
statements.doc:
Does there exist a minimal basis $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ with positive density
such that, for any $n \in A$, the (upper) density of integers which
cannot be represented without using $n$ is positive?

Neither set is asked to have a density, only to have positive upper density, so
`Set.upperDensity` is used for both rather than `Set.HasPosDensity`. As with many of Erdős'
questions "positive density" here most likely means positive upper density, and in [Er80] he
considers either the lower or the upper density for the integers not representable without a
fixed `n`. Requiring the density to exist would ask a strictly harder question than the one
posed. See #3979.

Such a set exists, so the answer is yes. The linked proof gives one of order `2`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_330_statement :
    ∃ (A : Set ℕ), ∃ h, MinAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder A h ∧
    0 < A.upperDensity ∧ ∀ n ∈ A, 0 < (UnrepWithout A n h).upperDensity

problems.title: Erdős Problem 331
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/331](https://www.erdosproblems.com/331)
- [ErFr84] Erdős, P. and Freud, R., On disjoint sets of differences. J. Number Theory (1984),
  99--109.

statements.name: Erdos331.erdos_331
statements.doc:
Let $A,B\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all large $N$$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg
N^{1/2}$$and$$\lvert B\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2}.$$
Is it true that there are infinitely many solutions to $a_1-a_2=b_1-b_2\neq 0$ with $a_1,a_2\in A$
and $b_1,b_2\in B$?

Ruzsa has observed that there is a simple counterexample: take $A$ to be the set of numbers whose
binary representation has only non-zero digits in even places, and $B$ similarly but with non-zero
digits only in odd places. It is easy to see $A$ and $B$ both grow like $\gg N^{1/2}$ and yet for
any $n\geq 1$ there is exactly one solution to $n=a+b$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$.

This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_331 :
    ¬ ∀ A B : Set ℕ,
    (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ)) =O[atTop] (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (count (· ∈ A) n : ℝ)) →
    (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ)) =O[atTop] (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (count (· ∈ B) n : ℝ)) →
    { s : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | let ⟨a₁, a₂, b₁, b₂⟩ := s
      a₁ ∈ A ∧ a₂ ∈ A ∧ b₁ ∈ B ∧ b₂ ∈ B ∧
      a₁ ≠ a₂ ∧ a₁ + b₂ = a₂ + b₁ }.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos331.erdos_331.variants.ruzsa
statements.doc:
Ruzsa suggests that a non-trivial variant of this problem arises if one imposes the stronger
condition that $|A \cap \{1,\dots,N\}| \sim c_A N^{1/2}$ for some constant $c_A>0$, and similarly
for $B$.

The answer is yes. Write $A(N) = |A \cap \{1,\dots,N\}|$ and $B(N) = |B \cap \{1,\dots,N\}|$.
Erdős and Freud [ErFr84, Theorem 4] proved that if $a_1 - a_2 = b_1 - b_2$ has only trivial
solutions and $\liminf_N \min(A(N), B(N)) / N^{1/2} > 0$, then neither $A(N) / N^{1/2}$ nor
$B(N) / N^{1/2}$ tends to a limit. If there were only finitely many non-trivial solutions, removing
the finitely many elements of $A$ that occur in them would give sets with the same asymptotics and
no non-trivial solution.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_331.variants.ruzsa :
    ∀ A B : Set ℕ,
    (∃ c_A > 0, (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (count (· ∈ A) n : ℝ)) ~[atTop] (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ c_A * (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ))) →
    (∃ c_B > 0, (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ (count (· ∈ B) n : ℝ)) ~[atTop] (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ c_B * (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ))) →
    { s : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | let ⟨a₁, a₂, b₁, b₂⟩ := s
      a₁ ∈ A ∧ a₂ ∈ A ∧ b₁ ∈ B ∧ b₂ ∈ B ∧
      a₁ ≠ a₂ ∧ a₁ + b₂ = a₂ + b₁ }.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 332
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/332](https://www.erdosproblems.com/332)

statements.name: Erdos332.erdos_332
statements.doc:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $D(A)$ be the set of those numbers which occur infinitely often as
$a_1 - a_2$ with $a_1, a_2\in A$. What conditions on $A$ are sufficient to ensure $D(A)$ has bounded
gaps?

The sufficient conditions are the unknown `erdos_332.answer`. In order to solve this problem one
has to provide what the sufficient conditions are, and proof that they imply the desired condition.
If the condition is a solution to the problem is up to human judgement.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_332 (A : Set ℕ) : erdos_332.answer A → HasBoundedGaps (D_A A)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 333
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/333](https://www.erdosproblems.com/333)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErNe77] Erdős, P. and Newman, D. J., *Bases for sets of integers*. J. Number Theory (1977),
  420-425.

statements.name: Erdos333.erdos_333
statements.doc:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of density zero. Does there exist a $B$ such that
$A\subseteq B+B$ and
$$\lvert B\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert =o(N^{1/2})$$
for all large $N$?

The answer is no. Erdős and Newman [ErNe77] have proved this is true when $A$ is the set of
squares. In fact, Theorem 2 of [ErNe77] already implies a negative answer to this problem, but
this seems to have been overlooked by Erdős and Graham.

See also [806].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_333 :
    ¬ ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.HasDensity 0 →
      ∃ B : Set ℕ, A ⊆ B + B ∧
        (fun N => ((B ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop]
          fun N => Real.sqrt N

problems.title: Erdős Problem 337
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/337](https://www.erdosproblems.com/337)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErGr80b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On bases with an exact order*. Acta Arith. (1980),
  201-207.
- [RT85] Ruzsa, I. Z. and Turjányi, S., *A note on additive bases of integers*. Publ. Math.
  Debrecen (1985), 101-104.
- [Tu84] Turjányi, S., *A note on basis sequences*. Topics in classical number theory, Vol. I, II
  (Budapest, 1981) (1984), 1571-1576.

statements.name: Erdos337.erdos_337
statements.doc:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an additive basis (of any finite order) such that
$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert=o(N)$. Is it true that
$$
\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{\lvert (A+A)\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}
{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}=\infty?
$$

The answer is no, and a counterexample was provided by Turjányi [Tu84]. This was generalised (to
the replacement of $A+A$ by the $h$-fold sumset $hA$ for any $h\geq 2$) by Ruzsa and Turjányi
[RT85].

"Additive basis" is `Set.IsAsymptoticAddBasis`: some finite $h$ has $hA$ containing every
sufficiently large integer. The exact notion `Set.IsAddBasis`, which asks that $hA$ be all of
$\mathbb{N}$, would force $0, 1 \in A$ and is not the class these results are about.

The linked file states the basis hypothesis as `∃ N₀, Set.Ici N₀ ⊆ iterated_sumset A k` and
indexes both counting functions by a real $x$ through $\lfloor x\rfloor$, where the counting
functions here are indexed by $N : \mathbb{N}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_337 :
    ¬ ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.IsAsymptoticAddBasis →
      (fun N : ℕ ↦ ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun N : ℕ ↦ (N : ℝ)) →
      Tendsto (fun N : ℕ ↦ (((A + A) ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ) / ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ))
        atTop atTop

statements.name: Erdos337.erdos_337.variants.h_fold
statements.doc:
This was generalised (to the replacement of $A+A$ by the $h$-fold sumset $hA$ for any $h\geq 2$)
by Ruzsa and Turjányi [RT85].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_337.variants.h_fold : ∀ h : ℕ, 2 ≤ h →
    ∃ A : Set ℕ, A.IsAsymptoticAddBasis ∧
      (fun N : ℕ ↦ ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun N : ℕ ↦ (N : ℝ)) ∧
      ¬ Tendsto (fun N : ℕ ↦
          ((h • A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ) / ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ))
        atTop atTop

statements.name: Erdos337.erdos_337.variants.ruzsa_turjanyi
statements.doc:
Ruzsa and Turjányi do prove (under the same hypotheses) that
$$
\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{\lvert (A+A+A)\cap \{1,\ldots,3N\}\rvert}
{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}=\infty,
$$
and conjecture that the same should be true with $(A+A)\cap \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ in the numerator.

This follows from the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality applied to $B=A\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}$: if $A$ is a
basis of order $h$ then $hB$ contains every element of $\{N_0,\ldots,N\}$, so
$(\lvert B+B\rvert/\lvert B\rvert)^h\geq \lvert hB\rvert/\lvert B\rvert\gg N/\lvert B\rvert$,
which tends to infinity since $\lvert B\rvert=o(N)$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_337.variants.ruzsa_turjanyi :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.IsAsymptoticAddBasis →
      (fun N : ℕ ↦ ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun N : ℕ ↦ (N : ℝ)) →
      Tendsto (fun N : ℕ ↦
          (((A + A) ∩ Icc 1 (2 * N)).ncard : ℝ) / ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ))
        atTop atTop

statements.name: Erdos337.erdos_337.variants.three_fold
statements.doc:
Ruzsa and Turjányi do prove (under the same hypotheses) that
$$
\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{\lvert (A+A+A)\cap \{1,\ldots,3N\}\rvert}
{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}=\infty.
$$

This is weaker than `Erdos337.erdos_337.variants.ruzsa_turjanyi`: translating by a fixed
$a\in A$ with $1\leq a\leq N$ embeds $(A+A)\cap\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ into
$(A+A+A)\cap\{1,\ldots,3N\}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_337.variants.three_fold :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.IsAsymptoticAddBasis →
      (fun N : ℕ ↦ ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun N : ℕ ↦ (N : ℝ)) →
      Tendsto (fun N : ℕ ↦
          (((A + A + A) ∩ Icc 1 (3 * N)).ncard : ℝ) / ((A ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ))
        atTop atTop

problems.title: Erdős Problem 338
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/338](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErGr80b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On bases with an exact order*. Acta Arith. (1980),
  201-207.
- [HHP07] Hegyvári, Norbert and Hennecart, François and Plagne, Alain, *Answer to a question by
  Burr and Erdős on restricted addition, and related results*. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2007),
  747--756.
- [He05] Hennecart, François, *On the restricted order of asymptotic bases of order two*.
  Ramanujan J. (2005), 123--130.
- [Ke57] Kelly, John B., *Restricted bases*. Amer. J. Math. (1957), 258-264.
- [Pa33] Pall, Gordon, *On Sums of Squares*. Amer. Math. Monthly (1933), 10-18.
- [Sc54] Schinzel, A., *Sur la décomposition des nombres naturels en sommes de nombres
  triangulaires distincts*. Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Cl. III. (1954), 409-410.

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338
statements.doc:
The restricted order of a basis $A$ is the least integer $t$ (if it exists) such that every large
integer is the sum of at most $t$ distinct summands from $A$. What are necessary and sufficient
conditions that this exists?

A solution must fill in `Erdos338.erdos_338.answer` with the condition and prove the
equivalence. Whether a condition is a satisfactory answer is up to human judgement.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338 :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∃ h, HasOrder A h) → ((∃ t, HasRestrictedOrder A t) ↔ erdos_338.answer A)

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.bounded_by_order
statements.doc:
Can the restricted order of a basis be bounded (when it exists) in terms of the order of the
basis?

`HasOrder A h` only says that the order of $A$ is at most $h$. This gives the same question,
since $f$ can be replaced by its running maximum. Kelly [Ke57] showed that $f(2) = 4$ works, and
Hennecart [He05] showed that $4$ is optimal. Hegyvári, Hennecart and Plagne [HHP07] showed that
any such $f$ has $f(k) \geq 2^{k-2}+k-1$ for $k \geq 3$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.bounded_by_order :
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, ∀ (A : Set ℕ) (h : ℕ), HasOrder A h →
      (∃ t, HasRestrictedOrder A t) → HasRestrictedOrder A (f h)

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.eq_order
statements.doc:
What are necessary and sufficient conditions that the restricted order of a basis $A$ is equal to
the order of $A$?

For a basis, `basisOrder A` is finite, so the equality also says that the restricted order exists.
The condition is `Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.eq_order.answer`, as in `Erdos338.erdos_338`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.eq_order :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∃ h, HasOrder A h) →
      (restrictedOrder A = basisOrder A ↔ erdos_338.variants.eq_order.answer A)

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.basis_after_finite_removal
statements.doc:
Is it true that if $A \setminus F$ is a basis for all finite sets $F$ then $A$ must have a
restricted order?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.basis_after_finite_removal :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∀ F : Set ℕ, F.Finite → ∃ h, HasOrder (A \ F) h) →
      ∃ t, HasRestrictedOrder A t

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.same_order_after_finite_removal
statements.doc:
Is it true that if the sets $A \setminus F$, for all finite sets $F$, are bases of the same order,
then $A$ must have a restricted order?

We read "the same order" literally: every $A \setminus F$ has the same exact order $h$. This is
equivalent to asking that the orders of the sets $A \setminus F$ are bounded. Removing elements can
only raise the order, so if the orders are bounded, their maximum is attained at some $F_0$, and
$A \setminus F_0 \subseteq A$ satisfies the literal hypothesis.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.same_order_after_finite_removal :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ,
      (∃ h : ℕ, ∀ F : Set ℕ, F.Finite → basisOrder (A \ F) = (h : ℕ∞)) →
      ∃ t, HasRestrictedOrder A t

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.bateman
statements.doc:
Bateman observed that for $h \geq 3$ the set $A = \{1\} \cup \{x > 0 : h \mid x\}$ is a basis of
order $h$ with no restricted order.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.bateman (h : ℕ) (hh : 3 ≤ h) :
    basisOrder (insert 1 {x : ℕ | 0 < x ∧ h ∣ x}) = h ∧
      ¬ ∃ t, HasRestrictedOrder (insert 1 {x : ℕ | 0 < x ∧ h ∣ x}) t

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.kelly
statements.doc: Kelly [Ke57] showed that any basis of order $2$ has restricted order at most $4$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_338.variants.kelly (A : Set ℕ) (hA : HasOrder A 2) : HasRestrictedOrder A 4

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.kelly_lowerDensity
statements.doc:
Kelly [Ke57] showed that any basis of order $2$ with positive lower density has restricted order
at most $3$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.kelly_lowerDensity (A : Set ℕ) (hA : HasOrder A 2)
    (hd : 0 < A.lowerDensity) : HasRestrictedOrder A 3

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.kelly_conjecture
statements.doc:
Kelly [Ke57] conjectured that any basis of order $2$ has restricted order at most $3$.

This was disproved by Hennecart [He05], who constructed a basis of order $2$ with restricted
order $4$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.kelly_conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ A : Set ℕ, HasOrder A 2 → HasRestrictedOrder A 3

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.squares
statements.doc:
The set of squares has order $4$ and restricted order $5$ (see [Pa33]).

Here $0$ is a square. The order is $4$ by Lagrange's four-square theorem, and is not $3$ because
no integer $\equiv 7 \pmod 8$ is a sum of three squares.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.squares :
    basisOrder (Set.range fun k : ℕ ↦ k ^ 2) = 4 ∧
      restrictedOrder (Set.range fun k : ℕ ↦ k ^ 2) = 5

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.triangular
statements.doc:
The set of triangular numbers has order $3$ and restricted order $3$ (see [Sc54]).

Here $0$ is a triangular number.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.triangular :
    basisOrder (Set.range fun k : ℕ ↦ k * (k + 1) / 2) = 3 ∧
      restrictedOrder (Set.range fun k : ℕ ↦ k * (k + 1) / 2) = 3

statements.name: Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.hegyvari_hennecart_plagne
statements.doc:
Hegyvári, Hennecart and Plagne [HHP07] showed that for all $k \geq 2$ there exists a basis of
order $k$ which has restricted order at least $2^{k-2}+k-1$.

The basis built in the proof of Theorem 4 of [HHP07] (for $k \geq 3$) has order exactly $k$ and a
finite restricted order, equal to $2^{k-2}+k-1$. The finiteness matters: without it, Bateman's
example `Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.bateman` would already give the bound. For $k = 2$ the bound
is $2$, and $A = \{1\} \cup \{x : 2 \mid x\}$ works.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_338.variants.hegyvari_hennecart_plagne :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → ∃ A : Set ℕ,
      basisOrder A = k ∧ restrictedOrder A = (2 ^ (k - 2) + k - 1 : ℕ)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 340
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/340](https://www.erdosproblems.com/340)

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340
statements.doc:
Let $A = \{1, 2, 4, 8, 13, 21, 31, 45, 66, 81, 97, \ldots\}$ be the greedy Sidon sequence:
we begin with $1$ and iteratively include the next smallest integer that preserves the
Sidon property (i.e. there are no non-trivial solutions to $a + b = c + d$). What is the
order of growth of $A$? Is it true that $|A \cap \{1, \ldots, N\}| \gg N^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$
for all $\varepsilon > 0$ and large $N$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340 (ε : ℝ) (hε : ε > 0) :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ √n / n ^ ε) =O[atTop]
      fun n : ℕ ↦ ((Set.range greedySidon ∩ Set.Icc 1 n).ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants.isTheta
statements.doc:
Let $A = \{1, 2, 4, 8, 13, 21, 31, 45, 66, 81, 97, \ldots\}$ be the greedy Sidon sequence:
we begin with $1$ and iteratively include the next smallest integer that preserves the
Sidon property (i.e. there are no non-trivial solutions to $a + b = c + d$). What is the
order of growth of $A$? Is it true that $|A \cap \{1, \ldots, N\}| \gg N^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$
for all $\varepsilon > 0$ and large $N$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants.isTheta (ε : ℝ) (hε : ε > 0) :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ ((Set.range greedySidon ∩ Set.Icc 1 n).ncard : ℝ)) =Θ[atTop]
      erdos_340.variants.isTheta.answer

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants.third
statements.doc: It is trivial that this sequence grows at least like $\gg N^{1/3}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants.third (ε : ℝ) (hε : ε > 0) :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 3)) =O[atTop]
      fun n : ℕ ↦ ((Set.range greedySidon ∩ Set.Icc 1 n).ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants.sub_hasPosDensity
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also asked about the difference set $A - A$ and whether this has
positive density.

[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants.sub_hasPosDensity :
    Set.HasPosDensity (Set.range greedySidon - Set.range greedySidon)

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants._22_mem_sub
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also asked about the difference set $A - A$ and whether this
contains $22$, which it does.

[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants._22_mem_sub :
    22 ∈ Set.range greedySidon - Set.range greedySidon

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants._33_mem_sub
statements.doc: The smallest integer which is unknown to be in $A - A$ is $33$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants._33_mem_sub :
    33 ∈ Set.range greedySidon - Set.range greedySidon

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants.cofinite_sub
statements.doc: It may be true that all or almost all integers are in $A - A$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants.cofinite_sub :
    ∀ᶠ n in cofinite, n ∈ Set.range greedySidon - Set.range greedySidon

statements.name: Erdos340.erdos_340.variants.co_density_zero_sub
statements.doc: It may be true that all or almost all integers are in $A - A$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_340.variants.co_density_zero_sub :
    ∃ S : Set ℕ, S.HasDensity 0 ∧ ∀ n ∈ Sᶜ, n ∈ Set.range greedySidon - Set.range greedySidon

problems.title: Erdős Problem 341
problems.doc:
*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/341](https://www.erdosproblems.com/341)
* [Ben Green's Open Problem 7](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.1)
* [Li26] Li, Z., *Counterexamples to Erdős Problem 341* (2026),
  https://github.com/LiAlreadyExists/Erdos-341/blob/main/paper/Erdos341.pdf

statements.name: Erdos341.erdos_341
statements.doc:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ be a finite set of integers and extend it to an infinite
sequence $\overline{A}=\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ by defining $a_{n+1}$ for $n \geq k$ to be
the least integer exceeding $a_n$ which is not of the form $a_i + a_j$ with $i,j \leq n$.
Is it true that the sequence of differences $a_{m+1}-a_m$ is eventually periodic?

This problem is discussed under Problem 7 on Green's open problems list.

The answer is no: Li [Li26] (with GPT-5.6 Sol) showed that the greedy extension of the seed set
$A = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 22, 27, 28, 32, 36, 40, 47, 48, 52, 63, 71, 77, 81, 89, 97\}$ has a
sequence of differences that is not eventually periodic. The linked formal proof
exhibits such a sequence `a : ℕ → ℕ` (strictly increasing, with the greedy rule holding from
some index on, and with `n ↦ a (n + 1) - a n` not eventually periodic); casting it to `ℤ`
gives a counterexample to the statement below.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_341 :
    ¬ ∀ (a : ℕ → ℤ),
      (∀ᶠ n in atTop,
        IsLeast { x | a n < x ∧ x ∉ { a i + a j | (i ≤ n) (j ≤ n) } } (a (n + 1))) →
      let d := fun i ↦ a (i + 1) - a i
      ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ m in atTop, d (m + p) = d m

problems.title: Erdős Problem 342
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/342](https://www.erdosproblems.com/342)
- [Ben Green's Open Problem 7](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.7)
- [OEIS A002858](https://oeis.org/A002858)
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., *Unsolved problems in number theory* (2004), xviii+437.

statements.name: Erdos342.erdos_342.parts.i
statements.doc: Do infinitely many pairs $(a, a+2)$ occur in Ulam's sequence?

statements.name: Erdos342.erdos_342.parts.ii
statements.doc: Does Ulam's sequence eventually have periodic differences? That is, is $a(n+1) - a(n)$ eventually periodic?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_342.parts.ii :
    ∀ a : ℕ → ℕ, IsUlamSequence a →
      let d (n : ℕ) : ℤ := a (n + 1) - a n
      ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ m in atTop, d (m + p) = d m

statements.name: Erdos342.erdos_342.parts.iii
statements.doc: Part (iii), is the density of the sequence 0?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_342.parts.iii :
    ∀ a : ℕ → ℕ, IsUlamSequence a →
      Set.upperDensity (Set.range a) = 0

problems.title: Erdős Problem 344
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/344](https://www.erdosproblems.com/344)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er61b] Erdős, P., *On the representation of large integers as sums of distinct summands
  taken from a fixed set*. Acta Arith. (1961/62), 345-354.
- [Fo66] Folkman, J., *On the representation of integers as sums of distinct terms from a
  fixed sequence*. Canadian J. Math. 18 (1966), 643-655.
- [SzVu06] Szemerédi, E. and Vu, V., *Long arithmetic progressions in sumsets: thresholds and
  bounds*. J. Amer. Math. Soc. 19 (2006), 119-169.
- [SzVu06b] Szemerédi, E. and Vu, V., *Finite and infinite arithmetic progressions in sumsets*.
  Ann. of Math. 163 (2006), 1-35.

statements.name: Erdos344.erdos_344
statements.doc:
If $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a set of integers such that
$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\gg N^{1/2}$$
for all $N$ then must $A$ be subcomplete? That is, must
$$P(A) = \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A\textrm{ finite }\right\}$$
contain an infinite arithmetic progression?

This is true, and was proved by Szemerédi and Vu [SzVu06].

The implied constant is absolute, as in [SzVu06b, Corollary 1.4].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_344 :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ A : Set ℕ,
      (∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, C * Real.sqrt N ≤ A.countUpTo N) → IsSubcomplete A

statements.name: Erdos344.erdos_344.variants.sqrt_two
statements.doc:
The stronger conjecture that this is true under
$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\geq (2N)^{1/2}$$
seems to be still open (this would be best possible as shown by [Er61b]).

The bound is required for all sufficiently large $N$: at $N=1$, it is impossible since
$\lvert A\cap\{1\}\rvert\leq 1<\sqrt{2}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_344.variants.sqrt_two :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, Real.sqrt (2 * N) ≤ A.countUpTo N) →
      IsSubcomplete A

statements.name: Erdos344.erdos_344.variants.folkman
statements.doc:
Folkman proved this under the stronger assumption that
$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\gg N^{1/2+\epsilon}$$
for some $\epsilon>0$ [Fo66].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_344.variants.folkman :
    ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ c : ℝ, 0 < c → ∀ A : Set ℕ,
      (∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop, c * (N : ℝ) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 2 + ε) ≤ A.countUpTo N) →
      IsSubcomplete A

problems.title: Erdős Problem 345
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/345](https://www.erdosproblems.com/345)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980), p. 55.
- [Ki17] Kim, D., *On the largest integer that is not a sum of distinct positive nth powers*.
  Journal of Integer Sequences 20 (2017), Article 17.7.5.
  [arXiv:1610.02439](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02439)

statements.name: Erdos345.erdos_345
statements.doc:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a complete sequence, and define the threshold of completeness
$T(A)$ to be the least integer $m$ such that all $n\geq m$ are in
$$P(A) = \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A\textrm{ finite }\right\}$$
(the existence of $T(A)$ is guaranteed by completeness).

Is it true that there are infinitely many $k$ such that $T(n^k)>T(n^{k+1})$?

Here $T(n^k)$ means the threshold of the positive $k$-th powers. Least-threshold witnesses
ensure that the thresholds exist. We restrict to $k\geq 1$, since the zeroth powers form
$\{1\}$, which is incomplete. Positive powers are complete [Ki17].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_345 :
    {k : ℕ | 0 < k ∧ ∃ a b : ℕ, IsLeast (thresholds (kthPowers k)) a ∧
      IsLeast (thresholds (kthPowers (k + 1))) b ∧ b < a}.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos345.kthPowers_isAddComplete
statements.doc: Every set of positive $k$-th powers with $k\geq 1$ is complete [Ki17].
statements.statement: theorem kthPowers_isAddComplete : ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → IsAddComplete (kthPowers k)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 346
problems.doc:
*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346)
 - [Gr64d] Graham, R. L., A property of Fibonacci numbers. Fibonacci Quart. (1964), 1-10.
 - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
    theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
 -

statements.name: Erdos346.erdos_346
statements.doc:
Is it true that for every lacunary, strongly complete sequence `A` that is not complete whenever
infinitely many terms are removed from it, `lim A (n + 1) / A n = (1 + √5) / 2`?

The answer is no. A counterexample recorded at [erdosproblems.com/346] has all successive ratios
at least `6 / 5`, but has subsequences of successive ratios tending to two different limits,
`(1 + √5) / 2` and `(1 + √5) / 2 + 1 / 4`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_346 : ¬ ∀ {A : ℕ → ℕ}, IsLacunary A → IsAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq A →
    (∀ B : Set ℕ, B ⊆ range A → B.Infinite → ¬ IsAddComplete (range A \ B)) →
    Tendsto (fun n => A (n + 1) / (A n : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 ((1 + √5) / 2))

statements.name: Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.f_isAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq
statements.doc: The sequence `f` is strongly complete, and this is proved in [Gr64d].
statements.statement: theorem erdos_346.variants.f_isAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq : IsAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq f

statements.name: Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.f_not_isAddComplete
statements.doc:
The sequence `f` is not complete whenever infinitely many terms are removed from it, and this
is proved in [Gr64d].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_346.variants.f_not_isAddComplete {B : Set ℕ} (h : B ⊆ range f) (hB : B.Infinite) :
    ¬ IsAddComplete (range f \ B)

statements.name: Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.gt_goldenRatio_not_IsAddComplete
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] remark that it is easy to see that if `A (n + 1) / A n > (1 + √5) / 2`
then the second property is automatically satisfied.

statements.name: Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.example
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also say that it is not hard to construct very irregular sequences
satisfying the aforementioned properties: there is a strictly increasing sequence `A` that is
strongly complete and not complete whenever infinitely many terms are removed from it, but with
$\liminf_n A(n+1)/A(n) = 1$ and $\limsup_n A(n+1)/A(n) = \infty$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_346.variants.example : ∃ A : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono A ∧ IsAddStronglyCompleteNatSeq A ∧
    (∀ B : Set ℕ, B ⊆ range A → B.Infinite → ¬ IsAddComplete (range A \ B)) ∧
    liminf (fun n => A (n + 1) / (A n : ℝ)) atTop = 1 ∧
    limsup (fun n => A (n + 1) / (A n : ENNReal)) atTop = ⊤

problems.title: Erdős Problem 347
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/347](https://www.erdosproblems.com/347)

statements.name: Erdos347.erdos_347
statements.doc:
Is there a sequence $A=\{a_1\leq a_2\leq \cdots\}$ of integers with
$$\lim \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=2$$
such that
$$P(A')= \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A'\textrm{ finite }\right\}$$
has density $1$ for every cofinite subsequence $A'$ of $A$?

This has been solved in the affirmative by ebarschkis in the comments (based on idea of Tao and
van Doorn, also in the comments).

This was formalized in Lean by Barschkis using Aristotle.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_347 :
    ∃ a : ℕ → ℕ, (Monotone a) ∧
      (Tendsto (fun n ↦ (a (n + 1) : ℝ) / (a n : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 2)) ∧
      (∀ ι : ℕ → ℕ, (range ι)ᶜ.Finite → HasDensity (𝓟 (range (a ∘ ι))) 1)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 348
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/348](https://www.erdosproblems.com/348)
- [Ge26] Geneson, J., *Deletion thresholds and exponential examples for complete sequences*.
  [arXiv:2609.25107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25107) (2026).

statements.name: Erdos348.erdos_348
statements.doc:
For what values of $0 \leq m < n$ is there a complete sequence
$A = \{a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots\}$ of integers such that
 1. $A$ remains complete after removing any $m$ elements, but
 2. $A$ is not complete after removing any $n$ elements.

Geneson [Ge26, Theorem 1] proved that the pairs are exactly those with $m \leq 1$.
Completeness allows finitely many exceptions, and deletions remove indexed occurrences.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_348 :
    { (m, n) | (m) (n) (_ : m < n) (a : ℕ → ℕ) (_ : Monotone a)
      (_ : ∀ s, s.card = m → IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (Function.updateFinset a s 0))
        (_ : ∀ t, t.card = n → ¬IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (Function.updateFinset a t 0)) } =
    erdos_348.answer

problems.title: Erdős Problem 349
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)

statements.name: Erdos349.erdos_349
statements.doc:
For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete
(that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_349 :
    {(t, α) | 0 < t ∧ 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α} = erdos_349.answer

statements.name: Erdos349.complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio
statements.doc:
It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all
for all $t>0$ and all $1 < \alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
statements.statement:
theorem complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t)
    (hα : α ∈ Set.Ioo 1 ((1 + √5) / 2)) : IsGoodPair t α

statements.name: Erdos349.exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segments
statements.doc:
For any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha > 0$
such that the sequence $\lfloor t_k\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete consists of at least $k$
disjoint line segments, that is, it has at least $k$ connected components.
statements.statement:
theorem exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segments (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ t ∈ Ioo 0 1,
      let S := {α | 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α}
      k ≤ (connectedComponentIn S '' S).encard

statements.name: Erdos349.erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_odd
statements.doc:
Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are odd infinitely
often and even infinitely often?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_odd :
    {n | Odd ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos349.erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_even
statements.doc: Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are even infinitely often?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_even :
    {n | Even ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos349.alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair
statements.doc:
For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively
complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős
Problem 349: it complements `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio`.

The proof is recorded via the `formal_proof` mechanism rather than written inline, as it exceeds
the repository's proof-length guideline.
statements.statement: theorem alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t) (hα : 2 < α) : ¬ IsGoodPair t α

statements.name: Erdos349.alpha_le_one_not_isGoodPair
statements.doc:
For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: every term
$\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ lies in the finite interval $[0, \lfloor t\rfloor]$ (since
$\alpha^n \le 1$), so every subset sum is bounded by the constant $\sum_{i \in [0,\lfloor t\rfloor]} i$,
and no large integer can be a subset sum. A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349,
complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases.
statements.statement:
theorem alpha_le_one_not_isGoodPair (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t) (hα0 : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1) :
    ¬ IsGoodPair t α

statements.name: Erdos349.exists_finsetSum_two_pow
statements.doc:
**Binary expansion.** Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is
a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction:
subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder. A textbook-level building
block for `one_two_isGoodPair` below; it says nothing about `IsGoodPair` itself.
statements.statement:
theorem exists_finsetSum_two_pow (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ E : Finset ℕ, k = ∑ i ∈ E, 2 ^ i

statements.name: Erdos349.one_two_isGoodPair
statements.doc:
**The pair $(1, 2)$ is good.** The powers of two $\lfloor 1\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^n$ form an
additively complete set: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum of distinct powers of two.
statements.statement: theorem one_two_isGoodPair : IsGoodPair 1 2

statements.name: Erdos349.dyadic_two_isGoodPair
statements.doc:
**The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$.** For every $k$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the
sequence $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ is additively complete because at index $n = m + k$ it equals
the exact power $2^m$, so its range contains all powers of two, which already form an additively
complete set. Uses monotonicity `IsAddComplete.mono`.
statements.statement: theorem dyadic_two_isGoodPair (k : ℕ) : IsGoodPair (1 / 2 ^ k) 2

statements.name: Erdos349.int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair
statements.doc:
**Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness.** For every integer base
$\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor =
t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every subset sum is too, but two consecutive large integers
cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial result
on Erdős Problem 349.
statements.statement:
theorem int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair (t : ℤ) (ht : 2 ≤ t) (α : ℤ) :
    ¬ IsGoodPair (t : ℝ) (α : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos349.integer_isGoodPair_iff
statements.doc:
**Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs.** For integers
$t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is
additively complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 2)$. Assembles the four partial results: $(1,2)$ is
good, $\alpha \le 1$ fails, $2 < \alpha$ fails (`alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair`), and integer
$t \ge 2$ fails.
statements.statement:
theorem integer_isGoodPair_iff (t α : ℤ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) (hα : 1 ≤ α) :
    IsGoodPair (t : ℝ) (α : ℝ) ↔ t = 1 ∧ α = 2

statements.name: Erdos349.three_halves_two_not_isGoodPair
statements.doc:
**The pair $(3/2, 2)$ is NOT good.** The negative companion of `dyadic_two_isGoodPair`:
while every dyadic coefficient $1/2^k$ gives a good pair at $\alpha = 2$, the non-dyadic rational
$t = 3/2$ does not. The sequence $\lfloor (3/2)\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, \ldots$ is not
additively complete because every term but the first $\lfloor 3/2\rfloor = 1$ is a multiple of
$3$ (namely $\lfloor (3/2)\cdot 2^{n+1}\rfloor = 3\cdot 2^n$), so every subset sum is
$\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 3$; the infinitely many integers $\equiv 2 \pmod 3$ are never reached.
A partial result on Erdős Problem 349 in the same divisibility family as
`int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair` (here the modulus is $3$).
statements.statement: theorem three_halves_two_not_isGoodPair : ¬ IsGoodPair (3 / 2) 2

problems.title: Erdős Problem 350
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/350](https://www.erdosproblems.com/350)
