problems.title: Erdős Problem 358
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
- [Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)

statements.name: Erdos358.f_id
statements.doc: When $A_n = n$, the function $f$ defined above counts the number of odd divisors of $n$.
statements.statement: theorem f_id : f id = fun n ↦ #{d ∈ n.divisors | Odd d}

statements.name: Erdos358.erdos_358.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of
solutions to $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.$$
Is there such an $A$ for which $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$?

Tao [Ta26] constructed such a sequence with $f(n) \gg \log n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_358.parts.i :
    ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ atTop.Tendsto (f A) atTop

statements.name: Erdos358.erdos_358.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of
solutions to $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.$$
Is there an $A$ such that $f(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$?

This also follows from Tao's construction with $f(n) \gg \log n$ [Ta26].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_358.parts.ii :
    ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ ∀ᶠ n in atTop, 2 ≤ f A n

statements.name: Erdos358.erdos_358.variants.prime_set
statements.doc:
When $A =\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ corresponds to the set of primes, it is conjectured that the
$\limsup$ of the number of representations $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$$ is infinite.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_358.variants.prime_set :
    atTop.limsup (fun n ↦ (f (Nat.nth Nat.Prime) n : ℕ∞)) = ⊤

statements.name: Erdos358.erdos_358.variants.prime_set_density_representation
statements.doc:
When $A =\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ corresponds to the set of primes, it is conjectured that the set of
numbers $n$ that have representations $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$$ has positive upper density.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_358.variants.prime_set_density_representation :
    0 < {n : ℕ | intervalRepresentations (Nat.nth Nat.Prime) n |>.Nonempty}.upperDensity

statements.name: Erdos358.erdos_358.variants.one_le
statements.doc:
In [ErGr80] Erdős and Graham further asked whether there is an $A$ with $f(n)\geq 1$ for all
large $n$. Egami observed that this holds trivially for $a_n=n$, so they may have intended to
count only those representations $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$$ that use at least two consecutive
terms, which is what $g$ counts.

This follows from Tao's construction [Ta26], which gives $f(n)\gg\log n$: see
`erdos_358.parts.ii` and `one_le_g_of_two_le_f`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_358.variants.one_le :
    ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ ∀ᶠ n in atTop, 1 ≤ g A n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 359
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/359](https://www.erdosproblems.com/359)

statements.name: Erdos359.erdos_359.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $a_1< a_2 < ⋯ $ be an infinite sequence of integers such that $a_1=1$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the
least integer which is not a sum of consecutive earlier $a_j$s. Show that $a_k / k \to \infty$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_359.parts.i (A : ℕ → ℕ) (hA : IsGoodFor A 1) :
    atTop.Tendsto (fun k ↦ (A k : ℝ) / k) atTop

statements.name: Erdos359.erdos_359.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $a_1< a_2 < ⋯ $ be an infinite sequence of integers such that $a_1=1$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the
least integer which is not a sum of consecutive earlier $a_j$s. Show that $a_k / k ^ {1 + c} \to 0$
for any $c > 0$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_359.parts.ii (A : ℕ → ℕ) (hA : IsGoodFor A 1) (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 < c):
    atTop.Tendsto (fun k ↦ A k / (k : ℝ) ^ (1 + c)) (nhds 0)

statements.name: Erdos359.erdos_359.variants.isGoodFor_1_asymptotic
statements.doc:
Suppose monotone sequence $A$ satisfies the following: `A 0 = 1` and for all `j`, `A (j + 1)` is the
smallest natural number that cannot be written as a sum of consecutive terms of `A 0, ..., A j`.
Then it is conjectured that $$a_k ~ \frac{k \log k}{\log \log k}$$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_359.variants.isGoodFor_1_asymptotic (A : ℕ → ℕ) (hA : IsGoodFor A 1) :
    (fun k ↦ (A k : ℝ)) ~[atTop] (fun k ↦ k * (k : ℝ).log / (k : ℝ).log.log)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 360
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/360](https://www.erdosproblems.com/360)
- [AlEr96] Alon, Noga and Erdős, Paul, *Sure monochromatic subset sums*. Acta Arith. 74 (1996),
  269-272.
- [CFP21] Conlon, D. and Fox, J. and Pham, H. T., *Subset sums, completeness and colorings*.
  [arXiv:2104.14766](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14766) (2021).
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
- [Vu07] Vu, Van H., *Some new results on subset sums*. J. Number Theory 124 (2007), 229-233.

statements.name: Erdos360.erdos_360
statements.doc:
Let $f(n)$ be minimal such that $\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ can be partitioned into $f(n)$ classes so that
$n$ cannot be expressed as a sum of distinct elements from the same class. How fast does $f(n)$
grow?

A problem of Erdős and Graham [ErGr80]. Conlon, Fox, and Pham [CFP21, Theorem 1.5] determined
the order of growth of $f(n)$ up to a multiplicative constant, proving
$$f(n) \asymp \frac{n^{1/3}(n/\phi(n))}{(\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}}.$$
Here $\phi$ is Euler's totient function, and the statement is asymptotic ($n \to \infty$).
statements.statement: theorem erdos_360 : (fun n : ℕ ↦ (f n : ℝ)) =Θ[atTop] erdos_360.answer

statements.name: Erdos360.erdos_360.variants.alon_erdos
statements.doc:
Alon and Erdős [AlEr96] proved that $f(n) = n^{1/3+o(1)}$, and more precisely
$$\frac{n^{1/3}}{(\log n)^{4/3}}\ll f(n) \ll
  \frac{n^{1/3}}{(\log n)^{1/3}}(\log\log n)^{1/3}.$$
This is the two-sided bound, which implies the first claim.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_360.variants.alon_erdos :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 3 : ℝ) / Real.log n ^ (4 / 3 : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
        (fun n : ℕ ↦ (f n : ℝ)) ∧
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ (f n : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
        (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 3 : ℝ) / Real.log n ^ (1 / 3 : ℝ) *
          Real.log (Real.log n) ^ (1 / 3 : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos360.erdos_360.variants.vu
statements.doc:
Vu [Vu07] improved the lower bound to
$$f(n) \gg \frac{n^{1/3}}{\log n}.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_360.variants.vu :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 3 : ℝ) / Real.log n) =O[atTop] (fun n : ℕ ↦ (f n : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 361
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/361](https://www.erdosproblems.com/361)

statements.name: Erdos361.erdos_361
statements.doc:
Let $c > 0$ and $n$ be some large integer. What is the size of the largest set
$A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, \lfloor c n \rfloor\}$ such that $n$ is not a sum of a subset of $A$?
Does this depend on $n$ in an irregular way?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_361 (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 < c) :
    subsetSumAvoidanceNumber c = erdos_361.answer

problems.title: Erdős Problem 362
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/362](https://www.erdosproblems.com/362)
- [Er65] Erdős, P., *Extremal problems in number theory*. Proc. Sympos. Pure Math., Vol. VIII
  (1965), 181-189.
- [Er73] Erdős, P., *Problems and results on combinatorial number theory*. A survey of
  combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971)
  (1973), 117-138.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [SaSz65] Sárközi, A. and Szemerédi, E., *Über ein Problem von Erdős und Moser*. Acta Arith.
  (1965), 205-208.
- [St80] Stanley, Richard P., *Weyl groups, the hard Lefschetz theorem, and the Sperner property*.
  SIAM J. Algebraic Discrete Methods (1980), 168-184.
- [Ha77] Halász, G., *Estimates for the concentration function of combinatorial number theory and
  probability*. Period. Math. Hungar. (1977), 197-211.

statements.name: Erdos362.erdos_362
statements.doc:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a finite set of size $N$. Is it true that, for any fixed $t$,
there are
$$\ll \frac{2^N}{N^{3/2}}$$
many $S\subseteq A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}n=t$?

Erdős and Moser [Er65] proved the first bound with an additional factor of $(\log n)^{3/2}$.
This was removed by Sárközy and Szemerédi [SaSz65], thereby answering the first question in the
affirmative. Stanley [St80] has shown that this quantity is maximised when
$A=\{-\lfloor \frac{N-1}{2}\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor\frac{N}{2}\rfloor\}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_362 : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ (A : Finset ℕ) (t : ℕ), A.Nonempty →
    ({S ∈ A.powerset | ∑ n ∈ S, n = t}.card : ℝ) ≤ C * 2 ^ A.card / (A.card : ℝ) ^ (3 / 2 : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos362.erdos_362.variants.fixed_card
statements.doc:
If we further ask that $\lvert S\rvert=l$ (for any fixed $l$) then is the number of solutions
$$\ll \frac{2^N}{N^2},$$
with the implied constant independent of $l$ and $t$?

The second question was answered in the affirmative by Halász [Ha77], as a consequence of a more
general multi-dimensional result.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_362.variants.fixed_card : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ (A : Finset ℕ) (l t : ℕ),
    A.Nonempty →
      ({S ∈ A.powersetCard l | ∑ n ∈ S, n = t}.card : ℝ) ≤ C * 2 ^ A.card / (A.card : ℝ) ^ 2

problems.title: Erdős Problem 363
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/363](https://www.erdosproblems.com/363)
- [BaBe07] Bauer, Mark and Bennett, Michael A., *On a question of Erd\H{o}s
  and Graham*. Enseign. Math. (2) (2007), 259--264.
- [BeVL12] Bennett, Michael A. and Van Luijk, Ronald, *Squares from blocks of
  consecutive integers: a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham*. Indag. Math. (N.S.)
  (2012), 123--127.
- [Ul05] Ulas, Maciej, *On products of disjoint blocks of consecutive integers*.
  Enseign. Math. (2) (2005), 331--334.

statements.name: Erdos363.erdos_363
statements.doc:
Is it true that, for each fixed $n$ and fixed sizes $k_1,\ldots,k_n \geq 4$, there are only finitely
many collections of disjoint intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ of size $\lvert I_i\rvert = k_i$ for
$1\leq i\leq n$ such that$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}\prod_{m\in I_i}m$$is a square?

The number of intervals and their sizes are fixed: the list `ks` of sizes determines both. Without
this restriction finiteness fails, by a result of Skałba (see [Ul05]).

This is false: Ulas [Ul05] constructed infinitely many such collections with $n = 4$ and
$k_1 = \cdots = k_4 = 4$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_363 : ¬ ∀ ks : List ℕ,
    {S : List (Finset ℕ) | IsValidCollection S ∧ S.map Finset.card = ks}.Finite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 364
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/364](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364)

statements.name: Erdos364.erdos_364
statements.doc: There is no consecutive triple of powerful numbers.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_364 :
    ¬ ∃ (n : ℕ), Powerful n ∧ Powerful (n + 1) ∧ Powerful (n + 2)

statements.name: Erdos364.erdos_364.variants.strong
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er76d] conjectured a stronger statement: if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number,
then $n_{k+2} - n_k > n_k^c$ for some constant $c > 0$.

[Er76d] Erdős, P., Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics (Univ. Manitoba, Winnipeg, Man., 1975) (1976), 25-44.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_364.variants.strong :
    ∃ (c : ℝ) (h : c > 0), ∀ (k : ℕ),
    Nat.nth Powerful (k + 2) - Nat.nth Powerful k > (Nat.nth Powerful k : ℝ) ^ c

statements.name: Erdos364.erdos_364.variants.weak
statements.doc:
There is no quadruple of powerful numbers, since at least one of the four numbers must be
$2 \pmod{4}$, which cannot be powerful (since $2$ divides it, but $2^2$ does not).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_364.variants.weak :
    ¬ ∃ (n : ℕ), Powerful n ∧ Powerful (n + 1) ∧ Powerful (n + 2) ∧ Powerful (n + 3)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 365
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/365](https://www.erdosproblems.com/365)
- [Go70] Golomb, S. W., *Powerful numbers*. Amer. Math. Monthly (1970), 848-855.
- [Gu04] Guy, R. K., *Unsolved problems in number theory* (2004), Problem B16.
- [Wa76] Walker, D. T., *Consecutive integer pairs of powerful numbers and related
  Diophantine equations*. Fibonacci Quart. (1976), 111-116.

statements.name: Erdos365.erdos_365.parts.i
statements.doc:
Do all pairs of consecutive powerful numbers $n$ and $n+1$ come from solutions to Pell
equations? In other words, must either $n$ or $n+1$ be a square?

The answer to the first question is no: Golomb [Go70] observed that both $12167=23^3$ and
$12168=2^3 3^2 13^2$ are powerful.

We require $n>0$ since `Nat.Powerful` also includes $0$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_365.parts.i :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → Nat.Powerful n → Nat.Powerful (n + 1) →
      IsSquare n ∨ IsSquare (n + 1)

statements.name: Erdos365.erdos_365.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Is the number of positive $n\leq x$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful bounded
by $(\log x)^{O(1)}$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_365.parts.ii :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∃ k : ℕ, ∀ᶠ x : ℕ in Filter.atTop,
      ({n : ℕ | 0 < n ∧ n ≤ x ∧ Nat.Powerful n ∧ Nat.Powerful (n + 1)}.ncard : ℝ) ≤
        C * (Real.log x) ^ k

problems.title: Erdős Problem 366
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)

statements.name: Erdos366.erdos_366
statements.doc: Are there any $2$-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is $3$-full?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_366 : ∃ n > 0, (2).Full n ∧ (3).Full (n + 1)

statements.name: Erdos366.erdos_366.variants.three_two
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham asked whether $(8, 9)$ is the only pair of consecutive integers $n$, $n+1$
with $n$ $3$-full and $n+1$ $2$-full. The answer is no: $12167 = 23^3$ and
$12168 = 2^3 3^2 13^2$ is another such pair, already known to Golomb [Go70].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_366.variants.three_two :
    ¬ ∀ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n + 1) → n = 8

statements.name: Erdos366.erdos_366.variants.weaker
statements.doc: Are there any consecutive pairs of $3$-full integers?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_366.variants.weaker :
    ∃ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (3).Full (n + 1)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 367
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)
- [ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory*, L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).

statements.name: Erdos367.erdos_367.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $B_2(n)$ be the $2$-full part of $n$ (that is, $B_2(n)=n/n'$ where $n'$ is the product of all
primes that divide $n$ exactly once). Is it true that, for every fixed $k \geq 1$,
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_2(m) \ll n^{2+o(1)}$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_367.parts.i : ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k →
    ∃ e : ℕ → ℝ,
      e =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ) ∧
      ∀ᶠ n in atTop,
        ((∏ m ∈ .Ico n (n + k), B 2 m : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) ^ (2 + e n)

statements.name: Erdos367.erdos_367.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Or perhaps even $\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_2(m) \ll_k n^2$?

van Doorn notes in the comments that this fails for all $k \geq 3$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_367.parts.ii : ¬ ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k →
    (fun n ↦ ((∏ m ∈ .Ico n (n + k), B 2 m : ℕ) : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      fun n ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (2 : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos367.erdos_367.variants.k_le_two
statements.doc:
van Doorn notes in the comments that for $k \leq 2$ we trivially have
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_2(m) \ll n^2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_367.variants.k_le_two : ∀ k : ℕ, k ≤ 2 →
    (fun n ↦ ((∏ m ∈ .Ico n (n + k), B 2 m : ℕ) : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      fun n ↦ (n : ℝ) ^ (2 : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos367.erdos_367.variants.k_ge_three_lower
statements.doc:
But this fails for all $k \geq 3$, and in fact
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+3} B_2(m) \gg n^2 \log n$ infinitely often.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_367.variants.k_ge_three_lower :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∃ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop,
      c * ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * Real.log (n : ℝ)) ≤
        ((∏ m ∈ .Ico n (n + 3), B 2 m : ℕ) : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos367.erdos_367.variants.higher_full_parts
statements.doc:
It would also be interesting to find upper and lower bounds for the analogous product with $B_r$
for $r \geq 3$, where $B_r(n)$ is the $r$-full part of $n$ (that is, the product of prime powers
$p^a \mid n$ such that $p^{a+1} \nmid n$ and $a \geq r$). Is it true that, for every fixed
$r \geq 3$ and $k \geq 2$, there is some $\epsilon = \epsilon(r, k) > 0$ with
$\limsup \frac{\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_r(m)}{n^{1+\epsilon}} = \infty$?

The webpage writes "for every fixed $r,k \geq 2$ and $\epsilon > 0$", but van Doorn observes in
the [comments](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/367#post-1766) that the intended
reading lets $\epsilon$ depend on $r$ and $k$. Since $B_r(m) \mid m$, the product is at most
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} m$, so the reading with $\epsilon$ universally quantified is false.

The answer is yes: $\epsilon = 1/(2r)$ works. For $j \geq r$ let $x = 2^j + 1$ and $n = x^r - 1$;
then $B_r(n+1) = x^r$ and $2^j \mid n$ gives $B_r(n) \geq 2^j$, so the product over $[n, n+k)$ is at
least $2^j x^r \geq (\sqrt{x}/2)\, n^{1 + 1/(2r)}$, which is unbounded. A stronger exponent
(any $\epsilon < (r+1)/r^2$) is claimed in the [forum](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/367)
but is not formalised.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_367.variants.higher_full_parts :
    ∀ r k : ℕ, 3 ≤ r → 2 ≤ k → ∃ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε ∧
      atTop.limsup (fun n ↦
        ((∏ m ∈ .Ico n (n + k), B r m : ℕ) / (n : ℝ) ^ (1 + ε) |>.toEReal)) = ⊤

problems.title: Erdős Problem 368
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/368](https://www.erdosproblems.com/368)
- [Er76d] Erdős, P., Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive
  integers and related questions. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical
  Mathematics (1976), 25–44.
- [Po18] Pólya, Georg, Zur arithmetischen Untersuchung der Polynome.
  Math. Z. (1918), 143–148.
- [Sc67b] Schinzel, A., On two theorems of Gelfond and some of their applications.
  Acta Arith. (1967/68), 177–236.

statements.name: Erdos368.erdos_368.lower_bound
statements.doc:
How large is the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$?
The truth is probably $F(n)\gg (\log n)^2$ for all $n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_368.lower_bound :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → c * Real.log n ^ 2 ≤ (F n : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos368.erdos_368.upper_bound
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er76d] conjectured that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$
such that $F(n)<(\log n)^{2+\epsilon}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_368.upper_bound :
    ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (F n : ℝ) < Real.log n ^ (2 + ε)

statements.name: Erdos368.erdos_368.variants.tendsto
statements.doc: Pólya [Po18] proved that $F(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_368.variants.tendsto : Tendsto F atTop atTop

statements.name: Erdos368.erdos_368.variants.subpower
statements.doc:
For every $\delta>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ with $F(n)\leq n^\delta$.
This follows from Schinzel's [Sc67b] observation that, for infinitely many $n$,
$F(n)\leq n^{O(1/\log\log\log n)}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_368.variants.subpower :
    ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∃ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (F n : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) ^ δ

problems.title: Erdős Problem 369
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/369](https://www.erdosproblems.com/369)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [EgSe76] Eggleton, R. B. and Selfridge, J. L., *Consecutive integers with no large prime factors*.
  J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1976), 1--11.
- [BFMW20] Bober, J. W. and Fretwell, D. and Martin, G. and Wooley, T. D., *Smooth values of
  polynomials*. J. Aust. Math. Soc. (2020), 245--261.
- [BaWo98] Balog, Antal and Wooley, Trevor D., *On strings of consecutive integers with no large
  prime factors*. J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1998), 266-276.

statements.name: Erdos369.erdos_369
statements.doc:
Let $\epsilon>0$ and $k\geq 2$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there is a
sequence of $k$ consecutive integers in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ all of which are $n^\epsilon$-smooth?

The problem is trivially true as written (simply taking $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and $n>k^{1/\epsilon}$).
There are (at least) two possible variants which are non-trivial, and it is not clear which
Erdős and Graham meant. We formalize the second: each $m\in P$ (where $P$ is the sequence of $k$
consecutive integers sought for) must be in $[n/2,n]$. In this case a positive answer also
follows directly from the result of Balog and Wooley [BaWo98] for infinitely many $n$. Proving
this is true for all large $n$ does not follow immediately from [BaWo98], but can be deduced
using a similar construction, as shown by SkyYang.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_369 :
    ∀ (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k),
      ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, ∃ a : ℕ, n / 2 ≤ a + 1 ∧ a + k ≤ n ∧
        ∀ j < k, ∀ p ∈ (a + 1 + j).primeFactors, (p : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) ^ ε

problems.title: Erdős Problem 370
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/370](https://www.erdosproblems.com/370)

statements.name: Erdos370.erdos_370
statements.doc:
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the largest prime factor of $n$ is $< n^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and
the largest prime factor of $n + 1$ is $< (n + 1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Steinerberger has pointed out this problem has a trivial solution.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_370 :
    { n | Nat.maxPrimeFac n < √n ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) < √(n + 1) }.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 371
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/371](https://www.erdosproblems.com/371)
- [OAI26a] OpenAI, *The joint Dickman law for consecutive integers*. OpenAI Math Release preprint
  (2026).
  https://github.com/openai/math/blob/adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a/preprints/The-joint-Dickman-law-for-consecutive-integers-September-24-2026/paper.pdf

statements.name: Erdos371.erdos_371
statements.doc:
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. Show that the set of $n$
with $P(n+1) > P(n)$ has density $\frac{1}{2}$.

This was proved by an internal OpenAI model in September 2026 [OAI26a]; see the linked Lean proof.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_371 :
    { n | Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) > Nat.maxPrimeFac n }.HasDensity (1/2)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 372
problems.doc:
*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/372](https://www.erdosproblems.com/372)

Conjectured by Erdős and Pomerance. Proved by Balog, who showed the stronger quantitative result
that this holds for $\gg \sqrt{x}$ many $n\leq x$, for all large $x$.

statements.name: Erdos372.erdos_372
statements.doc:
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. There are infinitely many $n$ such that
$P(n)>P(n+1)>P(n+2)$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_372 :
    {n : ℕ | Nat.maxPrimeFac n > Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) ∧
      Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) > Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 2)}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 373
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/373](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373)

statements.name: Erdos373.erdos_373
statements.doc:
Show that the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has
only finitely many solutions.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_373 : S.Finite

statements.name: Erdos373.erdos_373.variants.of_limit
statements.doc:
Show that if `P(n(n+1)) / log n → ∞` where `P(m)` denotes the largest prime factor of `m`, then
the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with `n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has only
finitely many solutions.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_373.variants.of_limit
    (H : Filter.atTop.Tendsto (fun (n : ℕ) => (n*(n+1)).maxPrimeFac / (n : ℝ).log) Filter.atTop) :
    S.Finite

statements.name: Erdos373.erdos_373.variants.of_lower_bound
statements.doc:
Show that if `P(n(n−1)) > 4 log n` for large enough `n`, where `P(m)` denotes the
largest prime factor of `m`, then the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with
`n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, has only finitely many solutions.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_373.variants.of_lower_bound
    (H : ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, 4*(n : ℝ).log < (n*(n-1 : ℕ)).maxPrimeFac) :
    S.Finite

statements.name: Erdos373.erdos_373.variants.maximal_solution
statements.doc:
Hickerson conjectured the largest solution the equation `n!=a_1!a_2!···a_k!`, with
`n−1 > a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ··· ≥ a_k`, is `16!=14!5!2!`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_373.variants.maximal_solution :
    (16, [14, 5, 2]) ∈ S ∧ ∀ s ∈ S, s.fst ≤ 16

statements.name: Erdos373.erdos_373.variants.suranyi
statements.doc:
Surányi was the first to conjecture that the only non-trivial solution to `a!b!=n!`
is `6!7!=10!`.

problems.title: Erdős Problem 375
problems.doc:
*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
 - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
    theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
 - [RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to
    factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124.
 -

statements.name: Erdos375.erdos_375
statements.doc: Is `Erdos375Prop` true?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_375 : Erdos375Prop

statements.name: Erdos375.erdos_375.variants.bounded_gap
statements.doc:
If `Erdos375Prop` is true, then `(n + 1).nth Prime - n.nth Prime < (n.nth Prime) ^ (1 / 2 - c)`
for some `c > 0`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_375.variants.bounded_gap : Erdos375Prop →
    ∃ c > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (n + 1).nth Nat.Prime - n.nth Nat.Prime
    < (n.nth Nat.Prime : ℝ) ^ (1 / (2 : ℝ) - c)

statements.name: Erdos375.erdos_375.variants.legendre
statements.doc: In particular, if `Erdos375Prop` is true, then Legendre's conjecture is asymptotically true.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_375.variants.legendre : Erdos375Prop →
    (∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ p ∈ Set.Ioo (n ^ 2) ((n + 1) ^ 2), Nat.Prime p)

statements.name: Erdos375.erdos_375.variants.le_two
statements.doc:
It is easy to see that for any `n ≥ 1` and `k ≤ 2`, if `n + 1, ..., n + k` are all composite,
then there are distinct primes `p₁, ... pₖ` such that `pᵢ ∣ n + i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ k`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_375.variants.le_two : ∀ n ≥ 1, ∀ k ≤ 2, (∀ i < k, ¬ (n + i + 1).Prime) →
    ∃ p : Fin k → ℕ, p.Injective ∧ ∀ i, (p i).Prime ∧ p i ∣ n + i + 1

statements.name: Erdos375.erdos_375.variants.log
statements.doc:
There exists a constant `c > 0` such that for all `n`, if
`k < c * (log n / (log (log n))) ^ 3 → (∀ i < k, ¬ (n + i + 1).Prime)`, then
there are distinct primes `p₁, ... pₖ` such that `pᵢ ∣ n + i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ k`. This is proved
in [RST75]. There is no need to only consider sufficiently large `n` because one can always take
`c` small enough so that `k < c * (log n / (log (log n))) ^ 3` implies that `k = 0` until `n` is
large.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_375.variants.log : ∃ c > 0, ∀ n k : ℕ,
    k < c * (Real.log n / (Real.log (Real.log n))) ^ 3 → (∀ i < k, ¬ (n + i + 1).Prime) →
    ∃ p : Fin k → ℕ, p.Injective ∧ ∀ i, (p i).Prime ∧ p i ∣ n + i + 1

problems.title: Erdős Problem 376
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/376](https://www.erdosproblems.com/376)

statements.name: Erdos376.erdos_376
statements.doc: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that ${2n\choose n}$ is coprime to $105$?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_376 : { (n : ℕ) | n.centralBinom.Coprime 105 }.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos376.erdos_376.variants.prime
statements.doc:
Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75] have shown that, for any two odd primes $p$ and $q$,
there are infinite many $n$ such that ${2n\choose n}$ is coprime to $pq$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_376.variants.prime {p q : ℕ} (h₁ : p.Prime)
    (h₂ : Odd p) (h₃ : q.Prime) (h₄ : Odd q) :
    { (n : ℕ) | n.centralBinom.Coprime (p * q) }.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 377
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)

statements.name: Erdos377.erdos_377
statements.doc:
Is there some absolute constant $C > 0$ such that
$$
  \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p} \leq C
$$
for all $n$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_377 :
    ∃ C > (0 : ℝ), ∀ (n : ℕ), sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n ≤ C

statements.name: Erdos377.erdos_377.variants.limit.i
statements.doc:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then
$$
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x} f(n) = \gamma_0
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_377.variants.limit.i (γ₀ : ℝ)
    (hγ₀ : γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), (k + 2 : ℝ).log / 2 ^ (k + 2)) :
    Tendsto (fun (x : ℕ) => (1 : ℝ) / x * ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 x, sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n)
      atTop (𝓝 γ₀)

statements.name: Erdos377.erdos_377.variants.limit.ii
statements.doc:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then
$$
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x} f(n)^2 = \gamma_0^2
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_377.variants.limit.ii (γ₀ : ℝ)
    (hγ₀ : γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), (k + 2 : ℝ).log / 2 ^ (k + 2)) :
    Tendsto (fun (x : ℕ) =>
      (1 : ℝ) / x * ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 x, sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n ^ 2)
      atTop (𝓝 (γ₀ ^ 2))

statements.name: Erdos377.erdos_377.variants.ae
statements.doc:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then for almost all integers $f(m) = \gamma_0 + o(1)$, i.e. for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the set of
$n$ with $|f(n) - \gamma_0| < \varepsilon$ has natural density one.

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_377.variants.ae (γ₀ : ℝ) (hγ₀ : γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), (k + 2 : ℝ).log / 2 ^ (k + 2)) :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), {n : ℕ | |sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n - γ₀| < ε}.HasDensity 1

statements.name: Erdos377.erdos_377.variants.ub
statements.doc:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
then there is some constant $c < 1$ such that for all large $n$
$$
  f(n) \leq c \log\log n.
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_377.variants.ub : ∃ c < (1 : ℝ),
      ∀ᶠ n in atTop, sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n ≤ c * (n : ℝ).log.log

problems.title: Erdős Problem 379
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/379](https://www.erdosproblems.com/379)

statements.name: Erdos379.erdos_379
statements.doc:
Let $S(n)$ denote the largest integer such that, for all $1 ≤ k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by $p^S(n)$ for some prime $p$ (depending on $k$).Then
$\limsup S(n) = \infty$.

This was formalized in Lean by Tao.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_379 : atTop.limsup (fun n => (S n : ℕ∞)) = ⊤

problems.title: Erdős Problem 382
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/382](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

statements.name: Erdos382.lt_two_mul_of_largestPrimeRepeated
statements.doc:
If the condition holds, then $v < 2u$.

Otherwise $2u \leq v$, and by Bertrand's postulate there is a prime $q$ with $v/2 < q \leq v$, so
$u \leq q \leq v$. The largest prime $p$ of the product satisfies $p \geq q > v/2$. Hence $p$
divides exactly one factor $m \in [u, v]$, namely $m = p$, and $p$ appears with exponent $1$.
statements.statement:
theorem lt_two_mul_of_largestPrimeRepeated {u v : ℕ} (h : LargestPrimeRepeated u v) :
    v < 2 * u

statements.name: Erdos382.erdos_382.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $u \leq v$ be such that the largest prime dividing $\prod_{u \leq m \leq v} m$ appears with
exponent at least $2$. Is it true that $v - u = v^{o(1)}$?

We read this as: for every $\epsilon > 0$, every such pair with $v$ large enough satisfies
$v - u \leq v^{\epsilon}$. Cambie observed that this question reduces to old conjectures on gaps
between primes; for example, it follows from Cramér's conjecture. See also Erdős Problems 380 and
383.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_382.parts.i :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ v : ℕ in atTop, ∀ u : ℕ, LargestPrimeRepeated u v →
      ((v - u : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (v : ℝ) ^ ε

statements.name: Erdos382.erdos_382.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $u \leq v$ be such that the largest prime dividing $\prod_{u \leq m \leq v} m$ appears with
exponent at least $2$. Can $v - u$ be arbitrarily large?

That is, for every $k$, is there such a pair with $v - u \geq k$? Cambie gives a heuristic that
suggests the answer is yes.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_382.parts.ii :
    ∀ k : ℕ, ∃ u v : ℕ, LargestPrimeRepeated u v ∧ k ≤ v - u

statements.name: Erdos382.erdos_382.variants.ramachandra
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] report that it follows from results of Ramachandra that
$v - u \leq v^{1/2+o(1)}$ for every pair $u \leq v$ as in `Erdos382.erdos_382.parts.i`.

That is, for every $\epsilon > 0$, every such pair with $v$ large enough satisfies
$v - u \leq v^{1/2+\epsilon}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_382.variants.ramachandra :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ v : ℕ in atTop, ∀ u : ℕ, LargestPrimeRepeated u v →
      ((v - u : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (v : ℝ) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 2 + ε)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 383
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/383](https://www.erdosproblems.com/383)

statements.name: Erdos383.erdos_383
statements.doc:
Is it true that for every $k$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that the largest prime
divisor of
$$
  \prod_{i = 0}^k (p ^ 2 + i)
$$
is $p$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_383 :
    ∀ k, {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 0 k, (p ^ 2 + i)) = p}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 384
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/384](https://www.erdosproblems.com/384)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Ec69] Ecklund, Jr., E. F., *On prime divisors of the binomial coefficient*. Pacific J. Math.
  (1969), 267-270.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., *Unsolved problems in number theory*. (2004), xviii+437.

statements.name: Erdos384.erdos_384
statements.doc:
If $1<k<n-1$ then $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by a prime $p\leq n/2$ (except
$\binom{7}{3}=\binom{7}{4}=5\cdot 7$).

A conjecture of Erdős and Selfridge [ErGr80]. Proved by Ecklund [Ec69], who made the stronger
conjecture that whenever $n>k^2$ the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by a prime
$p<n/k$. Discussed in problem B31 and B33 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. Stronger forms of this
conjecture are [1094](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1094) and
[1095](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1095).

Ecklund's theorem is stated for $n \geq 2k$ with the single exception $\binom{7}{3}$; by the
symmetry $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$ this is the form above, where $\binom{7}{4}$ is the
second exception. The prime bound is $p \leq n/2$ (that is, $2p \leq n$); see
`erdos_384.variants.strict` for the strict inequality.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_384 (n k : ℕ) (hk : 1 < k) (hkn : k < n - 1) (h₃ : (n, k) ≠ (7, 3))
    (h₄ : (n, k) ≠ (7, 4)) :
    ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ p ∣ n.choose k ∧ 2 * p ≤ n

statements.name: Erdos384.erdos_384.variants.strict
statements.doc:
With the strict inequality $p < n/2$ the statement is false: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ has no prime
divisor $p < 2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_384.variants.strict :
    ¬ ∀ n k : ℕ, 1 < k → k < n - 1 → (n, k) ≠ (7, 3) → (n, k) ≠ (7, 4) →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ p ∣ n.choose k ∧ 2 * p < n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 385
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/385](https://www.erdosproblems.com/385)

statements.name: Erdos385.erdos_385.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $F(n) := \max\{m + p(m) \mid  \textrm{$m < n$ composite}\}\}$ where $p(m)$ is the least
prime divisor of $m$. Is it true that $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_385.parts.i : ∀ᶠ n in atTop, n < F n

statements.name: Erdos385.erdos_385.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $F(n) := \max\{m + p(m) \mid  \textrm{$m < n$ composite}\}\}$ where $p(m)$ is the least
prime divisor of $m$. Does $F(n) - n \to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_385.parts.ii : atTop.Tendsto (fun n ↦ F n - n) atTop

statements.name: Erdos385.erdos_385.variants.lb
statements.doc:
A question of Erdős, Eggleton, and Selfridge, who write that in fact it is possible that
this quantity is always at least $n+(1-o(1))\sqrt{n}$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_385.variants.lb : ∃ (e : ℕ → ℝ) (he : e =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)),
    ∀ n, n + (1 - e n) * √n ≤ F n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 386
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/386](https://www.erdosproblems.com/386)

statements.name: Erdos386.erdos_386
statements.doc:
Let $2 \le k \le n - 2$. Can $\binom{n}{k}$ be the product of consecutive primes infinitely
often? Here $k$ may vary with $n$: the question asks for infinitely many admissible binomial
coefficients, not for a single $k$ that works infinitely often.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_386 :
    ∃ᶠ n in .atTop, ∃ k ≥ 2,
      k ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose k = ∏ i ∈ .Ico p q, nth Nat.Prime i

statements.name: Erdos386.erdos_386.variants.forall
statements.doc:
For all $2 \le k \le n - 2$,
can $\binom{n}{k}$ be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_386.variants.forall :
    ∀ k ≥ 2, ∃ᶠ n in .atTop,
      k ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose k = ∏ i ∈ .Ico p q, nth Nat.Prime i

statements.name: Erdos386.erdos_386.variants.two
statements.doc: Can $\binom{n}{2}$ be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_386.variants.two :
    ∃ᶠ n in .atTop,
      2 ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose 2 = ∏ i ∈ .Ico p q, nth Nat.Prime i

problems.title: Erdős Problem 387
problems.doc:
*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/387](https://www.erdosproblems.com/387)
 - [ErGr76b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On the prime factors of
   ${n \choose k}$*. Fibonacci Quart. (1976), 348-352.
 - [Er78g] Erdős, Pál, *On prime factors of binomial coefficients. II*. Mat. Lapok
   (1978/82), 307-316.
 - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
   number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
 - [Sc58] Schinzel, A., *Sur un problème de P. Erdős*. Colloq. Math. (1958), 198-204.
 - [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
 - [Fa66] Faulkner, M. "On a theorem of Sylvester and Schur." Journal of the London Mathematical
    Society 1.1 (1966): 107-110.
 - [BNPZ26] Bui, H., Naprienko, S., Pratt, K., and Zaharescu, A. Binomial coefficients with
    divisors avoiding an interval. arXiv:2605.21221 (2026).

statements.name: Erdos387.erdos_387
statements.doc:
Is there an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that, for all $1 \leq k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn, n]$?

Bui, Naprienko, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BNPZ26] answered this negatively.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_387 : ¬ ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → k < n →
    ∃ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioc (c * n) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k

statements.name: Erdos387.erdos_387.variants.schinzel
statements.doc: The following is Schinzel's conjecture, which appears in [Gu04].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_387.variants.schinzel :
    ∀ᶠ k in atTop, ¬ IsPrimePow k → ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ i < k, ¬ n - i ∣ n.choose k

statements.name: Erdos387.erdos_387.variants.easy
statements.doc: It is easy to see that `n.choose k` has a divisor in `[n / k, n]`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_387.variants.easy {n : ℕ} {k : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hk : k ≤ n) : ∃ d : ℕ,
    (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Icc (n / k : ℝ) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k

statements.name: Erdos387.erdos_387.variants.guy
statements.doc:
Is it true for any $c < 1$ and all $n$ sufficiently large, for all $1 \leq k < n$,
$\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn, n]$?

This variant appears in [Gu04]. Bui, Naprienko, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BNPZ26] answered it
negatively.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_387.variants.guy : ¬ ∀ c : ℝ, c < 1 → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k →
    k < n → ∃ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioc (c * n) n ∧ d ∣ n.choose k

problems.title: Erdős Problem 388
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/388](https://www.erdosproblems.com/388)
- [Er76d] Erdős, P., *Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers
  and related questions*. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics
  (Univ. Manitoba, Winnipeg, Man., 1975) (1976), 25-44.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er92e] Erdős, Pál, *Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics*.
  Eureka (1992), 44-48.

statements.name: Erdos388.erdos_388
statements.doc:
Are there only finitely many solutions of
$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)$$
with $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$?

Here $m_1, m_2 \geq 0$, so every factor is positive and the condition $m_1 + k_1 \leq m_2$ makes the
two blocks disjoint. Negative $m_1$ would give trivial solutions such as
$(-5)(-4)(-3)(-2) = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5$. The source also asks to classify all solutions;
see `Erdos388.erdos_388.variants.classification`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_388 :
    {(m₁, k₁, m₂, k₂) : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | 3 < k₁ ∧ 3 < k₂ ∧ m₁ + k₁ ≤ m₂ ∧
      ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (m₁ + i) = ∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (m₂ + j)}.Finite

statements.name: Erdos388.erdos_388.variants.classification
statements.doc:
Can one classify all solutions of
$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)$$
with $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$?

A solution must supply the set of all solutions $(m_1, k_1, m_2, k_2)$. Whether a description of
this set is a satisfactory classification is up to human judgement.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_388.variants.classification :
    {(m₁, k₁, m₂, k₂) : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | 3 < k₁ ∧ 3 < k₂ ∧ m₁ + k₁ ≤ m₂ ∧
      ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (m₁ + i) = ∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂,
        (m₂ + j)} = erdos_388.variants.classification.answer

statements.name: Erdos388.erdos_388.variants.general
statements.doc:
More generally, if $k_1>2$ then for fixed $a$ and $b$ the equation
$$a\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=b\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)$$
should have only finitely many solutions.

The source states no condition on $a$, $b$, $k_2$ or the position of the blocks, so this is our
reading: $a$ and $b$ are positive integers, we keep the condition $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$ of the main
problem (the $k_1$-block lies below the $k_2$-block), and we assume $k_2 > 2$ as well. Without
these conditions there are infinite families of solutions:
- for $k_2 = 1$ and $b = 1$, take $m_2 + 1 = a\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)$;
- for $k_2 = 2$, $a = 1$ and $b = 4$, the identity $(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4) = Y(Y+2)$ with
  $Y = (n+1)(n+4)$ even gives a solution with $m_2 + 1 = Y/2$ for every $n \geq 2$;
- overlapping blocks give $2\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(k-1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k}(k+j)$ for every
  $k \geq 2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_388.variants.general (a b : ℕ) (ha : 0 < a) (hb : 0 < b) :
    {(m₁, k₁, m₂, k₂) : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | 2 < k₁ ∧ 2 < k₂ ∧ m₁ + k₁ ≤ m₂ ∧
      a * ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (m₁ + i) = b * ∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (m₂ + j)}.Finite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 389
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/389](https://www.erdosproblems.com/389)

statements.name: Erdos389.erdos_389
statements.doc:
Is it true that for every $n \geq 1$ there is a $k$ such that
$$
  n(n + 1) \cdots (n + k - 1) \mid (n + k) \cdots (n + 2k - 1)?
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_389 :
    ∀ n ≥ 1, ∃ k ≥ 1, ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (n + i) ∣ ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (n + k + i)

statements.name: Erdos389.erdos_389.variants.mehta_four
statements.doc:
Bhavik Mehta has computed the minimal such $k$ for $1 \leq n \leq 18$.
For example, the minimal $k$ for $n = 4$ is $207$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_389.variants.mehta_four :
    IsLeast
      { k | 1 ≤ k ∧ ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (4 + i) ∣ ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (4 + k + i) }
      207

problems.title: Erdős Problem 390
problems.doc:
*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/390](https://www.erdosproblems.com/390)
 - [EGS82] Erdős, P., R. K. Guy, and J. L. Selfridge. "Another Property of 239 and some related
    questions." Congr. Numer. 34 (1982): 243-257.
 -

statements.name: Erdos390.erdos_390.variants.theta
statements.doc: `f n - 2 * n = θ (n / log n)`. This is proved in [EGS82].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_390.variants.theta :
    (fun n => f n - 2 * n : ℕ → ℝ) =Θ[atTop] (fun n => n / log (n : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos390.erdos_390
statements.doc: Does there exists a constant `c` such that `f n - 2 * n ~ c * (n / log n)`?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_390 :
    ∃ c,
      (fun n => f n - 2 * n : ℕ → ℝ) ~[atTop] (fun n => c * n / log (n : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 391
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/391](https://www.erdosproblems.com/391)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er96b] Erdős, Paul, *Some problems I presented or planned to present in my short talk*.
  Analytic number theory, Vol. 1 (Allerton Park, IL, 1995) (1996), 333-335.
- [AlGr77] Alladi, Krishnaswami and Grinstead, Charles, *On the decomposition of $n!$ into prime
  powers*. J. Number Theory (1977), 452-458.
- [ACRSTUV25] B. Alexeev, E. Conway, M. Rosenfeld, A. Sutherland, T. Tao, M. Uhr, and K.
  Ventullo, *Decomposing a factorial into large factors*. arXiv:2503.20170 (2025).

statements.name: Erdos391.erdos_391
statements.doc:
Let $t(n)$ be maximal such that there is a representation
$$n!=a_1\cdots a_n$$
with $t(n)=a_1\leq \cdots \leq a_n$. Obtain good bounds for $t(n)/n$. In particular, is it true
that
$$\lim \frac{t(n)}{n}=\frac{1}{e}?$$

It is easy to see that $\lim \frac{t(n)}{n}\leq \frac{1}{e}$. Erdős [Er96b] wrote he, Selfridge,
and Straus had proved a corresponding lower bound, so that $\lim \frac{t(n)}{n}=\frac{1}{e}$, and
'believed that Straus had written up our proof. Unfortunately Straus suddenly died and no trace
was ever found of his notes. Furthermore, we never could reconstruct our proof, so our assertion
now can be called only a conjecture.'

Alladi and Grinstead [AlGr77] have obtained similar results when the $a_i$ are restricted to
prime powers.

Both questions were answered by Alexeev, Conway, Rosenfeld, Sutherland, Tao, Uhr, and Ventullo
[ACRSTUV25], who proved that
$$\frac{t(n)}{n}= \frac{1}{e}-\frac{c_0}{\log n}+O\left(\frac{1}{(\log n)^{1+c}}\right),$$
where $c_0=0.3044\cdots$ is an explicit constant, for some $c>0$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_391 :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (t n : ℝ) / n) atTop (𝓝 (1 / Real.exp 1))

statements.name: Erdos391.erdos_391.variants.deficit
statements.doc:
Furthermore, does there exist some constant $c>0$ such that
$$\frac{t(n)}{n} \leq \frac{1}{e}-\frac{c}{\log n}$$
for infinitely many $n$?

This was answered in the affirmative by Alexeev, Conway, Rosenfeld, Sutherland, Tao, Uhr, and
Ventullo [ACRSTUV25].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_391.variants.deficit : ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧
    {n : ℕ | (t n : ℝ) / n ≤ 1 / Real.exp 1 - c / Real.log n}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 392
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/392](https://www.erdosproblems.com/392)

statements.name: Erdos392.erdos_392
statements.doc:
Let $A(n)$ denote the least value of $t$ such that
$$
  n! = a_1 \cdots a_t
$$
with $a_1 \leq \cdots \leq a_t\leq n^2$. Then
$$
  A(n) = \frac{n}{2} - \frac{n}{2\log n} + o\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right).
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_392 (A : ℕ → ℕ) (h : ∀ n > 0,
    IsLeast { t + 1 | (t) (_ : ∃ a : Fin (t + 1) → ℕ, (n)! = ∏ i, a i ∧
      Monotone a ∧ a (Fin.last t) ≤ n ^ 2) } (A n)) :
    ((fun (n : ℕ) => (A n - n / 2 + n / (2 * Real.log n) : ℝ)) =o[atTop] fun n => n / Real.log n)

statements.name: Erdos392.erdos_392.variants.lower
statements.doc:
If we change the condition to $a_t \leq n$ it can be shown that
$$
  A(n) = n - \frac{n}{\log n} + o\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_392.variants.lower (A : ℕ → ℕ)
    (hA : ∀ n > 0, IsLeast
      { t + 1 | (t) (_ : ∃ a : Fin (t + 1) → ℕ, (n)! = ∏ i, a i ∧
        Monotone a ∧ a (Fin.last t) ≤ n) } (A n)) :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => (A n - n + n / Real.log n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] fun n => n / Real.log n

statements.name: Erdos392.erdos_392.variants.implication
statements.doc:
Cambie has observed that a positive answer follows from the result above with $a_t \leq n$, simply
by pairing variables together, e.g. taking $a'_i = a_{2i-1}a_{2i}$ (and the lower bound follows from
Stirling's approximation).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_392.variants.implication (h : type_of% erdos_392.variants.lower) :
    type_of% erdos_392

problems.title: Erdős Problem 393
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/393](https://www.erdosproblems.com/393)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [BeOs92] Berend, Daniel and Osgood, Charles F., *On the equation $P(x)=n!$ and a question of
  Erdős*. J. Number Theory 42 (1992), 189-193.
- [BPZ23] Bui, Hung M. and Pratt, Kyle and Zaharescu, Alexandru, *Power savings for counting
  solutions to polynomial-factorial equations*. Adv. Math. 422 (2023), Paper No. 109021, 32 pp.
  [arXiv:2204.08423](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08423)
- [Lu02] Luca, Florian, *The Diophantine equation $P(x)=n!$ and a result of M. Overholt*.
  Glas. Mat. Ser. III 37 (2002), 269-273.
- [OEIS A388302](https://oeis.org/A388302): the values $f(n)$ for $n \geq 2$.

statements.name: Erdos393.erdos_393
statements.doc:
Let $f(n)$ denote the minimal $m\geq 1$ such that
$$n! = a_1\cdots a_t$$
with $a_1<\cdots <a_t=a_1+m$. What is the behaviour of $f(n)$?

We formalise the question as: does $f(n) \to \infty$? A result of Luca [Lu02] implies a positive
answer, conditional on the $abc$ conjecture (see `Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.luca`).
statements.statement: theorem erdos_393 : Tendsto f atTop atTop

statements.name: Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.infinitely_often_one
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80, p. 76] write that they do not even know whether $f(n) = 1$ for infinitely
many $n$, that is, whether a factorial is the product of two consecutive integers infinitely
often.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_393.variants.infinitely_often_one :
    {n : ℕ | f n = 1}.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.berend_osgood
statements.doc:
Let $F_m(N)$ count the number of $n \leq N$ such that $f(n) = m$. A theorem of Berend and
Osgood [BeOs92] implies that, for each fixed $m$, $F_m(N) = o(N)$, that is,
$\{n : f(n) = m\}$ has natural density $0$.

They proved that, for every $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree at least $2$, the set of $n$ such
that $P(x) = n!$ has an integer solution has density $0$. For $m \geq 1$ this applies because
$f(n) = m$ gives $n! = P(a_1)$ for one of the finitely many polynomials
$P(x) = \prod_{j \in S} (x + j)$ with $\{0, m\} \subseteq S \subseteq \{0, \ldots, m\}$. For
$m = 0$ the set is $\{0, 1\}$ (the junk values), so the statement is trivial.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_393.variants.berend_osgood (m : ℕ) :
    {n : ℕ | f n = m}.HasDensity 0

statements.name: Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.bui_pratt_zaharescu
statements.doc:
A theorem of Bui, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BPZ23] implies that, for each fixed $m$,
$$F_m(N) \ll_m N^{33/34},$$
where $F_m(N)$ is the number of $n \leq N$ such that $f(n) = m$.

They proved that, for every $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree at least $2$, the number of
$N \leq n < 2N$ such that $P(x) = n!$ has an integer solution is $\ll_P N^{33/34}$. Summing over
the finitely many polynomials in `Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.berend_osgood` and over the dyadic
ranges $[2^i, 2^{i+1})$ gives the bound for $n \leq N$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_393.variants.bui_pratt_zaharescu (m : ℕ) :
    (fun N : ℕ ↦ (({n : ℕ | f n = m} ∩ Set.Iic N).ncard : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      (fun N : ℕ ↦ (N : ℝ) ^ (33 / 34 : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.luca
statements.doc:
Luca [Lu02] proved that the $abc$ conjecture implies that, for every $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of
degree at least $2$, the equation $P(x) = n!$ has only finitely many solutions. As remarked on
erdosproblems.com, this implies that $f(n) \to \infty$, conditional on the $abc$ conjecture
(`ABC.abc`).
statements.statement: theorem erdos_393.variants.luca (habc : type_of% ABC.abc) : Tendsto f atTop atTop

problems.title: Erdős Problem 394
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/394](https://www.erdosproblems.com/394)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErHa78] Erdős, P. and Hall, R. R., On some unconventional problems on the divisors of integers.
  J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1978), 479--485.

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.parts.i
statements.doc: Is it true that $\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{x^2}{(\log x)^c}$ for some $c>0$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_394.parts.i :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), (fun x ↦ ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊,
    (t 2 n : ℝ)) ≪ (fun x ↦ x ^ 2 / (Real.log x) ^ c)

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.parts.ii
statements.doc: Is it true that, for $k\geq 2$, $\sum_{n\leq x}t_{k+1}(n) =o\left(\sum_{n\leq x}t_k(n)\right)?$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_394.parts.ii :
    ∀ k ≥ 2, (fun (x : ℝ) ↦ ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊,
    (t (k + 1) n : ℝ)) =o[atTop]
    (fun (x : ℝ) ↦ ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊,
    (t k n : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.variants.hall_bound
statements.doc:
In [ErGr80] they mention a conjecture of Erdős that the sum is $o(x^2)$. This was proved by Erdős
and Hall [ErHa78], who proved that in fact
$\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}x^2.$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_394.variants.hall_bound :
    (fun x ↦ ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊, (t 2 n : ℝ)) ≪
    (fun x ↦ x ^ 2 * (Real.log (Real.log (Real.log x)) / Real.log (Real.log x)))

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.variants.hall_conjecture
statements.doc: Erdős and Hall conjecture that the sum is $o(x^2/(\log x)^c)$ for any $c<\log 2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_394.variants.hall_conjecture :
    ∀ c < Real.log 2, (fun x ↦ ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊,
    (t 2 n : ℝ)) =o[atTop]
    (fun x ↦ x ^ 2 / (Real.log x) ^ c)

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.variants.lower_bound
statements.doc: Since $t_2(p)=p-1$ for prime $p$ it is trivial that $\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\gg \frac{x^2}{\log x}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_394.variants.lower_bound :
    (fun x ↦ x ^ 2 / Real.log x) ≪
    (fun x ↦ ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊, (t 2 n : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.variants.factorial_gap_conjecture
statements.doc:
They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$ and also ask whether, for infinitely many $n$,
$t_k(n!)< t_{k-1}(n!)-1$ for all $1\leq k < n$.

statements.name: Erdos394.erdos_394.variants.factorial_gap_10
statements.doc: They proved (with Selfridge) that this holds for $n=10$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_394.variants.factorial_gap_10 :
    ∀ (k : ℕ), 2 ≤ k → k < 10 →
    t k (10 !) <
    t (k - 1) (10 !) - 1

problems.title: Erdős Problem 395
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/395](https://www.erdosproblems.com/395)
- [Er45] Erdős, P., *On a lemma of Littlewood and Offord*. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (1945),
  898--902.
- [CaCa11] Carnielli, Walter and Carolino, Pietro K., *Adjusting a conjecture of Erdős*. Contrib.
  Discrete Math. (2011), 154--159.
- [HJNS24] X. He, T. Juškevičius, B. Narayanan, and S. Spiro, *The Reverse Littlewood-Offord
  problem of Erdős*. arXiv:2408.11034 (2024).

statements.name: Erdos395.erdos_395
statements.doc:
If $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in \mathbb{C}$ with $\lvert z_i\rvert=1$ then is it true that the probability
that
$$\lvert \epsilon_1z_1+\cdots+\epsilon_nz_n\rvert \leq \sqrt{2},$$
where $\epsilon_i\in \{-1,1\}$ uniformly at random, is $\gg 1/n$?

A reverse Littlewood-Offord problem. Erdős originally asked this with $\sqrt{2}$ replaced by $1$,
but Carnielli and Carolino [CaCa11] observed that this is false, choosing $z_1=1$ and $z_k=i$
for $2\leq k\leq n$, where $n$ is even, since then the sum is at least $\sqrt{2}$ always.

Solved in the affirmative by He, Juškevičius, Narayanan, and Spiro [HJNS24]. The bound of $1/n$
is the best possible, as shown by taking $z_k=1$ for $1\leq k\leq n/2$ and $z_k=i$ otherwise.

See also [498](https://www.erdosproblems.com/498).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_395 : ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ∀ z : Fin n → ℂ,
    (∀ i, ‖z i‖ = 1) → c / n ≤ (signedSumCount z √2 : ℝ) / 2 ^ n

statements.name: Erdos395.erdos_395.variants.one
statements.doc:
Erdős originally asked [erdős_395](https://www.erdosproblems.com/395) with $\sqrt{2}$ replaced by
$1$, but Carnielli and Carolino [CaCa11] observed that this is false, choosing $z_1=1$ and $z_k=i$
for $2\leq k\leq n$, where $n$ is even, since then the sum is at least $\sqrt{2}$ always.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_395.variants.one : ¬ ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
    ∀ z : Fin n → ℂ, (∀ i, ‖z i‖ = 1) → c / n ≤ (signedSumCount z 1 : ℝ) / 2 ^ n

statements.name: Erdos395.erdos_395.variants.sharp
statements.doc:
The bound of $1/n$ in [erdős_395](https://www.erdosproblems.com/395) is the best possible, as
shown by taking $z_k=1$ for $1\leq k\leq n/2$ and $z_k=i$ otherwise.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_395.variants.sharp : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ∃ z : Fin n → ℂ,
    (∀ i, ‖z i‖ = 1) ∧ (signedSumCount z √2 : ℝ) / 2 ^ n ≤ C / n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 396
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/396](https://www.erdosproblems.com/396)

statements.name: Erdos396.erdos_396
statements.doc:
Is it true that for every $k$ there exists $n$ such that
$$\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(n-i) \mid \binom{2n}{n}?$$
statements.statement: theorem erdos_396 : ∀ k : ℕ, ∃ n : ℕ, descFactorial n (k + 1) ∣ centralBinom n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 397
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/397](https://www.erdosproblems.com/397)
- [MathOverflow] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/138209/product-of-central-binomial-coefficients)

statements.name: Erdos397.erdos_397
statements.doc:
Are there only finitely many solutions to
$$
  \prod_i \binom{2m_i}{m_i}=\prod_j \binom{2n_j}{n_j}
$$
with the $m_i,n_j$ distinct?

Somani, using ChatGPT, has given a negative answer. In fact, for any $a\geq 2$, if $c=8a^2+8a+1$,
$\binom{2a}{a}\binom{4a+4}{2a+2}\binom{2c}{c}= \binom{2a+2}{a+1}\binom{4a}{2a}\binom{2c+2}{c+1}.$
Further families of solutions are given in the comments by SharkyKesa.

This was earlier asked about in a [MathOverflow] question, in response to which Elkies also gave an
alternative construction which produces solutions - at the moment it is not clear whether Elkies'
argument gives infinitely many solutions (although Bloom believes that it can).

This was formalized in Lean by Wu using Aristotle.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_397 :
    ¬ {(M, N) : Finset ℕ × Finset ℕ | Disjoint M N ∧
    ∏ i ∈ M, centralBinom i = ∏ j ∈ N, centralBinom j}.Finite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 398
problems.doc:
*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/398](https://www.erdosproblems.com/398)
 - [Wikipedia: Brocard's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brocard%27s_problem)

statements.name: Erdos398.erdos_398
statements.doc:
**Brocard's Problem**
Does $n! + 1 = m^2$ have integer solutions other than $n = 4, 5, 7$?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_398 : {n | ∃ m, n ! + 1 = m ^ 2} = {4, 5, 7}

problems.title: Erdős Problem 399
problems.doc:
Is it true that there are no solutions to $n! = x^k \pm y^k$ with $x,y,n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with $xy > 1$ and $k > 2$?

*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/399](https://www.erdosproblems.com/399)
- [Br32] Breusch, Robert, Zur Verallgemeinerung des Bertrandschen Postulates, da\ss zwischen $x$
  und 2 $x$ stets Primzahlen liegen. Math. Z. (1932), 505--526.
- [ErOb37] Erdős, P. and Obláth, R., \"Über diophantische Gleichungen der Form $n!=x^p+y^p$ und
  $n!\pmd m!=x^p$. Acta Litt. ac Sci. Reg. Univ. Hung. Fr.-Jos., Sect. Sci. Math. (1937), 241-255.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., Unsolved problems in number theory. (2004), xviii+437.
- [PoSh73] Pollack, Richard M. and Shapiro, Harold N., The next to last case of a factorial
  diophantine equation. Comm. Pure Appl. Math. (1973), 313-325.

statements.name: Erdos399.erdos_399
statements.doc:
Is it true that there are no solutions to `n! = x^k ± y^k` with `x,y,n ∈ ℕ`, `x*y > 1`, and
`k > 2`?

The answer is no: Jonas Barfield found the counterexample `10! = 48^4 - 36^4` (equivalently,
`10! + 36^4 = 48^4`).

This is discussed in problem D2 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

This was formalized in Lean by Lu using Codex.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_399 :
    ∃ (n x y k : ℕ), 1 < x * y ∧ 2 < k ∧ (n ! = x ^ k + y ^ k ∨ n ! + y ^ k = x ^ k)

statements.name: Erdos399.erdos_399.variants.erdos_oblath
statements.doc: Erdős and Obláth [ErOb37] proved this is true when $(x,y)=1$ and $k\neq 4$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_399.variants.erdos_oblath {n x y k : ℕ} :
    x.Coprime y → 1 < x * y → 2 < k → k ≠ 4 →
      n ! ≠ x ^ k + y ^ k ∧ n ! + y ^ k ≠ x ^ k

statements.name: Erdos399.erdos_399.variants.pollack_shapiro
statements.doc: Pollack and Shapiro [PoSh73] proved there are no solutions to $n!=x^4-1$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_399.variants.pollack_shapiro (n x : ℕ) : n ! + 1 ≠ x ^ 4

statements.name: Erdos399.erdos_399.variants.cambie
statements.doc:
Cambie has also observed that considerations modulo $8$ rule out any solutions to $n!=x^4+y^4$ with
$(x,y)=1$ and $xy>1$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_399.variants.cambie {n x y : ℕ} :
    x.Coprime y → 1 < x * y → n ! ≠ x ^ 4 + y ^ 4

statements.name: Erdos399.erdos_399.variants.sum_two_squares
statements.doc:
Erdős and Obláth observed that the Bertrand-style fact (first proved by Breusch [Br32]) that, if
$q_i$ is the sequence of primes congruent to $3\pmod{4}$ then $q_{i+1}<2q_i$ except for $q_1=3$,
together with Fermat's theorem on the sums of two squares implies that the only solution to
$n!=x^2+y^2$ is $6!=12^2+24^2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_399.variants.sum_two_squares :
    ∀ {n x y : ℕ}, 1 < x * y → n ! = x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 →
      n = 6 ∧ (x = 12 ∧ y = 24 ∨ x = 24 ∧ y = 12)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 400
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/400](https://www.erdosproblems.com/400)

statements.name: Erdos400.erdos_400.parts.i
statements.doc: Can one show that $\sum_{n\leq x}g_k(n) \sim c_k x\log x$ for some constant $c_k$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_400.parts.i :
    ∀ᵉ (k ≥ 2), ∃ c : ℝ,
      (fun x : ℕ ↦ (∑ n ∈ Icc 1 x, (g k n : ℝ))) ~[atTop]
      (fun x : ℕ ↦ c * x * Real.log x)

statements.name: Erdos400.erdos_400.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Is it true that there is a constant $c_k$ such that for almost all $n < x$ we have
$g_k(n)=c_k\log x+o(\log x)$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_400.parts.ii :
    ∀ᵉ (k ≥ 2), ∃ c : ℝ, ∀ ε > 0,
      Tendsto (fun x : ℕ ↦
        (((Icc 1 x).filter (fun n ↦
          |(g k n : ℝ) - c * Real.log x| ≤ ε * Real.log x)).card : ℝ) / x)
        atTop (𝓝 1)

statements.name: Erdos400.erdos_400.variants.upper_bound
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham write that it is easy to show that $g_k(n) \ll_k \log n$ always, but the best
possible constant is unknown.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_400.variants.upper_bound (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≥ 2) :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ (g k n : ℝ)) ≪ (fun n : ℕ ↦ Real.log (n : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 401
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/401](https://www.erdosproblems.com/401)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

statements.name: Erdos401.erdos_401
statements.doc:
Is there some function $f(r)$ such that $f(r)\to \infty$ as $r\to\infty$, such that, for
infinitely many $n$, there exist $a_1,a_2$ with
$$a_1+a_2> n+f(r)\log n$$
such that $a_1!a_2! \mid n!2^n3^n\cdots p_r^n$?

It is ambiguous in [ErGr80] what the intended quantifiers are on the variables (they write 'is
it true that we can find $a_1+a_2>n+f(r)\log n$...'). Comparing to previous problems such as
[728] and [729] it seems most likely that they intended to ask the formulation in the problem
statement.

The answer is yes: Barreto and Leeham have used ChatGPT to provide a proof of the stated problem
(in fact essentially the same construction as their solution to [729]).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_401 :
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℝ, Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧
      ∀ (r : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r),
        {n : ℕ | ∃ a₁ a₂ : ℕ, 0 < a₁ ∧ 0 < a₂ ∧
          (a₁ : ℝ) + a₂ > n + f r * Real.log n ∧
          a₁.factorial * a₂.factorial ∣
            n.factorial * (∏ i ∈ Finset.range r, Nat.nth Nat.Prime i) ^ n}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 402
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/402](https://www.erdosproblems.com/402)

statements.name: Erdos402.erdos_402
statements.doc:
Prove that, for any finite set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$, there exist $a, b\in A$ such
that
$$
  \gcd(a, b)\leq a/|A|.
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_402 (A : Finset ℕ) (h₁ : 0 ∉ A) (h₂ : A.Nonempty) : ∃ᵉ (a ∈ A) (b ∈ A),
    a.gcd b ≤ (a / A.card : ℚ)

statements.name: Erdos402.erdos_402.variants.equality
statements.doc:
A conjecture of Graham [Gr70], who also conjectured that (assuming $A$ itself
has no common divisor) the only cases where equality is achieved are when
$A = \{1, \dots, n\}$ or $A = \{L/1, \dots, L/n\}$ (where $L = \operatorname{lcm}(1, \dots, n)$) or
$A = \{2, 3, 4, 6\}$.
Note: The source [BaSo96] mentioned on the Erdős page makes it clear what
quantifiers to use for "where equality is achieved". See Theorem 1.1 there.

TODO(firsching): Consider if we should have the other direction here as well or
an iff statement.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_402.variants.equality (A : Finset ℕ) (h₁ : 0 ∉ A) (h₂ : A.Nonempty)
    (h₃ : A.gcd id = 1)
    (h : ∀ᵉ (a ∈ A) (b ∈ A), (a / A.card : ℚ) ≤ a.gcd b) :
    A = Finset.Icc 1 A.card ∨
    A = (Finset.Icc 1 A.card).image ((Finset.Icc 1 A.card).lcm id / ·) ∨
    A = {2, 3, 4, 6}

statements.name: Erdos402.erdos_402.variants.szegedy_zaharescu_weak
statements.doc:
Proved for all sufficiently large sets (including the sharper version which
characterises the case of equality) independently by Szegedy [Sz86] and
Zaharescu [Za87]. The following is taken from [Sz86].

There exists an effectively computable $n_0$ with the following properties:
(i) if $n \ge n_0$ and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are distinct natural numbers then
$\max_{i, j} \frac{a_i}{(a_i, a_j)} \ge n$.
(ii) If equality holds then the system $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ is either of the
type $\{k, 2k, \dots, nk\}$ or of the type
$\left\{\frac{k}{1}, \frac{k}{2}, \dots, \frac{k}{n}\right\}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_402.variants.szegedy_zaharescu_weak : ∀ᶠ n in atTop,
    ∀ (A : Finset ℕ), A.card = n → 0 ∉ A →
      (n ≤ (A ×ˢ A).sup (fun x => x.1 / x.1.gcd x.2)) ∧
      (n = (A ×ˢ A).sup (fun x => x.1 / x.1.gcd x.2) ↔
        ∃ k > 0, A = (Finset.Icc 1 n).image (k * ·) ∨
          A = (Finset.Icc 1 n).image (k * (Finset.Icc 1 n).lcm id / ·))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 403
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/403](https://www.erdosproblems.com/403)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
  number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
- [Li76] Lin, S., *On two problems of Erdős concerning sums of distinct factorials*.
  Bell Laboratories internal memorandum (1960).

statements.name: Erdos403.erdos_403
statements.doc:
Does the equation
$$2^m=a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$$
with $a_1<a_2<\cdots <a_k$ have only finitely many solutions?

Asked by Burr and Erdős. Frankl and Lin [Li76] independently showed that the answer is yes, and
the largest solution is
$$2^7=2!+3!+5!.$$
In fact Lin showed that the largest power of $2$ which can divide a sum of distinct factorials
containing $2$ is $2^{254}$, and that there are only 5 solutions to $3^m=a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$
(when $m=0,1,2,3,6$).

See also [404].

A solution is encoded below as a pair $(m, s)$ where $s$ is the finite set
$\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k\}$ of positive integers, so the distinctness of the $a_i$ is
given by set membership. The empty set contributes no solutions since $2^m \geq 1 > 0$.

The linked proof gives more than finiteness: it classifies the solutions outright, as
$(0,\{1\})$, $(1,\{2\})$, $(3,\{2,3\})$, $(5,\{2,3,4\})$ and $(7,\{2,3,5\})$, so the set below
has exactly five elements.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_403 :
    {p : ℕ × Finset ℕ | (∀ a ∈ p.2, 0 < a) ∧
      2 ^ p.1 = ∑ a ∈ p.2, a.factorial}.Finite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 405
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/405](https://www.erdosproblems.com/405)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980)
- [BrEr91] Brindza, B. and Erdős, P., On some {D}iophantine problems involving powers and
factorials. J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A (1991), 1--7.
- [YuLi96] Yu, Kunrui and Liu, Dehua, A complete resolution of a problem of {E}rdős and {G}raham.
Rocky Mountain J. Math. (1996), 1235--1244.

statements.name: Erdos405.erdos_405
statements.doc:
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Is it true that the equation $(p-1)!+a^{p-1}=p^k$ has only finitely many
solutions?

Originally proposed by Erdős and Graham [ErGr80].
Brindza and Erdős [BrEr91] proved that there are finitely many such solutions.

statements.name: Erdos405.erdos_405.variants.nonodd_p
statements.doc:
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] ask this allowing $p=2$, but this is presumably an oversight, since clearly
there are infinitely many solutions when $p=2$.

Observe that this creates $1! + a = 2^k$. For all $k$, fix $a = 2^k - 1$.

statements.name: Erdos405.erdos_405.variants.yu_liu
statements.doc:
Yu and Liu [YuLi96] showed that the only solutions to $(p-1)! + a^(p-1) = p^k$
for an odd prime p are:
$$
2! + 1^2 = 3\\
2! + 5^2 = 3^3\\
4! + 1^4 = 5^2
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_405.variants.yu_liu :
    { x : ℕ × ℕ × ℕ | let (a, k, p) := x; p.Prime ∧ Odd p ∧
      Nat.factorial (p - 1) + a ^ (p - 1) = p ^ k } =
    {(1, 1, 3), (5, 3, 3), (1, 2, 5)}

problems.title: Erdős Problem 406
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/406](https://www.erdosproblems.com/406)

statements.name: Erdos406.erdos_406
statements.doc:
Is it true that there are only finitely many powers of $2$ which have only the digits $0$
and $1$ when written in base $3$?
statements.statement: theorem erdos_406 : { n | n.isPowerOfTwo ∧ Nat.digits 3 n ⊆ [0, 1] }.Finite

statements.name: Erdos406.erdos_406.variants.one_two
statements.doc:
If we only allow the digits $1$ and $2$ then $2^{15}$ seems to be the largest such power
of $2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_406.variants.one_two :
    IsGreatest { n | n.isPowerOfTwo ∧ Nat.digits 3 n ⊆ [1, 2] } (2 ^ 15)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 407
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/407](https://www.erdosproblems.com/407)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [EGST88] Evertse, J.-H. and Győry, K. and Stewart, C. L. and Tijdeman, R., *$S$-unit equations
  and their applications*. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 110-174.
- [TiWa88] Tijdeman, R. and Wang, Lian Xiang, *Sums of products of powers of given prime
  numbers*. Pacific J. Math. (1988), 177-193.
- [BaBe24] Bajpai, Prajeet and Bennett, Michael A., *Effective $S$-unit equations beyond three
  terms: Newman's conjecture*. Acta Arith. (2024), 421-458.

statements.name: Erdos407.erdos_407
statements.doc:
Let $w(n)$ count the number of solutions to
$$n=2^a+3^b+2^c3^d$$
with $a,b,c,d\geq 0$ integers. Is it true that $w(n)$ is bounded by some absolute constant?

A conjecture originally due to Newman.

This is true, and was proved by Evertse, Győry, Stewart, and Tijdeman [EGST88].

Quantitative bounds were provided by Tijdeman and Wang [TiWa88], who proved that (if $w(n)$ only
counts distinct solutions, where we call two solutions distinct if the sets
$\{2^a,3^b,2^{c}3^d\}$ are distinct) then $w(n) \leq 4$ for all large $n$.

This was made effective by Bajpai and Bennett [BaBe24], who proved that $w(n)\leq 4$ if
$n\geq 131082$ and $w(n)\leq 9$ for all $n$. (The largest $n$ for which $w(n)=9$ is $299$.)
statements.statement: theorem erdos_407 : ∃ C : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, w n ≤ C

problems.title: Erdős Problem 408
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/408](https://www.erdosproblems.com/408)
- [OEIS A003434](https://oeis.org/A003434): the values $f(n)$ for $n \geq 2$.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
- [Pi29] Pillai, S. Sivasankaranarayana, *On a function connected with $\phi(n)$*. Bull. Amer.
  Math. Soc. 35 (1929), 837-841.
  [doi:10.1090/S0002-9904-1929-04800-6](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1929-04800-6)
- [Sh50] Shapiro, Harold N., *On the iterates of a certain class of arithmetic functions*. Comm.
  Pure Appl. Math. 3 (1950), 259-272.
- [EGPS90] Erdős, P., Granville, A., Pomerance, C. and Spiro, C., *On the normal behavior of the
  iterates of some arithmetic functions*. Analytic number theory (Allerton Park, IL, 1989),
  Progr. Math. 85 (1990), 165-204.
- [Gu04] Guy, Richard K., *Unsolved problems in number theory*. Third edition, Springer (2004),
  Problem B41.
- [FKL10] Ford, K., Konyagin, S. V. and Luca, F., *Prime chains and Pratt trees*. Geom. Funct.
  Anal. 20 (2010), 1231-1258. [arXiv:0904.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/0904.0473)
  [doi:10.1007/s00039-010-0089-0](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-010-0089-0)

statements.name: Erdos408.erdos_408.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $\phi(n)$ be the Euler totient function and $\phi_k(n)$ be the iterated $\phi$ function, so
that $\phi_1(n)=\phi(n)$ and $\phi_k(n)=\phi(\phi_{k-1}(n))$. Let
$$f(n) = \min\{k : \phi_k(n)=1\}.$$
Does $f(n)/\log n$ have a distribution function?

We ask for a distribution function $F$ (non-decreasing, with $F(-\infty) = 0$ and
$F(+\infty) = 1$) such that, for every continuity point $c$ of $F$, the set
$\{n : f(n)/\log n \leq c\}$ has natural density $F(c)$. For $n \leq 1$ the quotient is $0$ in
Lean, which does not affect densities. Erdős, Granville, Pomerance and Spiro [EGPS90] proved
that the answer is yes, conditional on a form of the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_408.parts.i :
    ∃ F : ℝ → ℝ, Monotone F ∧ Tendsto F atBot (𝓝 0) ∧ Tendsto F atTop (𝓝 1) ∧
      ∀ c : ℝ, ContinuousAt F c →
        {n : ℕ | (f n : ℝ) / Real.log n ≤ c}.HasDensity (F c)

statements.name: Erdos408.erdos_408.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Is $f(n)/\log n$ almost always constant?

We read this as: is there a constant $\alpha$ such that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, the set of
$n$ with $|f(n)/\log n - \alpha| < \epsilon$ has natural density $1$? Erdős, Granville,
Pomerance and Spiro [EGPS90] proved that, conditional on a form of the Elliott–Halberstam
conjecture, $f(n)$ has normal order $\alpha \log n$ for some constant $\alpha > 0$, so that the
answer is yes under this hypothesis.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_408.parts.ii :
    ∃ α : ℝ, ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ),
      {n : ℕ | |(f n : ℝ) / Real.log n - α| < ε}.HasDensity 1

statements.name: Erdos408.erdos_408.variants.pillai
statements.doc:
Pillai [Pi29] proved that, for all $n \geq 2$,
$$\left\lfloor \frac{\log n - \log 2}{\log 3} \right\rfloor + 1 \leq f(n) \leq
  \left\lfloor \frac{\log n}{\log 2} \right\rfloor + 1.$$
These are Theorems I and III of [Pi29]; Pillai's function $R(n)$ is the least $r$ with
$\phi_r(n) = 1$, which is $f(n)$. The lower bound is attained at $n = 2 \cdot 3^k$, and
$f(2^k) = k$ (`Erdos408.f_two_pow`), so the upper bound cannot be replaced by $f(n) < \log_2 n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_408.variants.pillai (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    ⌊(Real.log n - Real.log 2) / Real.log 3⌋₊ + 1 ≤ f n ∧
      f n ≤ ⌊Real.log n / Real.log 2⌋₊ + 1

statements.name: Erdos408.erdos_408.variants.ford_konyagin_luca
statements.doc:
The third question asks what can be said about the largest prime factor $P^+(\phi_k(n))$ when,
say, $k = \log\log n$; it is open-ended and is not formalised. The site remarks that it is likely
true that, if $k \to \infty$ however slowly with $n$, then $P^+(\phi_k(n)) \leq n^{o(1)}$ for
almost all $n$.

Ford, Konyagin and Luca [FKL10, Theorem 5] proved that for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $\delta > 0$
there is an integer $k$ such that, for all large $x$, at least $(1 - \epsilon)x$ integers
$n \leq x$ satisfy $P^+(\phi_k(n)) \leq x^{\delta}$. Since $P^+(\phi(m)) \leq P^+(m)$, this gives
the remark above for every $k = k(n) \to \infty$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_408.variants.ford_konyagin_luca (ε δ : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) (hδ : 0 < δ) :
    ∃ k : ℕ, ∀ᶠ x : ℝ in atTop, (1 - ε) * x ≤
      ((Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊).filter fun n ↦
        ((Nat.totient^[k] n).maxPrimeFac : ℝ) ≤ x ^ δ).card

problems.title: Erdős Problem 409
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/409](https://www.erdosproblems.com/409)

statements.name: Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i
statements.doc: How many iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ are needed before a prime is reached?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_409.parts.i (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) :
    IsLeast { i | (φ · + 1)^[i] n |>.Prime } erdos_409.parts.i.answer

statements.name: Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i.isTheta

    (h : ∀ n > 0, IsLeast { i | (φ · + 1)^[i] n |>.Prime } (c n)) :

Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ before a prime

statements.name: Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i.isLittleO
statements.doc:
Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ before a prime
is reached. Find the simplest function $g(n)$ such that $c(n) = o(g(n))$?
statements.statement:
