- [erdosproblems.com/621](https://www.erdosproblems.com/621)
- [EGT96] Erdős, Paul and Gallai, Tibor and Tuza, Zsolt, *Covering and independence in triangle
  structures*. Discrete Math. (1996), 89-101.
- [Er99] Erdős, Paul, *A selection of problems and results in combinatorics*.
  Combin. Probab. Comput. (1999), 1-6.
- [NoSu16] S. Norin and Y.-R. Sun, *Triangle-free independent sets vs. cuts*. arXiv:1602.04370
  (2016).

statements.name: Erdos621.erdos_621
statements.doc:
Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices, $\alpha_1(G)$ be the maximum number of edges that contain
at most one edge from every triangle, and $\tau_1(G)$ be the minimum number of edges that
contain at least one edge from every triangle.

Is it true that$$\alpha_1(G)+\tau_1(G) \leq \frac{n^2}{4}?$$

A problem of Erdős, Gallai, and Tuza [EGT96], who observe that this is probably quite difficult
since there are different examples where equality hold: the complete graph, the complete
bipartite graph, and the graph obtained from $K_{m,m}$ by adding one vertex joined to every
other.

This is true, and was proved by Norin and Sun [NoSu16], who in fact proved
that$$\alpha_1(G)+\tau_B(G) \leq \frac{n^2}{4},$$where $\tau_B(G)$ is the minimum number of
edges that need to be removed to make the graph bipartite.

Here $\alpha_1(G)$ and $\tau_1(G)$ are taken over subsets of the edge set of $G$, and the
inequality is stated multiplied through by $4$ so that it lives in the natural numbers.

The linked file states $\tau_1$ as the least number of edges whose deletion leaves $G$
triangle-free, which is the same as meeting every triangle of $G$, and quantifies over an
arbitrary `Fintype V` rather than `Fin n`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_621 :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (a t : ℕ),
      IsGreatest {k : ℕ | ∃ A ⊆ G.edgeFinset, A.card = k ∧
        ∀ x y z : Fin n, G.Adj x y → G.Adj y z → G.Adj x z →
          (({s(x, y), s(y, z), s(x, z)} : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n))) ∩ A).card ≤ 1} a →
      IsLeast {k : ℕ | ∃ T ⊆ G.edgeFinset, T.card = k ∧
        ∀ x y z : Fin n, G.Adj x y → G.Adj y z → G.Adj x z →
          (T ∩ ({s(x, y), s(y, z), s(x, z)} : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)))).Nonempty} t →
      4 * (a + t) ≤ n ^ 2

problems.title: Erdős Problem 623
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/623](https://www.erdosproblems.com/623)

statements.name: Erdos623.erdos_623
statements.doc:
Let $X$ be a set of cardinality $\aleph_\omega$ and $f$ be a function from the finite subsets of
$X$ to $X$ such that $f(A)\not\in A$ for all $A$. Must there exist an infinite $Y\subseteq X$
that is independent - that is, for all finite $B\subset Y$ we have $f(B)\not\in Y$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_623 : ∀ (X : Type u) (hX : #X = ℵ_ ω)
    (f : Finset X → X), (∀ A : Finset X, f A ∉ A) →
    (∃ Y : Set X, Set.Infinite Y ∧ (∀ (B : Finset X), ↑B ⊆ Y → f B ∉ Y))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 624
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/624](https://www.erdosproblems.com/624)

statements.name: Erdos624.erdos_624
statements.doc:
Let $X$ be a finite set of size $n$ and $H(n)$ be such that there is a function
$f:\{A : A\subseteq X\}\to X$ so that for every $Y\subseteq X$ with $\lvert Y\rvert \geq H(n)$
we have $\left\{ f(A) : A\subseteq Y\right\}=X$.
Prove that $H(n)-\log_2 n \to \infty$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_624 :
    atTop.Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => H n - Real.logb 2 (n : ℝ)) atTop

problems.title: Erdős Problem 626
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/626](https://www.erdosproblems.com/626)
- [Er59b] Erdős, P., *Graph theory and probability*. Canadian J. Math. (1959), 34-38.
- [Er62b] Erdős, P., *On circuits and subgraphs of chromatic graphs*. Mathematika (1962),
  170-175.
- [Er69b] Erdős, P., *Problems and results in chromatic graph theory*. Proof Techniques in Graph
  Theory (Proc. Second Ann Arbor Graph Theory Conf., Ann Arbor, Mich., 1968) (1969), 27-35.
- [Ko88] Kostochka, A. V., *Upper bounds on the chromatic number of graphs*. Trudy Inst. Mat.
  (Novosibirsk) (1988), 204-226, 265.

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $k \geq 4$ and let $g_k(n)$ denote the largest $m$ such that there is a graph on $n$
vertices with chromatic number $k$ and girth $> m$ (i.e. containing no cycle of length
$\leq m$). Does
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{g_k(n)}{\log n}$$
exist?

By `Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.kostochka` and `Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.erdos_upper`, the
limit, if it exists, is a positive real number.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.parts.i :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 4 ≤ k → ∃ L : ℝ,
      Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ (g k n : ℝ) / Real.log n) atTop (𝓝 L)

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.kostochka
statements.doc:
Kostochka [Ko88] proved that for $k \geq 4$
$$g_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{4\log k}\log n.$$
Kostochka's theorem gives this lower bound for the girth itself, and $g_k(n)$ is one less than the
largest possible girth, so the inequality above holds only up to $1$. The statement below is a
consequence of his theorem, not the theorem itself: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and all
sufficiently large $n$, $g_k(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{4\log k} - \varepsilon\right)\log n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.variants.kostochka :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 4 ≤ k → ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (1 / (4 * Real.log k) - ε) * Real.log n ≤ (g k n : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.erdos_upper
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er59b] proved that for $k \geq 4$
$$g_k(n) \leq \frac{2}{\log(k-2)}\log n + 1.$$
We state it for all sufficiently large $n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.variants.erdos_upper :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 4 ≤ k → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (g k n : ℝ) ≤ 2 * Real.log n / Real.log ((k : ℝ) - 2) + 1

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $h^{(m)}(n)$ be the maximal chromatic number of a graph on $n$ vertices with girth $> m$.
Does
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n}$$
exist, and what is its value? The value is asked for in
`Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_odd_conjecture` and `Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_even_conjecture`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.parts.ii :
    ∀ m : ℕ, ∃ L : ℝ,
      Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ Real.log (h m n : ℝ) / Real.log n) atTop (𝓝 L)

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_lower
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er59b] proved that
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n} \gg \frac{1}{m}.$$
The existence of the limit is open, so we state the lower bound for the lower limit: there is
an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that for every $m \geq 1$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, eventually
$h^{(m)}(n) \geq n^{c/m - \varepsilon}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.variants.h_lower :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ m : ℕ, 1 ≤ m → ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (n : ℝ) ^ (c / (m : ℝ) - ε) ≤ (h m n : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_upper_odd
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er59b] proved that for odd $m$
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n} \leq \frac{2}{m+1}.$$
The existence of the limit is open, so we state the bound for the upper limit: for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, eventually $h^{(m)}(n) \leq n^{2/(m+1) + \varepsilon}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.variants.h_upper_odd :
    ∀ m : ℕ, Odd m → ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (h m n : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) ^ (2 / ((m : ℝ) + 1) + ε)

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_odd_conjecture
statements.doc:
Erdős conjectured that the bound in `Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_upper_odd` is sharp: for
odd $m$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n} = \frac{2}{m+1}.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.variants.h_odd_conjecture :
    ∀ m : ℕ, Odd m → Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ Real.log (h m n : ℝ) / Real.log n) atTop
      (𝓝 (2 / ((m : ℝ) + 1)))

statements.name: Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_even_conjecture
statements.doc:
For even $m$, Erdős had no good guess for the value of the limit, other than that it should
lie in $\left[\frac{2}{m+2}, \frac{2}{m}\right]$. He could not prove this even for $m = 4$.

The existence of the limit is open, so we state the claim for the lower and upper limits: for
every $\varepsilon > 0$, eventually
$n^{2/(m+2) - \varepsilon} \leq h^{(m)}(n) \leq n^{2/m + \varepsilon}$. We require $m \geq 2$,
since $2/m$ is undefined for $m = 0$. The upper half is known: girth $> m$ implies girth
$> m - 1$, so $h^{(m)}(n) \leq h^{(m-1)}(n)$, and `Erdos626.erdos_626.variants.h_upper_odd` for
the odd number $m - 1$ gives the exponent $2/m$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_626.variants.h_even_conjecture :
    ∀ m : ℕ, Even m → 2 ≤ m → ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (n : ℝ) ^ (2 / ((m : ℝ) + 2) - ε) ≤ (h m n : ℝ) ∧
        (h m n : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) ^ (2 / (m : ℝ) + ε)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 627
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/627](https://www.erdosproblems.com/627)
- [AFM25] Araujo, I. and Filipe, R. and Miyazaki, R., *A note on the maximum ratio between
  chromatic number and clique number*. arXiv:2512.16062 (2025).
- [Er61d] Erdős, P., *Graph theory and probability. II*. Canadian J. Math. (1961), 346-352.
- [Er67c] Erdős, P., *Some remarks on chromatic graphs*. Colloq. Math. (1967), 253-256.
- [Er69b] Erdős, P., *Problems and results in chromatic graph theory*. Proof Techniques in Graph
  Theory (Proc. Second Ann Arbor Graph Theory Conf., Ann Arbor, Mich., 1968) (1969), 27-35.
- [My55] Mycielski, J., *Sur le coloriage des graphs*. Colloquium Mathematicum 3 (1955), 161–162.
  [doi:10.4064/cm-3-2-161-162](https://doi.org/10.4064/cm-3-2-161-162)
- [Zy52] Zykov, A. A., *On some properties of linear complexes*. Amer. Math. Soc. Translation
  (1952), 33.

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627
statements.doc:
Let $\omega(G)$ denote the clique number of $G$ and $\chi(G)$ the chromatic number. If $f(n)$ is
the maximum value of $\chi(G)/\omega(G)$, as $G$ ranges over all graphs on $n$ vertices, then
does
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{n/(\log_2n)^2}$$
exist?

Since $f(n) \asymp n/(\log_2 n)^2$ (see `Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.theta`), the limit, if it
exists, is a finite real number.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627 :
    ∃ L : ℝ, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ maxChromaticCliqueRatio n / ((n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2))
      atTop (𝓝 L)

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.theta
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er67c] proved that
$$f(n) \asymp \frac{n}{(\log_2 n)^2}.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.theta :
    (fun n : ℕ ↦ maxChromaticCliqueRatio n) =Θ[atTop]
      (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2)

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.lower
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er67c] proved the lower bound
$$f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{4} + o(1)\right) \frac{n}{(\log_2 n)^2}.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.lower :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (1 / 4 - ε) * ((n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2) ≤ maxChromaticCliqueRatio n

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.upper
statements.doc:
The method of Erdős [Er67c] gives the upper bound
$$f(n) \leq (4 + o(1)) \frac{n}{(\log_2 n)^2}.$$
Erdős states the constant as $1$, but Araujo, Filipe, and Miyazaki [AFM25] note that his method
gives $4$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.upper :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      maxChromaticCliqueRatio n ≤ (4 + ε) * ((n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2)

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.limit_bounds
statements.doc:
Consequently, if the limit in `Erdos627.erdos_627` exists, it lies in $[1/4, 4]$ [Er67c]
(with the correction of the upper constant from $1$ to $4$ noted in [AFM25]).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.limit_bounds :
    ∀ L : ℝ, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ maxChromaticCliqueRatio n / ((n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2))
      atTop (𝓝 L) → 1 / 4 ≤ L ∧ L ≤ 4

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.afm_upper
statements.doc:
Araujo, Filipe, and Miyazaki [AFM25, Theorem 1.3] improved the upper bound to
$$f(n) \leq (3.71943 + o(1)) \frac{n}{(\log_2 n)^2},$$
using recent improvements in the asymptotics of Ramsey numbers. [AFM25] is an arXiv preprint.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.afm_upper :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      maxChromaticCliqueRatio n ≤ (3.71943 + ε) * ((n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2)

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.conditional
statements.doc:
Araujo, Filipe, and Miyazaki [AFM25, Theorem 1.2]: suppose that $R(s,t) \leq R(k)$ for all
$s, t, k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $st \leq k^2$ (their Conjecture 1.1), and that
$\lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{\log_2 R(k)}{k}$ exists and equals $\ell$. Then
$$f(n) = (\ell^2 + o(1)) \frac{n}{(\log_2 n)^2},$$
so the limit in `Erdos627.erdos_627` exists and equals $\ell^2$. Here $R(s,t)$ is the
two-colour Ramsey number and $R(k) = R(k,k)$ (see [77]). [AFM25] is an arXiv preprint.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.conditional (ℓ : ℝ)
    (hR : ∀ s t k : ℕ, s * t ≤ k ^ 2 → classicalRamsey s t ≤ diagonalRamsey k)
    (hlim : Tendsto (fun k : ℕ ↦ Real.logb 2 (diagonalRamsey k : ℝ) / (k : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 ℓ)) :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ maxChromaticCliqueRatio n / ((n : ℝ) / Real.logb 2 n ^ 2))
      atTop (𝓝 (ℓ ^ 2))

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.tutte_zykov
statements.doc:
Tutte and Zykov [Zy52] independently proved that for every $k$ there is a graph with
$\omega(G) = 2$ and $\chi(G) = k$.

We require $k \geq 2$: a graph with $\omega(G) = 2$ has an edge, so $\chi(G) \geq 2$.
The proof here uses Mycielski's construction [My55].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.tutte_zykov :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → ∃ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)),
      G.cliqueNum = 2 ∧ G.chromaticNumber = (k : ℕ∞)

statements.name: Erdos627.erdos_627.variants.erdos_1961
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er61d] proved that for every (large) $n$ there is a graph on $n$ vertices with
$\omega(G) = 2$ and
$$\chi(G) \gg \frac{n^{1/2}}{\log n},$$
whence $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}/\log n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_627.variants.erdos_1961 :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∃ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      G.cliqueNum = 2 ∧
        c * Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) / Real.log (n : ℝ) ≤ (G.chromaticNumber.toNat : ℝ)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 628
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/628](https://www.erdosproblems.com/628)
- [BKPS09] Balogh, József and Kostochka, Alexandr V. and Prince, Noah and Stiebitz, Michael,
  *The Erdős-Lovász Tihany conjecture for quasi-line graphs*. Discrete Math. (2009), 3985-3991.
- [BrJu69] Brown, W. G. and Jung, H. A., *On odd circuits in chromatic graphs*. Acta Math. Acad.
  Sci. Hungar. (1969), 129-134.
- [Er68b] Erdős, P., *Problem 2*. Theory of Graphs (1968), 361.
- [So22] Song, Zi-Xia, *A survey on the Erdős-Lovász Tihany conjecture*. Adv. Math. (China)
  (2022), 259--274.

statements.name: Erdos628.erdos_628
statements.doc:
Let $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $k$ containing no $K_k$. If $a,b\geq 2$ and $a+b=k+1$
then must there exist two disjoint subgraphs of $G$ with chromatic numbers $\geq a$ and $\geq b$
respectively?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_628 (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ)
    (hG_chrom : G.chromaticNumber = (k : ℕ∞))
    (hG_clique : G.CliqueFree k)
    (a b : ℕ) (ha : a ≥ 2) (hb : b ≥ 2) (hab : a + b = k + 1) :
    ∃ (s : Set V),
      (G.induce s).chromaticNumber ≥ (a : ℕ∞) ∧
      (G.induce sᶜ).chromaticNumber ≥ (b : ℕ∞)

statements.name: Erdos628.erdos_628.variants.k_5_a_3_b_3
statements.doc: Erdős [Er68b] originally asked about $a=b=3$ which was proved by Brown and Jung [BrJu69] (who in fact prove that $G$ must contain two vertex disjoint odd cycles)..
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_628.variants.k_5_a_3_b_3 (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG_chrom : G.chromaticNumber = (5 : ℕ∞))
    (hG_clique : G.CliqueFree 5) :
    ∃ (s : Set V),
      (G.induce s).chromaticNumber ≥ (3 : ℕ∞) ∧
      (G.induce sᶜ).chromaticNumber ≥ (3 : ℕ∞)

statements.name: Erdos628.erdos_628.variants.quasi_line
statements.doc: Balogh, Kostochka, Prince, and Stiebitz [BKPS09] proved the conjecture for quasi-line graphs.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_628.variants.quasi_line (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG_quasi : IsQuasiLineGraph G)
    (k : ℕ)
    (hG_chrom : G.chromaticNumber = (k : ℕ∞))
    (hG_clique : G.CliqueFree k)
    (a b : ℕ) (ha : a ≥ 2) (hb : b ≥ 2) (hab : a + b = k + 1) :
    ∃ (s : Set V),
      (G.induce s).chromaticNumber ≥ (a : ℕ∞) ∧
      (G.induce sᶜ).chromaticNumber ≥ (b : ℕ∞)

statements.name: Erdos628.erdos_628.variants.independence_number_2
statements.doc: Balogh, Kostochka, Prince, and Stiebitz [BKPS09] proved the conjecture for graphs with independence number 2.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_628.variants.independence_number_2 (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG_indep : G.indepNum = 2)
    (k : ℕ)
    (hG_chrom : G.chromaticNumber = (k : ℕ∞))
    (hG_clique : G.CliqueFree k)
    (a b : ℕ) (ha : a ≥ 2) (hb : b ≥ 2) (hab : a + b = k + 1) :
    ∃ (s : Set V),
      (G.induce s).chromaticNumber ≥ (a : ℕ∞) ∧
      (G.induce sᶜ).chromaticNumber ≥ (b : ℕ∞)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 629
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/629](https://www.erdosproblems.com/629)
- [ERT80] Erdős, Paul and Rubin, Arthur L. and Taylor, Herbert, *Choosability in graphs*.
  Proceedings of the West Coast Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing (1979),
  Congress. Numer. XXVI (1980), 125-157. [PDF](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-07.pdf)
- [HMT96] Hanson, Denis and MacGillivray, Gary and Toft, Bjarne, *Choosability of bipartite
  graphs*. Ars Combin. (1996), 183-192.
- [RaSr00] Radhakrishnan, Jaikumar and Srinivasan, Aravind, *Improved bounds and algorithms for
  hypergraph $2$-coloring*. Random Structures Algorithms (2000), 4-32.

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629
statements.doc:
The list chromatic number $\chi_L(G)$ is defined to be the minimal $k$ such that for any
assignment of a list of $k$ colours to each vertex of $G$ (perhaps different lists for different
vertices) a colouring of each vertex by a colour on its list can be chosen such that adjacent
vertices receive distinct colours.

Determine the minimal number of vertices $n(k)$ of a bipartite graph $G$ such that
$\chi_L(G)>k$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_629 : n = erdos_629.answer

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629.variants.ert_bounds
statements.doc:
A problem of Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor [ERT80], who proved that
$$2^{k-1}<n(k) <k^22^{k+2}.$$

The chain of inequalities in [ERT80, p. 129] needs $k \geq 2$, since $m(1) = 1 = 2^0$; for
$k = 1$ the claim holds because $n(1) = 2$. The case $k = 0$ is degenerate ($n(0) = 1$).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_629.variants.ert_bounds (k : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k) :
    2 ^ (k - 1) < n k ∧ n k < k ^ 2 * 2 ^ (k + 2)

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629.variants.property_b
statements.doc:
They also prove that if $m(k)$ is the size of the smallest family of $k$-sets without property B
(i.e. the smallest number of $k$-sets in a graph with chromatic number $3$) then
$m(k)\leq n(k)\leq m(k+1)$.

[ERT80, p. 129] prints the upper bound as $2m(k)$; we state that form. Here $m(k)$ is
`Hypergraph.minChromaticEdges k 3`, as in Erdős Problem 901. We assume $k \geq 2$: for $k = 1$
this is `⊤`, since singleton edges admit no proper colouring, whereas $m(1) = 1$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_629.variants.property_b (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) :
    (Hypergraph.minChromaticEdges k 3).toNat ≤ n k ∧
      n k ≤ 2 * (Hypergraph.minChromaticEdges k 3).toNat

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629.variants.radhakrishnan_srinivasan
statements.doc:
The lower bounds on $m(k)$ by Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan [RaSr00] imply that
$$2^k \left(\frac{k}{\log k}\right)^{1/2}\ll n(k).$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_629.variants.radhakrishnan_srinivasan :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop,
      c * 2 ^ k * Real.sqrt (k / Real.log k) ≤ (n k : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629.variants.n_two
statements.doc: Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor [ERT80] proved $n(2)=6$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_629.variants.n_two : n 2 = 6

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629.variants.n_three
statements.doc: Hanson, MacGillivray, and Toft [HMT96] proved $n(3)=14$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_629.variants.n_three : n 3 = 14

statements.name: Erdos629.erdos_629.variants.hmt_recursion
statements.doc:
Hanson, MacGillivray, and Toft [HMT96] proved
$$n(k) \leq kn(k-2)+2^k.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_629.variants.hmt_recursion (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) :
    n k ≤ k * n (k - 2) + 2 ^ k

problems.title: Erdős Problem 633
problems.doc:
*Reference:*
* [erdosproblems.com/633](https://www.erdosproblems.com/633)
* [So09] Soifer, Alexander, How Does One Cut a Triangle? I
* [So09c] Soifer, Alexander, Is there anything beyond the solution?
* [BLZ26] Beeson, Michael, Laczkovich, Miklós, and Zhang, Yan,
  [*Solution of Erdős problem 633*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03609).

statements.name: Erdos633.isCuttable_iff_isSquare_of_linearIndependent
statements.doc:
A triangle whose side lengths and angles are integrally independent is cuttable only into
a non-zero square number of congruent triangles. This is proved in [So09c].
statements.statement:
lemma isCuttable_iff_isSquare_of_linearIndependent
    (hTsides : LinearIndependent ℤ
      ![dist (T.points 0) (T.points 1),
        dist (T.points 1) (T.points 2),
        dist (T.points 2) (T.points 0)])
    (hTangles : LinearIndependent ℤ
      ![∠ (T.points 0) (T.points 1) (T.points 2),
        ∠ (T.points 1) (T.points 2) (T.points 0),
        ∠ (T.points 2) (T.points 0) (T.points 1)]) :
    IsCuttable n T ↔ n ≠ 0 ∧ IsSquare n

statements.name: Erdos633.erdos_633
statements.doc:
Which triangles can only be decomposed into a square number of congruent triangles?

Beeson, Laczkovich, and Zhang [BLZ26] classify the triangles that can be tiled only into a square
number of congruent triangles, settling this problem. The classification is too involved to encode
in the answer slot here, so the answer is left as `sorry` and the reference records the result.
statements.statement:
lemma erdos_633 : T ∈ erdos_633.answer ↔
    ∀ n, IsCuttable n T → IsSquare n

statements.name: Erdos633.IsSimiliCuttable.of_ne_zero_two_three_five
statements.doc:
Every triangle is simili-cuttable into any number of similar triangles, except 0, 2, 3, 5.
This is proved in [So09].
statements.statement:
lemma IsSimiliCuttable.of_ne_zero_two_three_five (hn₀ : n ≠ 0) (hn₂ : n ≠ 2) (hn₃ : n ≠ 3)
    (hn₅ : n ≠ 5) : IsSimiliCuttable n T

statements.name: Erdos633.exists_isSimiliCuttable_iff_ne_zero_two_three_five
statements.doc:
There exists a triangle which isn't simili-cuttable into 0, 2, 3, 5 parts.
This is proved in [So09].
statements.statement:
lemma exists_isSimiliCuttable_iff_ne_zero_two_three_five :
    ∃ T, ∀ n, IsSimiliCuttable n T ↔ n ≠ 0 ∧ n ≠ 2 ∧ n ≠ 3 ∧ n ≠ 5

problems.title: Erdős Problem 636
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/636](https://www.erdosproblems.com/636)
- [AlKo09] Alon, N. and Kostochka, A. V., *Induced subgraphs with distinct sizes*.
  Random Structures Algorithms 34 (2009), 45-53.
- [Er93] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favorite solved and unsolved problems in graph theory*.
  Quaestiones Math. (1993), 333-350.
- [Er97d] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent problems and results in graph theory*. Discrete Math. (1997),
  81-85.
- [KwSu21] Kwan, M. and Sudakov, B., *Proof of a conjecture on induced subgraphs of Ramsey graphs*.
  Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 372 (2019), 5571-5594.
  [arXiv:1712.05656](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.05656)

statements.name: Erdos636.erdos_636
statements.doc:
Suppose $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices which contains no complete graph or independent set on
$\gg \log n$ many vertices. Must $G$ contain $\gg n^{5/2}$ induced subgraphs which pairwise differ
in either the number of vertices or the number of edges?

A problem of Erdős, Faudree, and Sós (although in [Er93] Erdős credits this question to Alon and
Bollobás). This was proved by Kwan and Sudakov [KwSu21].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_636 :
    ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ γ > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      (G.cliqueNum : ℝ) < C * Real.log n → (G.indepNum : ℝ) < C * Real.log n →
        HasManyDistinctInducedSubgraphs G (γ * (n : ℝ) ^ (5 / 2 : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos636.erdos_636.variants.erdos_faudree_sos
statements.doc:
Erdős, Faudree, and Sós proved that there exist $\gg n^{3/2}$ many such subgraphs, as stated on
erdosproblems.com. Section 2 of [KwSu21] describes two short proofs of this weaker bound.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_636.variants.erdos_faudree_sos :
    ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ γ > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      (G.cliqueNum : ℝ) < C * Real.log n → (G.indepNum : ℝ) < C * Real.log n →
        HasManyDistinctInducedSubgraphs G (γ * (n : ℝ) ^ (3 / 2 : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos636.erdos_636.variants.best_possible
statements.doc:
Erdős, Faudree, and Sós note that the exponent $5/2$ would be best possible: there are graphs on
$n$ vertices with no complete graph or independent set on $\gg \log n$ many vertices which contain
only $O(n^{5/2})$ induced subgraphs that pairwise differ in either the number of vertices or the
number of edges. For example, the random graph $G(n, 1/2)$ has this property with high
probability. This is the remark following Theorem 1.1 in [KwSu21], where it is proved in sketch
form by a concentration inequality and a union bound; see also [AlKo09, Section 4].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_636.variants.best_possible :
    ∃ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ K : ℝ, ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∃ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      (G.cliqueNum : ℝ) < C * Real.log n ∧ (G.indepNum : ℝ) < C * Real.log n ∧
        ¬ HasManyDistinctInducedSubgraphs G (K * (n : ℝ) ^ (5 / 2 : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 639
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/639](https://www.erdosproblems.com/639)
- [Er97d] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent problems and results in graph theory*. Discrete Math.
  (1997), 81-85.
- [KeSu04] Keevash, Peter and Sudakov, Benny, *On the number of edges not covered by monochromatic
  copies of a fixed graph*. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (2004), 41-53.
- [Py86] Pyber, L., *Clique covering of graphs*. Combinatorica (1986), 393-398.

statements.name: Erdos639.erdos_639
statements.doc:
Is it true that if the edges of $K_n$ are 2-coloured then there are at most $n^2/4$ many edges
which do not occur in a monochromatic triangle?

Solved by Erdős, Rousseau, and Schelp for large $n$, but unpublished. Alon has observed that this
also follows from a result of Pyber [Py86], which states that (for large enough $n$) at most
$\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+2$ monochromatic cliques cover all edges of a $2$-coloured $K_n$.

This problem was solved completely by Keevash and Sudakov [KeSu04], who proved that the correct
threshold is $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ for all $n\geq 7$, is $\binom{n}{2}$ for $n\leq 5$, and is
$10$ for $n=6$.

Since the bound fails for small $n$ (at $n=6$ the threshold is $10 > 6^2/4$), the statement is
formalized in the asymptotic reading in which the problem was posed and solved: for all
sufficiently large $n$, every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ leaves at most $n^2/4$ edges
not occurring in a monochromatic triangle. Edges of $K_n$ are the non-diagonal unordered pairs
`Sym2 (Fin n)`; an edge $\{x, y\}$ occurs in a monochromatic triangle if and only if there is a
third vertex $z$ with $C(\{x, z\}) = C(\{y, z\}) = C(\{x, y\})$.

The linked file proves the bound for every finite vertex type with at least $10$ vertices, which
gives the `atTop` reading below, and collects the uncovered edges as the edge set of a graph
rather than as a set of pairs.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_639 :
    ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, ∀ C : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 2,
      {e : Sym2 (Fin n) | ¬e.IsDiag ∧
        ∀ x y : Fin n, e = s(x, y) →
          ¬∃ z, z ≠ x ∧ z ≠ y ∧ C s(x, z) = C e ∧ C s(y, z) = C e}.ncard ≤ n ^ 2 / 4

statements.name: Erdos639.erdos_639.variants.exact
statements.doc:
The exact maximum number of uncovered edges is $\binom{n}{2}$ for $n\leq 5$, $10$ for
$n=6$, and $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ for $n\geq 7$ [KeSu04, Theorem 1.1].
`IsGreatest` states both the upper bound and its attainment by a colouring.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_639.variants.exact :
    ∀ n : ℕ, IsGreatest
      (Set.range fun C : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 2 => (uncoveredEdges C).ncard)
      (if n ≤ 5 then n.choose 2 else if n = 6 then 10 else n ^ 2 / 4)

statements.name: Erdos639.erdos_639.variants.ten_le
statements.doc:
Every two-colouring of $K_n$ with $n\geq 10$ has at most
$\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ uncovered edges [KeSu04, Proposition 2.1].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_639.variants.ten_le :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 10 ≤ n → ∀ C : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 2,
      (uncoveredEdges C).ncard ≤ n ^ 2 / 4

statements.name: Erdos639.erdos_639.variants.six_vertices
statements.doc: There is a two-colouring of $K_6$ with ten uncovered edges, exceeding $6^2/4$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_639.variants.six_vertices :
    ∃ C : Sym2 (Fin 6) → Fin 2, (uncoveredEdges C).ncard = 10 ∧
      6 ^ 2 / 4 < (uncoveredEdges C).ncard

problems.title: Erdős Problem 640
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/640](https://www.erdosproblems.com/640)
- [Er97d] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent problems and results in graph theory*. Discrete Math.
  (1997), 81–85, p.84.

statements.name: Erdos640.erdos_640
statements.doc:
For every $k \geq 3$, does there exist $f(k)$ such that every finite graph of chromatic
number at least $f(k)$ has an odd cycle whose vertices induce a graph of chromatic
number at least $k$? The cycle may have chords in the ambient graph.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_640 :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      (N : ℕ∞) ≤ G.chromaticNumber → HasHighChromaticOddCycle G k

statements.name: Erdos640.erdos_640.variants.three
statements.doc:
Every finite graph of chromatic number at least $3$ has an odd cycle whose vertices
induce a graph of chromatic number at least $3$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_640.variants.three (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n))
    (hG : (3 : ℕ∞) ≤ G.chromaticNumber) : HasHighChromaticOddCycle G 3

problems.title: Erdős Problem 641
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/641](https://www.erdosproblems.com/641)
- [Er92b] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite problems in various branches of combinatorics*.
  Le Matematiche (1992), 231–240.
- [Er97d] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent problems and results in graph theory*.
  Discrete Math. (1997), 81–85, p.84.
- [JSS24] Janzer, Barnabás, Steiner, Raphael, and Sudakov, Benny,
  *Chromatic number and regular subgraphs*. arXiv:2410.02437 (2024).

statements.name: Erdos641.erdos_641
statements.doc:
Is there some function $f$ such that for all $k\geq 1$ if a finite graph $G$ has chromatic
number $\geq f(k)$ then $G$ has $k$ edge disjoint cycles on the same set of vertices?

A problem of Erdős and Hajnal. This was resolved in the negative by Janzer, Steiner,
and Sudakov [JSS24] - in fact, this fails even at $k=2$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_641 : ¬ ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, ErdosHajnalProperty f

problems.title: Erdős Problem 642
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/642](https://www.erdosproblems.com/642)
- [CES96] Chen, Guantao and Erdős, Paul and Staton, William, *Proof of a conjecture of Bollobás
  on nested cycles*. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1996), 38--43.
- [DMMS24] Draganić, Nemanja and Methuku, Abhishek and Munhá Correia, David and Sudakov,
  Benny, *Cycles with many chords*. Random Structures Algorithms (2024), 3--16.
- [Er97d] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent problems and results in graph theory*. Discrete Math.
  (1997), 81-85.

statements.name: Erdos642.erdos_642
statements.doc:
Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices such that all cycles have more
vertices than chords. Is it true that $f(n)\ll n$?

A problem of Hamburger and Szegedy. A chord is an edge between two vertices of the cycle which are
not consecutive in the cycle.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_642 :
    (fun n : ℕ => (maxEdges n : ℝ)) =O[atTop] (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos642.erdos_642.variants.upper_bound_n_pow_three_halves
statements.doc: Chen, Erdős, and Staton [CES96] proved $f(n) \ll n^{3/2}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_642.variants.upper_bound_n_pow_three_halves :
    (fun n : ℕ => (maxEdges n : ℝ)) =O[atTop] (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) ^ (3 / 2 : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos642.erdos_642.variants.upper_bound_n_log_pow_eight
statements.doc:
Draganić, Methuku, Munhá Correia, and Sudakov [DMMS24] have improved this to
$$f(n) \ll n(\log n)^8.$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_642.variants.upper_bound_n_log_pow_eight :
    (fun n : ℕ => (maxEdges n : ℝ)) =O[atTop] (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ) * Real.log n ^ 8)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 643
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/643](https://www.erdosproblems.com/643)
- [Fu84] F\"uredi, Z., Hypergraphs in which all disjoint pairs have distinct unions. Combinatorica
  (1984), 161--168.
- [PiVe09] Pikhurko, Oleg and Verstra\"{e}te, Jacques, The maximum size of hypergraphs without
  generalized 4-cycles. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A (2009), 637--649.
- [HMY26] Huang, Hao, Ma, Jie, and Yang, Tianchi, *Extremal hypergraphs without generalized
  4-cycles*. [arXiv:2609.37744](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37744) (2026), Theorem 1.2.

statements.name: Erdos643.erdos_643.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $f(n;t)$ be minimal such that if a $t$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices contains at least
$f(n;t)$ edges then there must be four edges $A,B,C,D$ such that
$$A\cup B= C\cup D$$
and
$$A\cap B=C\cap D=\emptyset.$$
Estimate $f(n;t)$ - in particular, is it true that for $t\geq 3$
$$f(n;t)=(1+o(1))\binom{n}{t-1}?$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_643.parts.i :
    ∀ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t →
      (fun n ↦ (forcingThreshold n t : ℝ)) ~[atTop] erdos_643.parts.i.answer t

statements.name: Erdos643.erdos_643.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Is it true that $f(n;t)=(1+o(1))\binom{n}{t-1}$ for $t\geq 3$?

For $t\geq4$, Huang, Ma, and Yang [HMY26] prove the exact extremal formula below.
The case $t=3$ remains open.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_643.parts.ii :
    ∀ t : ℕ, 3 ≤ t →
    (fun n ↦ (forcingThreshold n t : ℝ)) ~[atTop]
        (fun n ↦ (n.choose (t - 1) : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos643.erdos_643.variants.exact_t_ge_four
statements.doc:
Huang, Ma, and Yang [HMY26, Theorem 1.2] determine the maximum size of an avoiding family
for each fixed $t\geq4$ and all sufficiently large $n$:
$$\binom{n-1}{t-1}+\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{t}\right\rfloor.$$
The forcing threshold is one larger.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_643.variants.exact_t_ge_four :
    ∀ t : ℕ, 4 ≤ t → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      Hypergraph.extremalNumber n t (fun H ↦ ¬ H.HasRepeatedDisjointUnion) =
        (n - 1).choose (t - 1) + (n - 1) / t

problems.title: Erdős Problem 644
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/644](https://www.erdosproblems.com/644)
- [EFKT92] Erdős, P. and Fon-Der-Flaass, D. and Kostochka, A. V. and Tuza, Zs., Small transversals in
  uniform hypergraphs. Siberian Adv. Math. (1992), 82-88.

statements.name: Erdos644.erdos_644.variants.elementary_upper_bound
statements.doc: For $r \geq 3$, the transversal bound satisfies $f(k,r) \leq 2k$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_644.variants.elementary_upper_bound (k r : ℕ) (hr : 3 ≤ r) :
    Hypergraph.subfamilyTransversalBound k r 2 ≤ ((2 * k : ℕ) : ℕ∞)

statements.name: Erdos644.erdos_644.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $f(k,r)$ be minimal such that if $A_1,A_2,\ldots$ is a family of sets, all of size $k$, such
that for every collection of $r$ of the $A_is$ there is some pair $\{x,y\}$ which intersects all of
the $A_j$, then there is some set of size $f(k,r)$ which intersects all of the sets $A_i$. Is it
true that
$$f(k,7)=(1+o(1))\frac{3}{4}k?$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_644.parts.i :
    (fun k ↦ ((Hypergraph.subfamilyTransversalBound k 7 2).toNat : ℝ)) ~[atTop]
      (fun k ↦ (3 / 4 : ℝ) * k)

statements.name: Erdos644.erdos_644.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Is it true that for any $r\geq 3$ there exists some constant $c_r$ such that
$$f(k,r)=(1+o(1))c_rk?$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_644.parts.ii :
    ∀ r : ℕ, 3 ≤ r → ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧
    (fun k ↦ ((Hypergraph.subfamilyTransversalBound k r 2).toNat : ℝ)) ~[atTop]
      (fun k ↦ c * k)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 645
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/645](https://www.erdosproblems.com/645)
- [BrLa99] Brown, Tom C. and Landman, Bruce M., Monochromatic arithmetic progressions with large
  differences. Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. (1999), 21--35.

statements.name: Erdos645.erdos_645
statements.doc:
If ℕ is $2$-coloured then there must exist a monochromatic three-term arithmetic progression
$x,x+d,x+2d$ such that $d>x$.

This was first proved by Brown and Landman [BrLa99], who in fact show that this is always possible
with $d>f(x)$ for any increasing function $f$.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_645 (c : ℕ → Bool) : ∃ x d, 0 < x ∧ x < d ∧
    (∃ C, c x = C ∧ c (x + d) = C ∧ c (x + 2 * d) = C)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 646
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/646](https://www.erdosproblems.com/646)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [Be97] Berend, Daniel, *On the parity of exponents in the factorization of $n!$*.
  J. Number Theory (1997), 13-19.

statements.name: Erdos646.erdos_646
statements.doc:
Let $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ be distinct primes. Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n!$ is
divisible by an even power of each of the $p_i$?

The answer is yes, proved by Berend [Be97], who further proved that the sequence of such $n$
has bounded gaps (where the bound depends on the initial set of primes).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_646 :
    ∀ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ S, p.Prime) →
      {n : ℕ | ∀ p ∈ S, Even (padicValNat p (n !))}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 647
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/647](https://www.erdosproblems.com/647)

statements.name: Erdos647.erdos_647
statements.doc:
Let $\tau(n)$ count the number of divisors of $n$. Is there some $n > 24$ such that
$$
  \max_{m < n}(m + \tau(m)) \leq n + 2?
$$
statements.statement: theorem erdos_647 : ∃ n > 24, ⨆ m : Fin n, m + σ 0 m ≤ n + 2

statements.name: Erdos647.erdos_647.variants.twenty_four
statements.doc: This is true for $n = 24$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_647.variants.twenty_four : ⨆ m : Fin 24, (m : ℕ) + σ 0 m ≤ 26

statements.name: Erdos647.erdos_647.variants.lim
statements.doc:
Erdős says 'it is extremely doubtful' that there are infinitely many such $n$, and in
fact suggests that
$$
  lim_{n\to\infty} \max_{m < n}(\tau(m) + m − n) = \infty.
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_647.variants.lim :
    atTop.Tendsto (fun n ↦ ⨆ m : Fin n, σ 0 m + m - n) atTop

statements.name: Erdos647.erdos_647.variants.infinite
statements.doc:
Erdős says it 'seems certain' that for every $k$ there are infinitely many $n$
for which
$$
  \max_{n−k < m < n}(m + \tau(m)) ≤ n + 2.
$$
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_647.variants.infinite :
    ∀ k, { n | ⨆ m : Set.Ioo (n - k) n, ↑m + σ 0 m ≤ n + 2 }.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 648
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/648](https://www.erdosproblems.com/648)
- [Er95c] Erdős, Paul, *Some problems in number theory*. Octogon Math. Mag. (1995), 3-5.
- [Ca25b] S. Cambie, *On Erdős problem #648*. arXiv:2503.22691 (2025).

statements.name: Erdos648.erdos_648
statements.doc:
Let $g(n)$ denote the largest $t$ such that there exist integers $2\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots <a_t <n$
such that $$P(a_1)>P(a_2)>\cdots >P(a_t)$$ where $P(m)$ is the greatest prime factor of $m$.
Estimate $g(n)$.

Stijn Cambie has proved [Ca25b] $$g(n) \asymp \left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/2}.$$
Cambie further asks whether there exists a constant $c$ such that
$$g(n) \sim c \left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/2}.$$
Cambie's proof shows that such a $c$ must satisfy $2\leq c\leq 2\sqrt{2}$.

The sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_t$ is packaged as a strictly monotone map `a : Fin t → ℕ`
with $2\leq a_i<n$, the greatest prime factor $P$ is `Nat.maxPrimeFac`, and $g(n)$ is the
supremum in `ℕ` of the achievable lengths $t$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_648 :
    (fun n => (g n : ℝ)) =Θ[atTop] fun n => Real.sqrt ((n : ℝ) / Real.log (n : ℝ))

problems.title: Erdős Problem 649
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/649](https://www.erdosproblems.com/649)
- [Ma35] Mahler, Kurt, *Über den grössten Primteiler spezieller Polynome zweiten Grades*. Archiv
  für math. og naturvid (1935).
- [Ro64b] Rotkiewicz, André, *Sur les nombres naturels $n$ et $k$ tels que les nombres $n$ et $nk$
  sont à la fois pseudopremiers*. Atti Accad. Naz. Lincei Rend. Cl. Sci. Fis. Mat. Nat. (8)
  (1964), 816-818.

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649
statements.doc:
Let $P(m)$ denote the greatest prime factor of $m$. Is it true that, for any two primes $p,q$,
there exists some integer $n$ such that $P(n)=p$ and $P(n+1)=q$?

In fact, the answer to this question as written is easily seen to be no, since there are no
solutions to $2^k\equiv -1\pmod{7}$, and hence this fails with $p=2$ and $q=7$. It is possible
that Erdős meant to exclude such obstructions, by amending this to 'odd primes' or 'all
sufficiently large primes' or such.

The statement below assumes $p \neq q$: for $p = q$ no such $n$ exists, because $p$ would divide
both $n$ and $n+1$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649 :
    ¬ ∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime → p ≠ q →
      ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649.variants.finite
statements.doc:
The number of solutions is finite for any fixed $p,q$ since the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$
tends to $\infty$ (Mahler [Ma35] showed that this is $\gg \log\log n$, see
[368](https://www.erdosproblems.com/368)).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649.variants.finite (p q : ℕ) :
    {n : ℕ | n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q}.Finite

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649.variants.no_solution_two_seven
statements.doc:
In fact, the answer to this question as written is easily seen to be no, since there are no
solutions to $2^k\equiv -1\pmod{7}$, and hence this fails with $p=2$ and $q=7$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649.variants.no_solution_two_seven :
    ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = 2 ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = 7

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649.variants.tong
statements.doc:
Even with such amendments, this problem is false in a strong sense: Alan Tong has provided the
following elegant elementary proof that, for any given prime $p$, there are infinitely many
primes $q$ such that this statement is false: let $m$ be the product of all primes $\leq p$, and
choose a prime $q$ congruent to $-1$ modulo $4m$. If $p$ is the greatest prime divisor of $n$
then, using quadratic reciprocity, every prime divisor of $n$ is a quadratic residue modulo $q$,
and hence $n$ is a quadratic residue modulo $q$. On the other hand, since $q\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ we
know that $-1$ is not a quadratic residue modulo $q$, and hence $n\not\equiv -1\pmod{q}$, so it
is impossible for $q\mid n+1$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649.variants.tong (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) :
    {q : ℕ |
      q.Prime ∧ ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q}.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649.variants.tong_question
statements.doc:
Tong asks whether, for any given odd prime $q$, there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that
there is no integer $n$ with $P(n)=p$ and $P(n+1)=q$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649.variants.tong_question :
    ∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → Odd q →
      {p : ℕ |
        p.Prime ∧ ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q}.Infinite

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649.variants.sampaio
statements.doc:
Sampaio independently observed that the answer to Erdős' original problem is no if one of the
primes can be $2$ - for example this is false with $p=19$ and $q=2$, since if $n+1=2^k$ and
$19\mid n$ then (since $2$ is a primitive root modulo $19$) we must have $18\mid k$, and hence
$73\mid 2^{18}-1\mid n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649.variants.sampaio :
    ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = 19 ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = 2

statements.name: Erdos649.erdos_649.variants.rmm_2020
statements.doc:
Problem 6 in the 12th Romanian Master of Mathematics Competitions in 2020 was to prove that there
exist infinitely many odd primes $p$ such that, for every $n$, $P(n)P(n+1)\neq 2p$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_649.variants.rmm_2020 :
    {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd p ∧
      ∀ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac * (n + 1).maxPrimeFac ≠ 2 * p}.Infinite

problems.title: Erdős Problem 650
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/650](https://www.erdosproblems.com/650)
- [Er78] Erdős, Paul, *Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number
  theory*. Proceedings of the Ninth Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory, and
  Computing (Florida Atlantic Univ., Boca Raton, Fla., 1978) (1978), 29-40.
- [Er86c] Erdős, P., *Some problems on number theory*. (1986), 53-67.
- [Er95c] Erdős, Paul, *Some problems in number theory*. Octogon Math. Mag. (1995), 3-5.
- [ErSu59] Erdős, Pál and Surányi, János, *Bemerkungen zu einer Aufgabe eines mathematischen
  Wettbewerbs*. Mat. Lapok (1959), 39-48.
- [VLT26] W. Van Doorn, Y. Li, and Q. Tang, *Optimal bounds for an Erdős problem on matching
  integers to distinct multiples*. arXiv:2603.28636 (2026).

statements.name: Erdos650.erdos_650.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $f(m)$ be such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has $\lvert A\rvert=m$ then every interval
in $[1,\infty)$ of length $2N$ contains $\geq f(m)$ many distinct integers $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ where
each $b_i$ is divisible by some $a_i\in A$, where $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ are distinct.

Estimate $f(m)$.

GPT 5.4 Pro (prompted by He, Li, and Tang) proved $f(m)\leq \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\rceil$. A
corresponding lower bound was given by GPT 5.4 Pro and Aristotle; it is now known (see the paper
of van Doorn, Li, and Tang [VLT26]) that
$$f(m) = \min(m, \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\rceil)$$
for all $m$.

This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_650.parts.i (m : ℕ) : f m = min m ⌈2 * Real.sqrt m⌉₊

statements.name: Erdos650.erdos_650.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $f(m)$ be such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has $\lvert A\rvert=m$ then every interval
in $[1,\infty)$ of length $2N$ contains $\geq f(m)$ many distinct integers $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ where
each $b_i$ is divisible by some $a_i\in A$, where $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ are distinct.

In particular is it true that $f(m)\leq \sqrt{m}$?

GPT 5.4 Pro (prompted by He, Li, and Tang) proved $f(m)\leq \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\rceil$. A
corresponding lower bound was given by GPT 5.4 Pro and Aristotle; it is now known (see the paper
of van Doorn, Li, and Tang [VLT26]) that
$$f(m) = \min(m, \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\rceil)$$
for all $m$.

This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_650.parts.ii : ¬ ∀ m : ℕ, (f m : ℝ) ≤ Real.sqrt m

statements.name: Erdos650.erdos_650.variants.erdos_suranyi
statements.doc: Erdős and Surányi [ErSu59] proved that $f(m)\geq\sqrt{m}$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_650.variants.erdos_suranyi (m : ℕ) : Real.sqrt m ≤ (f m : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos650.erdos_650.variants.erdos_selfridge
statements.doc:
Erdős and Selfridge proved (see [Er78] and [Er86c]) that $f(m^2)\leq 2m$, which implies
$f(m)\leq 2\lceil \sqrt{m}\rceil$ for all $m$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_650.variants.erdos_selfridge (m : ℕ) : f (m ^ 2) ≤ 2 * m

problems.title: Erdős Problem 651
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/651](https://www.erdosproblems.com/651)
- [Er97e] Erdős, P., *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [ErSz60] Erdős, P. and Szekeres, G., *On some extremum problems in elementary geometry*.
  Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest. Eötvös Sect. Math. 3-4 (1960/61), 53-62.
- [PoZa22] Pohoata, C. and Zakharov, D., *Convex polytopes from fewer points*.
  [arXiv:2208.04878](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04878) (2022).
- [Va96] Valtr, P., *Several results related to the Erdős-Szekeres theorem*. Doctoral
  dissertation, Charles University, Prague (1996).

statements.name: Erdos651.nonempty_cardSet
statements.doc:
For $k \geq 2$ and every $n$ there is an integer $N$ such that any $N$ points in general
position in $\mathbb{R}^k$ contain $n$ points in convex position. So $f_k(n)$ is well defined.

This is the higher-dimensional Erdős-Szekeres theorem. For $n \leq k + 1$ one can take $N = n$.
For larger $n$ it follows from Ramsey's theorem, which gives $f_k(n) \leq R_{k+2}(k+3, n)$, see
[PoZa22, Section 1].
statements.statement: theorem nonempty_cardSet {k : ℕ} (hk : 2 ≤ k) (n : ℕ) : (cardSet k n).Nonempty

statements.name: Erdos651.erdos_651
statements.doc:
Let $f_k(n)$ denote the smallest integer such that any $f_k(n)$ points in general position in
$\mathbb{R}^k$ contain $n$ which determine a convex polyhedron. Is it true that
$$
  f_k(n) > (1+c_k)^n
$$
for some constant $c_k>0$?

A problem of Erdős [Er97e]. We read "determine a convex polyhedron" as "are in convex position",
and the inequality as holding, with some $c_k > 0$, for all sufficiently large $n$. We ask the
question for every dimension $k \geq 3$. The planar case $k = 2$ is the Erdős-Klein-Szekeres
problem (see `erdos_651.variants.planar`).

The answer is no. Pohoata and Zakharov [PoZa22, Theorem 1.1] proved that $f_3(n) \leq 2^{o(n)}$,
and this implies $f_k(n) \leq 2^{o(n)}$ for every $k \geq 3$, see
`erdos_651.variants.pohoata_zakharov`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_651 :
    ¬ ∀ k : ℕ, 3 ≤ k → ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (1 + c) ^ n < (f k n : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos651.erdos_651.variants.pohoata_zakharov
statements.doc:
Pohoata and Zakharov [PoZa22, Theorem 1.1] proved that $ES_3(n) = 2^{o(n)}$, where $ES_k(n)$ is
the function $f_k(n)$ above: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and all large $n$, any set of at least
$2^{\varepsilon n}$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^3$ contains $n$ points in convex
position. By the projection argument of Valtr [Va96] (see `erdos_651.variants.antitone`) the same
holds in every dimension $k \geq 3$ [PoZa22, abstract and Section 1].

The theorem gives $f_k(n) \leq \lceil 2^{\varepsilon n} \rceil$. The form below follows by
applying it with $\varepsilon / 2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_651.variants.pohoata_zakharov {k : ℕ} (hk : 3 ≤ k) :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (f k n : ℝ) ≤ (2 : ℝ) ^ (ε * (n : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos651.erdos_651.variants.subexponential
statements.doc:
For every dimension $k \geq 3$ and every $c > 0$ one has $f_k(n) \leq (1+c)^n$ for all large
$n$. This is `erdos_651.variants.pohoata_zakharov` with $\varepsilon = \log_2(1 + c)$. In
particular, for every $c > 0$ the lower bound $f_k(n) > (1+c)^n$ fails not only for infinitely
many $n$ but for all large $n$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_651.variants.subexponential {k : ℕ} (hk : 3 ≤ k) :
    ∀ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (f k n : ℝ) ≤ (1 + c) ^ n

statements.name: Erdos651.erdos_651.variants.planar
statements.doc:
For $k = 2$ the lower bound of the question holds: $f_2(n) > (1+c)^n$ for some $c > 0$ and all
large $n$. Erdős and Szekeres [ErSz60] proved that
$2^{n-2} + 1 \leq f_2(n)$, see [PoZa22, abstract and Section 1], and $(3/2)^n < 2^{n-2} + 1$ for
all $n \geq 5$. The Erdős-Klein-Szekeres conjecture (Erdős Problem 107) states that
$f_2(n) = 2^{n-2} + 1$ for $n \geq 3$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_651.variants.planar :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (1 + c) ^ n < (f 2 n : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos651.erdos_651.variants.antitone
statements.doc:
The function $f_k(n)$ does not increase with the dimension: $f_{k+1}(n) \leq f_k(n)$ for
$k \geq 2$. Given a set in general position in $\mathbb{R}^{k+1}$ with at least $f_k(n)$ points,
project it to a generic hyperplane, find $n$ points in convex position in the projection, and
lift them back. This projection argument is due to Valtr [Va96]; see [PoZa22, Section 1, (1)].

The site states that $f_2(n) > f_3(n) > \cdots$. [PoZa22] gives only the non-strict inequality, so
we state that. The strict inequalities fail for small $n$: for example $f_2(3) = f_3(3) = 3$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_651.variants.antitone {k : ℕ} (hk : 2 ≤ k) (n : ℕ) : f (k + 1) n ≤ f k n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 652
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/652](https://www.erdosproblems.com/652)
- [Ma21] Mathialagan, Surya, *On bipartite distinct distances in the plane*.
  Electron. J. Combin. **28** (2021), no. 4, Paper No. 4.33, 25 pp.
  [doi:10.37236/9687](https://doi.org/10.37236/9687)
- [Discussion](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/652)

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652
statements.doc:
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and let
$R(x_i)=\#\{ \lvert x_j-x_i\rvert : j\neq i\}$, where the points are ordered such that
$$R(x_1)\leq \cdots \leq R(x_n).$$
Let $\alpha_k$ be minimal such that, for all large enough $n$, there exists a set of $n$ points
with $R(x_k)<\alpha_kn^{1/2}$. Is it true that $\alpha_k\to \infty$ as $k\to \infty$?

Mathialagan [Ma21] proved that given a set $P$ of $k$ points and a set $Q$ of $n$ points,
with $2\leq k\leq n^{1/3}$, there exists a point in $P$ which determines
$\gg (kn)^{1/2}$ distances to points in $Q$.
statements.statement: theorem erdos_652 : Tendsto alpha atTop atTop

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652.variants.first
statements.doc:
It is trivial that $R(x_1)=1$ is possible.
We require $n\geq 2$ because a singleton determines no distances to other points.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_652.variants.first (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    ∃ points : Finset ℝ², points.card = n ∧
      ∃ point ∈ points, distinctDistancesFrom points point = 1

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652.variants.product
statements.doc:
We always have $R(x_1)R(x_2)\gg n$.
Equivalently, the same bound holds for any two distinct points of the set.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_652.variants.product :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ points : Finset ℝ²,
      ∀ p ∈ points, ∀ q ∈ points, p ≠ q →
        c * points.card ≤
          (distinctDistancesFrom points p : ℝ) * distinctDistancesFrom points q

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652.variants.elekes
statements.doc:
Elekes proved that for every $k$ and $n$ sufficiently large there exists some set of
$n$ points with $R(x_k)\ll_k n^{1/2}$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_652.variants.elekes :
    ∀ k : ℕ, ∃ a : ℝ, AdmissibleConstant k a

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652.variants.mathialagan
statements.doc:
Mathialagan [Ma21, Theorem 14] proved that given a set $P$ of $k$ points and a set $Q$
of $n$ points, with $2\leq k\leq n^{1/3}$, there exists a point in $P$ which determines
$\gg (kn)^{1/2}$ distances to points in $Q$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_652.variants.mathialagan :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ P Q : Finset ℝ²,
      2 ≤ P.card → P.card ^ 3 ≤ Q.card →
        ∃ p ∈ P, c * Real.sqrt ((P.card : ℝ) * Q.card) ≤
          (Q.image fun q => dist p q).card

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652.variants.kth_lower_bound
statements.doc:
Mathialagan's bound immediately implies $R(x_k)\gg (kn)^{1/2}$ for
$2\leq k\leq n^{1/3}$: fewer than $k$ points have distance count below the bound.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_652.variants.kth_lower_bound :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ points : Finset ℝ², ∀ k : ℕ,
      2 ≤ k → k ^ 3 ≤ points.card →
        (points.filter fun point => (distinctDistancesFrom points point : ℝ) <
          c * Real.sqrt ((k : ℝ) * points.card)).card < k

statements.name: Erdos652.erdos_652.variants.order_sqrt
statements.doc:
Elekes' construction and Mathialagan's lower bound give
$\alpha_k=\Theta(\sqrt k)$, as noted by Zach Hunter in the discussion.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_652.variants.order_sqrt :
    ∃ c C : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ 0 < C ∧ ∀ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop,
      c * Real.sqrt k ≤ alpha k ∧ alpha k ≤ C * Real.sqrt k

problems.title: Erdős Problem 653
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/653](https://www.erdosproblems.com/653)

statements.name: Erdos653.erdos_653
statements.doc:
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and let $R(x_i)=\#\{ \lvert x_j-x_i\rvert : j\neq i\}$,
where the points are ordered such that
$$R(x_1)\leq \cdots \leq R(x_n).$$
Let $g(n)$ be the maximum number of distinct values the $R(x_i)$ can take. Is it true that
$g(n) \geq (1-o(1))n$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_653 : ∃ o : ℕ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (1 - o n) * n ≤ maximalDistinctDistancesFrom n

problems.title: Erdős Problem 654
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/654](https://www.erdosproblems.com/654)
- [Er87b] Erdős, P., *Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry*. Intuitive geometry
  (Siófok, 1985) (1987), 167-177.
- [ErPa90] Erdős, P. and Pach, J., *Variations on the theme of repeated distances*.
  Combinatorica (1990), 261--269.
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [Fe26] T. Feng et al, *Semi-Autonomous Mathematics Discovery with Gemini: A Case Study on the
  Erdős Problems*. arXiv:2601.22401 (2026).

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.parts.i
statements.doc:
Let $f(n)$ be such that, given any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with no four points on a
circle, there exists some $x_i$ with at least $f(n)$ many distinct distances to the other $x_j$.
Is it true that $f(n) > (1-o(1))n$?

Erdős asks this in [Er97e]. The answer is no: Aletheia [Fe26] constructed, for every $m \geq 10$,
a set of $n = 4m$ points with no four on a circle such that every point has fewer than
$\frac{3}{4}n$ distinct distances to the other points. This gives infinitely many $n$, which is
enough to refute the statement with $\varepsilon = 1/8$. See `Erdos654.erdos_654.variants.feng`.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.parts.i :
    ¬ ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², #A = n → NoFourConcyclic A →
      ∃ x ∈ A, (1 - ε) * (n : ℝ) < (distinctDistancesFrom A x : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.parts.ii
statements.doc:
Let $f(n)$ be as in `erdos_654.parts.i`. Is it true that $f(n) > (\frac{1}{3}+c)n$ for some
constant $c>0$ and all large $n$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.parts.ii :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², #A = n → NoFourConcyclic A →
      ∃ x ∈ A, (1 / 3 + c) * (n : ℝ) < (distinctDistancesFrom A x : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.variants.trivial_bound
statements.doc:
It is trivial that $f(n) \geq \frac{n-1}{3}$.

In fact every point $x$ has at least $\frac{n-1}{3}$ distinct distances to the other points: a
circle centred at $x$ contains at most three other points, since four would lie on a common
circle.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.variants.trivial_bound (A : Finset ℝ²) (hA : NoFourConcyclic A) :
    ∀ x ∈ A, ((#A : ℝ) - 1) / 3 ≤ (distinctDistancesFrom A x : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.variants.feng
statements.doc:
Aletheia [Fe26] showed that for every $m \geq 10$ there is a set of $n = 4m$ points in
$\mathbb{R}^2$, no four on a circle, such that every point has fewer than $\frac{3}{4}n = 3m$
distinct distances to the other points.

The construction places $2m$ points on each of two perpendicular lines, so it is not in general
position. Each point has at most $3m - 1$ distinct distances to the other points.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.variants.feng (m : ℕ) (hm : 10 ≤ m) :
    ∃ A : Finset ℝ², #A = 4 * m ∧ NoFourConcyclic A ∧
      ∀ x ∈ A, distinctDistancesFrom A x < 3 * m

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.variants.general_position
statements.doc:
Erdős [Er87b] and Erdős and Pach [ErPa90] ask the question of `erdos_654.parts.ii` under the
additional assumption that no three points are on a line. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with
no three points on a line and no four points on a circle. Is there some $x_i$ with at least
$(\frac{1}{3}+c)n$ distinct distances to the other $x_j$, for some constant $c>0$ and all large
$n$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.variants.general_position :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², #A = n → InGeneralPosition A →
      ∃ x ∈ A, (1 / 3 + c) * (n : ℝ) < (distinctDistancesFrom A x : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.variants.general_position_one_sub_eps
statements.doc:
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with no three points on a line and no four points on a
circle. Is there some $x_i$ with at least $(1-o(1))n$ distinct distances to the other $x_j$?

This is the general-position analogue of `Erdos654.erdos_654.parts.i`. The remark on
erdosproblems.com notes that the construction of [Fe26], which has all points on two lines, does
not settle the version in general position.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.variants.general_position_one_sub_eps :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², #A = n → InGeneralPosition A →
      ∃ x ∈ A, (1 - ε) * (n : ℝ) < (distinctDistancesFrom A x : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos654.erdos_654.variants.erdos_pach
statements.doc:
Erdős and Pach [ErPa90] suggest that the bound $(1-o(1))n$ holds under the assumption that every
circle centred at a point $x_i$ contains at most $2$ other points $x_j$. We state this for points
in general position (no three on a line and no four on a circle [Er87b, p. 167]), the setting in
which [Er87b] and [ErPa90] ask the weaker question. Without the assumption of no three points on a
line the statement is false: the sets of [Fe26] satisfy the circle condition.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_654.variants.erdos_pach :
    ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², #A = n → InGeneralPosition A →
      AtMostTwoPerCircle A → ∃ x ∈ A, (1 - ε) * (n : ℝ) < (distinctDistancesFrom A x : ℝ)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 655
problems.doc: *Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/655](https://www.erdosproblems.com/655)

statements.name: Erdos655.erdos_655
statements.doc:
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ be such that no circle whose centre is one
of the $x_i$ contains three other points. Are there at least
$$(1+c)\frac{n}{2}$$
distinct distances determined between the $x_i$, for some constant $c>0$ and
all $n$ sufficiently large?

The answer is **no**: as Zach Hunter observed, the regular `n`-gon (`n` points equally spaced on a
circle) is valid and determines only `⌊n/2⌋ < (1+c)n/2` distinct distances, for every `c > 0`.
(In the spirit of related conjectures of Erdős and others, presumably some kind of assumption that
the points are in general position was intended; see `erdos_655.variants.general_position`.)

The disproof — the regular `n`-gon construction together with its supporting lemmas — is formalised
at the linked commit.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_655 :
    ¬ ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ (X : Finset ℝ²), #X = n → IsValid X →
      (1 + c) * n / 2 ≤ distinctDistances X

statements.name: Erdos655.erdos_655.variants.general_position
statements.doc:
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ be such that no circle whose centre is one
of the $x_i$ contains three other points. Are there at least$$(1+c)\frac{n}{2}$$
distinct distances determined between the $x_i$, for some constant $c>0$ and
all $n$ sufficiently large?

In the spirit of related conjectures of Erdős and others, presumably
some kind of assumption that the points are in general position
(e.g. no three on a line and no four on a circle) was intended.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_655.variants.general_position :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ (X : Finset ℝ²), #X = n → IsValid X →
      InGeneralPosition X → (1 + c) * n / 2 ≤ distinctDistances X

problems.title: Erdős Problem 656
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/656](https://www.erdosproblems.com/656)
- [Er75b] Erdős, Paul, *Problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Journées
  Arithmétiques de Bordeaux (Conf., Univ. Bordeaux, Bordeaux, 1974) (1975), 295-310.
- [KMRR24] Kra, B., Moreira, J., Richter, F. K. and Robertson, D., *A proof of Erdős's $B+B+t$
  conjecture*. Commun. Am. Math. Soc. 4 (2024), 480-494.
  [arXiv:2206.12377](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.12377)

statements.name: Erdos656.erdos_656
statements.doc:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be a set with positive upper density. Must there exist an infinite set
$B\subseteq A$ and integer $t$ such that
$$\{b_1+b_2: b_1\neq b_2\in B\}+t\subseteq A?$$

Erdős [Er75b] posed this as a candidate for a density version of Hindman's theorem. This is true,
and was proved by Kra, Moreira, Richter, and Robertson [KMRR24, Theorem 1.2 (i)], even for sets of
positive upper Banach density and with $t \geq 0$.

The inclusion says that every $b_1+b_2+t$ is an element of `A`, as an integer.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_656 :
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, 0 < A.upperDensity →
      ∃ B ⊆ A, B.Infinite ∧ ∃ t : ℤ, ∀ b₁ ∈ B, ∀ b₂ ∈ B, b₁ ≠ b₂ →
        ∃ a ∈ A, (a : ℤ) = b₁ + b₂ + t

problems.title: Erdős Problem 657
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/657](https://www.erdosproblems.com/657)
- [Er73] Erdős, P., *Problems and results on combinatorial number theory*. A survey of
  combinatorial theory (Proc. Internat. Sympos., Colorado State Univ., Fort Collins, Colo., 1971)
  (1973), 117-138.
- [Er75f] Erdős, Paul, *On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry*. Ann. Mat.
  Pura Appl. (4) (1975), 99-108.
- [ErPa90] Erdős, P. and Pach, J., *Variations on the theme of repeated distances*.
  Combinatorica (1990), 261-269.
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [Du08] Dumitrescu, Adrian, *On distinct distances and λ-free point sets*. Discrete Math.
  (2008), 6533-6538.

statements.name: Erdos657.erdos_657
statements.doc:
Is it true that if $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a set of $n$ points such that every subset of $3$
points determines $3$ distinct distances (that is, $A$ has no isosceles triangles, degenerate
ones included) then $A$ determines at least $f(n)n$ distinct distances, for some function $f$
with $f(n)\to \infty$?
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_657 :
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℝ, Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧
      ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², A.card = n → (A : Set ℝ²).IsIsoscelesFree →
        f n * (n : ℝ) ≤ (distinctDistances A : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos657.erdos_657.variants.higher_dim
statements.doc:
In [Er73] Erdős attributes the problem, more generally in $\mathbb{R}^k$, to himself and Davies:
for every fixed $k \geq 1$, is there a function $f$ with $f(n)\to \infty$ such that every set of
$n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with no isosceles triangles determines at least $f(n)n$ distinct
distances?

Here the dimension $k$ is fixed and $f$ may depend on $k$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_657.variants.higher_dim :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → ∃ f : ℕ → ℝ, Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧
      ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ A : Finset (ℝ^k), A.card = n → (A : Set (ℝ^k)).IsIsoscelesFree →
        f n * (n : ℝ) ≤ (distinctDistances A : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos657.erdos_657.variants.dim_one
statements.doc:
The question on the real line, which Erdős [Er73] said was open, has a positive answer: there is
a function $f$ with $f(n)\to \infty$ such that every set of $n$ real numbers with no three-term
arithmetic progression determines at least $f(n)n$ distinct distances. This follows from the
lower bound of Dumitrescu [Du08].

On the line, a set has no isosceles triangle exactly when it has no three-term arithmetic
progression.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_657.variants.dim_one :
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℝ, Tendsto f atTop atTop ∧
      ∀ n : ℕ, ∀ A : Finset ℝ, A.card = n → (A : Set ℝ).IsIsoscelesFree →
        f n * (n : ℝ) ≤ (distinctDistances A : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos657.erdos_657.variants.dim_one_lower
statements.doc:
Dumitrescu [Du08] proved that there is a constant $c > 0$ such that, for all large $n$, every set
of $n$ real numbers with no three-term arithmetic progression determines at least
$n(\log n)^c$ distinct distances.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_657.variants.dim_one_lower :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      ∀ A : Finset ℝ, A.card = n → (A : Set ℝ).IsIsoscelesFree →
        (n : ℝ) * (Real.log n) ^ c ≤ (distinctDistances A : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos657.erdos_657.variants.dim_one_upper
statements.doc:
As noted in [Du08], Behrend's construction of large sets without three-term arithmetic
progressions shows that there is a constant $C > 0$ such that, for all large $n$, some set
of $n$ real numbers with no three-term arithmetic progression determines at most
$n 2^{C\sqrt{\log n}}$ distinct distances.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_657.variants.dim_one_upper :
    ∃ C > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      ∃ A : Finset ℝ, A.card = n ∧ (A : Set ℝ).IsIsoscelesFree ∧
        (distinctDistances A : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) * (2 : ℝ) ^ (C * √(Real.log n))

statements.name: Erdos657.erdos_657.variants.straus
statements.doc:
Straus observed that for every $k$ there is a set of $2^k$ points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with no
isosceles triangles which determines at most $2^k - 1$ distinct distances.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_657.variants.straus (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ A : Finset (ℝ^k), A.card = 2 ^ k ∧ (A : Set (ℝ^k)).IsIsoscelesFree ∧
      distinctDistances A ≤ 2 ^ k - 1

problems.title: Erdős Problem 658
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/658](https://www.erdosproblems.com/658)
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [FuKa91] Furstenberg, H. and Katznelson, Y., *A density version of the Hales-Jewett Theorem*.
  Journal d'Analyse Mathématique (1991), 64-119.
- [So04] Solymosi, J., *A Note on a Question of Erdős and Graham*. Combinatorics, Probability and
  Computing (2004), 263–267.

statements.name: Erdos658.erdos_658
statements.doc:
Let $\delta>0$ and $N$ be sufficiently large depending on $\delta$. Is it true that if
$A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}^2$ has $\lvert A\rvert \geq \delta N^2$ then $A$ must contain the
vertices of a square?

A problem of Graham, if the square is restricted to be axis-aligned. (It is unclear whether in
[Er97e] had this restriction in mind.)

This qualitative statement follows from the density Hales-Jewett theorem proved by Furstenberg
and Katznelson [FuKa91]. A quantitative proof (yet with very poor bounds) was given by Solymosi
[So04].

The square is taken to be axis-aligned (Graham's version), which implies the version allowing
arbitrary squares.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_658 : ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∀ᶠ N : ℕ in atTop,
    ∀ A : Finset (ℕ × ℕ), A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N ×ˢ Finset.Icc 1 N → δ * N ^ 2 ≤ A.card →
      ∃ a b d : ℕ, 0 < d ∧ (a, b) ∈ A ∧ (a + d, b) ∈ A ∧ (a, b + d) ∈ A ∧ (a + d, b + d) ∈ A

problems.title: Erdős Problem 659
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/659](https://www.erdosproblems.com/659)
- [MoOs06] Moree, Pieter and Osburn, Robert, Two-dimensional lattices with few distances. Enseign. Math. (2) (2006), 361--380
- [ErFi96] Erdős, Paul and Fishburn, Peter, Maximum planar sets that determine {$k$} distances. Discrete Math. (1996), 115--125.
- [Gr26](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09102): Benjamin Grayzel, Solution to a Problem of Erdős Concerning Distances and Points

statements.name: Erdos659.erdos_659
statements.doc:
Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at
least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is $\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$?

There does exist such a set: a suitable truncation of the lattice
$\{(a,b\sqrt{2}): a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ suffices. This construction appears to have been first
considered by Moree and Osburn \cite{MoOs06}, who proved that it has
 $\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ many distinct distances. This construction was independently found by
 [Lund and Sheffer](https://adamsheffer.wordpress.com/2014/07/16/point-sets-with-few-distinct-distances/),
 who further noted that this configuration contains no squares or equilateral triangles.

There are only six possible configurations of $4$ points which determine only $2$ distances
(first noted by Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi96]), and five of them contain either a square or an
equilateral triangle. The remaining configuration contains four points from a regular pentagon,
and Grayzel [Gr26] (using Gemini) has noted in the comments that this configuration can also be
ruled out, thus giving a complete solution to this problem.

Boris Alexeev provides a formalisation of the reduction, which is conditional on Bernays' theorem
(assumed as an axiom in the proof to obtain the $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ bound).
See the [formal proof](https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/226d5fad7143dcebea2bbb5ec87f18a3a1dcea69/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos659.lean).
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_659 : ∃ A : ℕ → Finset ℝ²,
   (∀ n, #(A n) = n ∧ ∀ S ⊆ A n, #S = 4 → 3 ≤ distinctDistances S) ∧
    (fun n ↦ distinctDistances (A n)) ≪ fun n ↦ n / sqrt (log n)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 660
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/660](https://www.erdosproblems.com/660)
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favorite problems and results*, The mathematics of Paul Erdős,
  I (1997), 47–67.
- [Al63] Altman, E., *On a problem of P. Erdős*, Amer. Math. Monthly (1963), 148–157.
- [Er75f] Erdős, Paul, *On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry*, Ann. Mat. Pura
  Appl. (4) (1975), 99–108.

statements.name: Erdos660.erdos_660
statements.doc:
Let $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be the vertices of a convex polyhedron. Are there at least
$$(1 - o(1)) \frac{n}{2}$$
many distinct distances between the $x_i$?

The $(1 - o(1)) \frac{n}{2}$ lower bound is formalised as: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, every set
of $n$ vertices of a convex polyhedron with $n$ sufficiently large determines at least
$(1 - \varepsilon) \frac{n}{2}$ distinct distances.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_660 :
    ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∀ P : Finset ℝ³,
      P.card = n → IsPolyhedronVertices P →
      (1 - ε) * ((n : ℝ) / 2) ≤ (distinctDistances P : ℝ)

statements.name: Erdos660.erdos_660.variants.altman_planar
statements.doc:
For the similar problem in $\mathbb{R}^2$ there are always at least $n/2$ distances, as proved by
Altman [Al63].
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_660.variants.altman_planar (n : ℕ) (P : Finset ℝ²)
    (hcard : P.card = n) (hconv : ConvexIndependent ℝ ((↑) : ↥(P : Set ℝ²) → ℝ²))
    (haff : affineSpan ℝ (P : Set ℝ²) = ⊤) :
    n / 2 ≤ distinctDistances P

statements.name: Erdos660.erdos_660.variants.Er75f
statements.doc:
In [Er75f] Erdős claims that Altman proved that the vertices determine $\gg n$ many distinct
distances, but gives no reference.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_660.variants.Er75f :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∀ P : Finset ℝ³,
      P.card = n → IsPolyhedronVertices P →
      c * n ≤ (distinctDistances P : ℝ)

problems.title: Erdős Problem 661
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/661](https://www.erdosproblems.com/661)
- [ErPa90] Erdős, P. and Pach, J., *Variations on the theme of repeated distances*.
  Combinatorica (1990), 261--269.
- [Er92e] Erdős, Pál, *Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics*.
  Eureka (1992), 44-48.
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*. Math. Japon. (1997), 527-537.
- [Er97f] Erdős, Paul, *Some unsolved problems*. Combinatorics, geometry and probability
  (Cambridge, 1993) (1997), 1-10.
- [Er46] Erdős, Paul, *On sets of distances of $n$ points*. Amer. Math. Monthly 53 (1946),
  248--250.

statements.name: Erdos661.erdos_661
statements.doc:
Are there, for all large $n$, some points $x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that
the number of distinct distances $d(x_i,y_j)$ is
$$o\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)?$$

We require all $2n$ points to be distinct; without any distinctness one could take all points
equal and get a single distance. Writing $F(n)$ for the minimal number of such distances
(`minimalCrossDistances ℝ² n`), the question asks whether $F(n) = o(n / \sqrt{\log n})$. This is
equivalent to the existence, for all large $n$, of configurations whose count is at most $g(n)$
for some fixed $g(n) = o(n / \sqrt{\log n})$, since the infimum is attained.

The source adds that one can also ask this for points in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Taken literally, the
question is easy there, since a cubic grid of $2n$ points determines only $O(n^{2/3})$ distinct
distances, so we do not state it.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_661 :
    (fun n => (minimalCrossDistances ℝ² n : ℝ)) =o[atTop]
      (fun (n : ℕ) => (n : ℝ) / (n : ℝ).log.sqrt)

statements.name: Erdos661.erdos_661.variants.grid_upper_bound
statements.doc:
Take $2n$ points of the smallest square grid with at least $2n$ points; by [Er46] they determine
$O(n / \sqrt{\log n})$ distinct distances. Splitting them into two halves of $n$ points shows
that $F(n) = O(n / \sqrt{\log n})$. So the question is whether this trivial bound can be
improved by more than a constant factor.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_661.variants.grid_upper_bound :
    (fun n => (minimalCrossDistances ℝ² n : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      (fun (n : ℕ) => (n : ℝ) / (n : ℝ).log.sqrt)

statements.name: Erdos661.erdos_661.variants.le_minimalDistinctDistances
statements.doc:
Every split of a set of $2n$ points into two halves of $n$ points gives a configuration for
$F(n)$, and the distances between the halves are among the distances of the whole set. Hence
$F(n) \leq f(2n)$, where $f(2n)$ is the minimal number of distinct distances determined by $2n$
points in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_661.variants.le_minimalDistinctDistances (n : ℕ) :
    minimalCrossDistances ℝ² n ≤ minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² (2 * n)

statements.name: Erdos661.erdos_661.variants.little_o_distinct_distances
statements.doc:
Let $F(2n)$ be the minimal number of distinct distances $d(x_i, y_j)$ for $2n$ distinct points
$x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$, and $f(2n)$ the minimal number of distinct
distances determined by any $2n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Is $F = o(f)$?

Here $F(2n)$ of erdosproblems.com is `minimalCrossDistances ℝ² n` (indexed by $n$ points on each
side) and $f(2n)$ is `minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² (2 * n)`. See also Erdős Problem 89.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_661.variants.little_o_distinct_distances :
    (fun n => (minimalCrossDistances ℝ² n : ℝ)) =o[atTop]
      (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² (2 * n) : ℝ))

statements.name: Erdos661.erdos_661.variants.lenz
statements.doc:
In $\mathbb{R}^4$ Lenz observed (as stated on erdosproblems.com/661) that for every $n$ there are
$2n$ distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in \mathbb{R}^4$ with $d(x_i,y_j)=1$ for all
$i,j$: take the $x_i$ on the circle of radius $1/\sqrt{2}$ about the origin in the plane of the
first two coordinates, and the $y_j$ on the circle of radius $1/\sqrt{2}$ about the origin in the
plane of the last two coordinates.
statements.statement:
theorem erdos_661.variants.lenz (n : ℕ) :
    ∃ A B : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 4)), #A = n ∧ #B = n ∧ Disjoint A B ∧
      ∀ x ∈ A, ∀ y ∈ B, dist x y = 1

problems.title: Erdős Problem 663
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/663](https://www.erdosproblems.com/663)
- [BEGL96] Burr, S. A., Erdős, P., Graham, R. L., and Li, W. W.-C.,
  *Complete sequences of sets of integer powers*. Acta Arith. (1996), 133–138.
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite unsolved problems*.
  Math. Japon. (1997), 527–537.
