statements.statement: theorem a_of_comesFromPrimeQuadruple {n : ℕ} (h : ComesFromPrimeQuadruple n) : A n

statements.name: OeisA56777.comesFromPrimeQuadruple_of_a
statements.doc: All members of the sequence A56777 come from prime quadruples.
statements.statement: theorem comesFromPrimeQuadruple_of_a {n : ℕ} (h : A n) : ComesFromPrimeQuadruple n

statements.name: OeisA56777.mod_72_of_comesFromPrimeQuadruple
statements.doc: Numbers coming from prime quadruples satisfy $n \equiv 65 \pmod{72}$.
statements.statement:
theorem mod_72_of_comesFromPrimeQuadruple {n : ℕ} (h : ComesFromPrimeQuadruple n) :
    n % 72 = 65

statements.name: OeisA56777.mod_100_of_comesFromPrimeQuadruple
statements.doc:
Numbers coming from prime quadruples satisfy $n \equiv 9 \pmod{100}$,
except the first value "65".
statements.statement:
theorem mod_100_of_comesFromPrimeQuadruple {n : ℕ} (h65 : 65 < n) (h : ComesFromPrimeQuadruple n) :
    n % 100 = 9

problems.title: Numerator of $1/\det(M)$ for $M[i,j] = 1/\operatorname{lcm}(i,j)$
problems.doc:
Numerator of $1/\det(M)$ where $M$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with
$M[i,j] = 1/\operatorname{lcm}(i,j)$.

*References:*
- [A060841](https://oeis.org/A060841)
- T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?",
  [arXiv:2608.11941](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11941) [cs.AI], 2026.

statements.name: OeisA60841.conjecture1
statements.doc:
"Conjecture: $1/\det(M)$ is an integer only for n: 1 to 34, 36 and 38." - _Robert G. Wilson v_,
Aug 02 2015
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture1 :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → (((lcmMatrix n).det)⁻¹.den = 1 ↔ n ∈ integerDetN)

statements.name: OeisA60841.conjecture2
statements.doc:
"All denominators are powers of two (A000079)." - _Robert G. Wilson v_, Aug 02 2015

This is false: for $n = 1807$ the denominator of $1/\det(M)$ is divisible by $3$.
See T. Adamczewski, OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?,
[arXiv:2608.11941](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11941). The Lean disproof there uses the closed
form $1/\det(M) = \prod_{k=1}^n k^2/\varphi(k)$ from the OEIS entry:
https://github.com/epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems-results/blob/fd09021e79869476ef83cda231312f1a2a89c8d7/runs/oeis-full-50usd-ant-j0j0g4uzligm1k41/oeis_60841_conjecture_0/Submission/Spec.lean#L272
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2 :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → ∃ k : ℕ, ((lcmMatrix n).det)⁻¹.den = 2 ^ k

problems.title: Number of different products of subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$
problems.doc:
The number of distinct products (including the empty product 1) of any subset
of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$.

*References:*
- [A060957](https://oeis.org/A060957)
- [Li26] Wentao Li, [A counterexample to the A060957 interpolation conjecture](https://github.com/VictorLiwentao/lean-oeis-proofs/blob/3be119e75ba5b31f034dc0c0b249975d17def711/proofs/new-proofs/A060957/PROOF.md), 2026.

statements.name: OeisA60957.counterexample
statements.doc:
An explicit counterexample from [Li26]: both endpoint products occur, but the intermediate
product with exponent $5$ does not. The definitions above specify every parameter, including
`Counterexample.circuitM` as a finite product.
statements.statement:
theorem counterexample :
    Counterexample.circuitPrime.Prime ∧ Counterexample.circuitPrime ≤ Counterexample.circuitN ∧
    Counterexample.circuitM ∈ productsOfSubsets Counterexample.circuitN ∧
    Counterexample.circuitPrime ^ 6 * Counterexample.circuitM ∈
      productsOfSubsets Counterexample.circuitN ∧
    0 < (5 : ℕ) ∧ 5 < (6 : ℕ) ∧
    Counterexample.circuitPrime ^ 5 * Counterexample.circuitM ∉
      productsOfSubsets Counterexample.circuitN

statements.name: OeisA60957.conjecture
statements.doc:
Conjecture: let $p \le n$ be prime. If $m$ and $p^a m$ are two such products, then so is $p^k m$
for all $0 < k < a$.
- Yan Sheng Ang, Feb 13 2020

This interpolation conjecture is false. Disproved by Wentao Li (2026), with AI assistance;
see [Li26]. The counterexample has
$p = 7 \cdot 2^{120} + 1$, $n = p \cdot 2^{189}$, $a = 6$, and $k = 5$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ (n p : ℕ), p.Prime → p ≤ n →
      ∀ (m a_exp : ℕ), m ∈ productsOfSubsets n → p ^ a_exp * m ∈ productsOfSubsets n →
        ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → k < a_exp → p ^ k * m ∈ productsOfSubsets n

problems.title: Reversible multiples $a(3^n) = 10^{3^{n-2}} - 1$ for powers of $3$
problems.doc:
First multiple of $n$ whose reverse is also divisible by $n$,
or 0 if no such multiple exists.

*References:*
- [A062567](https://oeis.org/A062567)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.

statements.name: OeisA62567.a_three_pow_eq
statements.doc:
The conjecture that $a(3^n) = 10^{3^{n-2}} - 1$ for $n > 1$ was shown to be false for $4 < n < 21$
by Farideh Firoozbakht, who conjectured that for all $n > 4$, $a(3^n) \neq 10^{3^{n-2}} - 1$.
This latter conjecture is proved here.

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
statements.statement:
theorem a_three_pow_eq (n : ℕ) :
    2 ≤ n → (a (3 ^ n) = 10 ^ (3 ^ (n - 2)) - 1 ↔ n = 2 ∨ n = 3 ∨ n = 4)

problems.title: Conjectures associated with A063880
problems.doc:
A063880 lists numbers $n$ such that $\sigma(n) = 2 \cdot \text{usigma}(n)$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the
sum of all divisors and $\text{usigma}(n)$ is the sum of unitary divisors.

Equivalently, these are numbers whose unitary and non-unitary divisors have equal sum.

The conjectures state that all members satisfy $n \equiv 108 \pmod{216}$, and that all
primitive terms (those whose proper divisors aren't in the sequence) are powerful numbers,
with $108$ being the only primitive term.

*References:*
- [A063880](https://oeis.org/A063880)

statements.name: OeisA63880.mod_216_of_a
statements.doc: All members of the sequence satisfy $n \equiv 108 \pmod{216}$.
statements.statement: theorem mod_216_of_a {n : ℕ} (h : A n) : n % 216 = 108

statements.name: OeisA63880.powerful_of_isPrimitiveTerm
statements.doc:
All primitive terms are powerful numbers: if `p` divided `n` exactly once, then `n / p` would
also be in the sequence.
statements.statement: theorem powerful_of_isPrimitiveTerm {n : ℕ} (h : IsPrimitiveTerm n) : n.Powerful

statements.name: OeisA63880.unique_primitive_108
statements.doc: $108$ is the only primitive term.
statements.statement: theorem unique_primitive_108 {n : ℕ} (h : IsPrimitiveTerm n) : n = 108

statements.name: OeisA63880.a_of_primitive_mul_squarefree
statements.doc:
If $m$ is a primitive term and $s$ is squarefree with $\gcd(m, s) = 1$, then $m \cdot s$
is in the sequence.
statements.statement:
theorem a_of_primitive_mul_squarefree (m s : ℕ) (hm : IsPrimitiveTerm m)
    (hs : Squarefree s) (hcoprime : m.Coprime s) : A (m * s)

statements.name: OeisA63880.exists_primitive_of_a
statements.doc:
Non-primitive terms have the form $m \cdot s$ where $m$ is primitive and $s$ is
squarefree with $\gcd(m, s) = 1$.
statements.statement:
theorem exists_primitive_of_a {n : ℕ} (h : A n) :
    ∃ m s, IsPrimitiveTerm m ∧ Squarefree s ∧ m.Coprime s ∧ n = m * s

problems.title: Numerator - denominator in $n$-th harmonic number
problems.doc:
$a(n) = \text{numerator}(H_n) - \text{denominator}(H_n)$, where
$H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/n$.

*References:*
- [A064169](https://oeis.org/A064169)

statements.name: OeisA64169.conjecture
statements.doc:
"Conjecture: for $n > 2$, $n$ divides $a(n-2)$ if and only if $n$ is a prime.
Checked up to 20000. - _Amiram Eldar_ and _Thomas Ordowski_, Jul 27 2019

This is false for the composite number $16843^2$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : ¬ ∀ (n : ℕ), 2 < n → ((n : ℤ) ∣ a (n - 2) ↔ n.Prime)

problems.title: Integer part of area of a regular polygon with $n$ sides each of length 1
problems.doc:
The area of a regular $n$-gon with side length 1 is given by
$\frac{n}{4} \cot(\pi / n) = \frac{n}{4 \tan(\pi / n)}$.

*References:*
- [A064313](https://oeis.org/A064313)

statements.name: OeisA64313.conjecture
statements.doc:
"Usually (perhaps always?) $\lfloor n^2 / (4\pi) - \pi / 12 \rfloor$ for a polygon of circumference $n$.
Note that the area of a circle with circumference $C$ is $C^2 / (4\pi)$."
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
    a n = (Int.floor ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 / (4 * Real.pi) - Real.pi / 12)).toNat

problems.title: Decimal encoding of the prime factorization of $n$
problems.doc:
If $n$ has prime factorization $p_1^{e_1} \dots p_r^{e_r}$ with $p_1 < \dots < p_r$,
then its decimal encoding is $p_1 e_1 \dots p_r e_r$.

*References:*
- [A067599](https://oeis.org/A067599)

statements.name: OeisA67599.conjecture
statements.doc:
"$a(31) = a(177147) = 311$. Is there any solution to $a(n) = n$?
- _Franklin T. Adams-Watters_, Dec 18 2006"
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ∃ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n ∧ a n = n

problems.title: Conjectures associated with A067720
problems.doc:
A067720 lists numbers $k$ such that $\varphi(k^2 + 1) = k \cdot \varphi(k + 1)$,
where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function.

The sequence exhibits a strong connection to primes: for almost all terms $k$,
$k + 1$ is prime. The conjecture states that $k = 8$ is the only exception.

*References:*
- [A067720](https://oeis.org/A067720)

statements.name: OeisA67720.a_of_primes
statements.doc: If $k + 1$ and $k^2 + 1$ are both prime, then $k$ is in the sequence.
statements.statement: theorem a_of_primes {k : ℕ} (hk : (k + 1).Prime) (hk' : (k ^ 2 + 1).Prime) : A k

statements.name: OeisA67720.prime_add_one_of_a
statements.doc: For members of the sequence other than $8$, we have $k + 1$ is prime.
statements.statement: theorem prime_add_one_of_a {k : ℕ} (h : A k) (hne : k ≠ 8) : (k + 1).Prime

problems.title: Euclid–Fortunate prime coverage
problems.doc:
OEIS A067836 starts with $2$. Each later term is the gap from the product of all previous terms to
the least prime strictly greater than that product plus one.

*References:*
- [OEIS A067836](https://oeis.org/A067836)

statements.name: OeisA67836.conjecture
statements.doc: [OEIS A067836](https://oeis.org/A067836) asks: "Do all primes occur in the sequence?"
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ∀ p, p.Prime → ∃ n ≥ 1, a n = p

problems.title: Sum of $a(k)/k!$ over divisors equals harmonic number
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ satisfies $\sum_{k \mid n} \frac{a(k)}{k!} = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{j} = H_n$,
where the sum on the left is over positive divisors $k$ of $n$. By Möbius inversion,
$$a(n) = n! \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(n/d) H_d$$
where $H_d = \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{j}$ is the $d$-th harmonic number.

*References:*
- [A067857](https://oeis.org/A067857)
- [A001221](https://oeis.org/A001221)

statements.name: OeisA67857.conjecture
statements.doc:
The terms are not all positive. The first negative one is
$a(30) = -22690644647302814715858124800000$.
Conjecture: $a(n) < 0$ if and only if A001221(n) is an odd number $\ge 3$.

This conjecture is false. A counterexample is the product of all primes at most $1000$,
which has $168$ distinct prime factors and a negative sequence value.

The counterexample and formal proof were developed by Codex (GPT-6),
prompted by Samuel Schlesinger.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
      (a n < 0 ↔ Odd (cardDistinctFactors n) ∧ 3 ≤ cardDistinctFactors n)

problems.title: Number of times $n^2 + s^2$ is prime for positive integers $s < n$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ counts the number of integers $s \in \{1, \dots, n-1\}$ such that
$n^2 + s^2$ is prime:
$$a(n) = \sum_{s=1}^{n-1} [\text{Prime}(n^2 + s^2)]$$

*References:*
- [A069004](https://oeis.org/A069004)
- [CE26] j2d9w5xtjn-png, [Counterexample to the upper bound](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/5453), 2026.
- [Li26] Wentao Li, [Lean certificate for the A069004 counterexample](https://github.com/VictorLiwentao/lean-oeis-proofs/blob/a16a2711b082ccab4ba941330148e7b7c78b11c1/proofs/new-formalization/A069004/PROOF.md), 2026.

statements.name: OeisA69004.conjecture1
statements.doc: Conjecture: $a(n) > 0$ for all $n > 1$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture1 (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 < n) : 0 < a n

statements.name: OeisA69004.conjecture2
statements.doc:
Stronger conjecture: Let pi(n) be the prime counting function (A000720). Then
pi(n) >= a(n) >= pi(n)/5 for n>1, with the following equalities: pi(2)=a(2),
pi(10)=a(10) and a(12)=pi(12)/5.
- T. D. Noe, Feb 26 2007

This conjunction is false. The upper bound fails at $n = 512720$:
a Lean certificate proves $a(512720) \ge 42494 > 42493 = \pi(512720)$.
The counterexample was recorded by j2d9w5xtjn-png [CE26].

Lean formalization by Wentao Li, with AI assistance, adapting Epoch Research's
certificate attempt; see [Li26].
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2 : ¬ (
    (∀ n : ℕ, 1 < n → Nat.primeCounting n ≥ a n) ∧
    (∀ n : ℕ, 1 < n → 5 * a n ≥ Nat.primeCounting n) ∧
    Nat.primeCounting 2 = a 2 ∧
    Nat.primeCounting 10 = a 10 ∧
    5 * a 12 = Nat.primeCounting 12)

statements.name: OeisA69004.conjecture2.variants.upper_bound_false
statements.doc:
The upper bound from T. D. Noe's stronger conjecture: "pi(n) >= a(n)" for "n>1".
It is false at $n = 512720$: $a(512720) \ge 42494 > 42493 = \pi(512720)$.
The counterexample was recorded by j2d9w5xtjn-png [CE26].

Lean formalization by Wentao Li, with AI assistance, adapting Epoch Research's
certificate attempt; see [Li26].
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2.variants.upper_bound_false :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 < n → Nat.primeCounting n ≥ a n

statements.name: OeisA69004.conjecture2.variants.without_upper_bound
statements.doc:
The part of the stronger conjecture that survives the counterexample to its upper bound:
$5 a(n) \ge \pi(n)$ for $n > 1$, together with the three claimed equalities
$\pi(2) = a(2)$, $\pi(10) = a(10)$ and $a(12) = \pi(12)/5$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2.variants.without_upper_bound :
    (∀ n : ℕ, 1 < n → 5 * a n ≥ Nat.primeCounting n) ∧
    Nat.primeCounting 2 = a 2 ∧
    Nat.primeCounting 10 = a 10 ∧
    5 * a 12 = Nat.primeCounting 12

problems.title: Determinant of prime sum indicator matrix
problems.doc:
Determinant of the $n \times n$ matrix with $(i,j)$-entry ($1 \le i, j \le n$) equal to $1$
if $i + j$ is prime, and $0$ otherwise.

*References:*
- [A069191](https://oeis.org/A069191)

statements.name: OeisA69191.conjecture_1
statements.doc:
Conjecture: Let $M(n)$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with $(i,j)$-entry equal to $1$ or $0$ according as
$i + j$ is prime or not. For each $n = 24, 25, \dots$, the characteristic polynomial of $M(n)$ is
irreducible over the field of rational numbers.
- _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Aug 25 2013
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture_1 (n : ℕ) (hn : 24 ≤ n) :
    Irreducible (primeMatrix ℚ n).charpoly

statements.name: OeisA69191.conjecture_2
statements.doc:
Conjecture: Let $M(n)$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with $(i,j)$-entry equal to $1$ or $0$ according as
$i + j$ is prime or not. For each $n = 24, 25, \dots$, the $n$ eigenvalues of $M(n)$ can be listed as
$\lambda(1), \dots, \lambda(n)$ such that
$\lambda(1) > -\lambda(2) > \lambda(3) > -\lambda(4) > \dots > (-1)^{n-1} \lambda(n) > 0$.
- _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Aug 25 2013
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture_2 (n : ℕ) (hn : 24 ≤ n) :
    ∃ ev : Fin n → ℝ,
      (primeMatrix ℝ n).charpoly = ∏ i : Fin n, (Polynomial.X - Polynomial.C (ev i)) ∧
      StrictAnti (fun i : Fin n => (-1 : ℝ) ^ (i : ℕ) * ev i) ∧
      ∀ i : Fin n, 0 < (-1 : ℝ) ^ (i : ℕ) * ev i

problems.title: Number of primes $p$ such that $n^n \le p \le n^n + n^2$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ counts the number of prime numbers in the interval $[n^n, n^n + n^2]$:
$$a(n) = |\{p \text{ prime} \mid n^n \le p \le n^n + n^2\}|$$

*References:*
- [A069922](https://oeis.org/A069922)

statements.name: OeisA69922.conjecture
statements.doc:
Question: for any $n > 0$, is there at least one prime $p$ such that $n^n \le p \le n^n + n^2$?
In this case, that would be stronger than the Schinzel conjecture: "for $m > 1$ there's at least
one prime $p$ such that $m \le p \le m + \log(m)^2$" since $n^2 < \log(n^n)^2 = n^2 \log(n)^2$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) : 1 ≤ a n

problems.title: Number of primes $p$ such that $2^n \le p \le 2^n + \mathrm{prime}(n)$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ counts the number of primes $p$ in the interval $[2^n, 2^n + p_n]$,
where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime ($p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, \dots$):
$$a(n) = |\{p \text{ prime} \mid 2^n \le p \le 2^n + p_n\}|$$
for $n \ge 1$, and $a(0) = 0$.

*References:*
- [A069923](https://oeis.org/A069923)

statements.name: OeisA69923.conjecture
statements.doc:
For any $n > 0$, is there always at least one prime $p$ such that
$2^n \le p \le 2^n + \mathrm{prime}(n)$?
(checked up to $n = 250$). In this case, that would be stronger than the Schinzel conjecture:
"for $m > 1$ there's at least one prime $p$ such that $m \le p \le m + \log(m)^2$" since,
for $n > 2$, $\mathrm{prime}(n) < \log(2^n)^2 = n^2 \log(2)$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) : 1 ≤ a n

problems.title: Value of $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial at $n$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n) = \Phi_n(n)$ gives the value of the $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial evaluated
at $n$:
$$a(n) = |\Phi_n(n)|$$

*References:*
- [A070518](https://oeis.org/A070518)

statements.name: OeisA70518.conjecture
statements.doc: $a(28341)$ is divisible by $283411^2$. What is the next $n$ such that $a(n)$ is not squarefree?
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    conjecture.answer =
      if h : ∃ n, 28341 < n ∧ ¬ Squarefree (a n) then
        some (sInf {n | 28341 < n ∧ ¬ Squarefree (a n)})
      else
        none

problems.title: Recurrence $a(n+2) = |a(n+1)a(n) - a(n)a(n+1)|$ via concatenation
problems.doc:
The sequence starts with $a(1) = 0, a(2) = 1$. For $n \ge 1$,
$$a(n+2) = |\text{concat}(a(n+1), a(n)) - \text{concat}(a(n), a(n+1))|$$
where concatenation is in decimal representation.

*References:*
- [A070823](https://oeis.org/A070823)

statements.name: OeisA70823.conjecture
statements.doc:
$a(n) \equiv 0 \pmod 3$ if $n > 2$. Is $a(n)$ always of the form $2^j \cdot 3^k \cdot s$
where $s$ is a squarefree number?

Answer: False, $a(20)$ is divisible by $13^2$ but not by $13^3$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 2 < n →
      a n ≡ 0 [MOD 3] ∧
        ∃ j k s : ℕ, a n = 2 ^ j * 3 ^ k * s ∧ Squarefree s

problems.title: Determinant of matrix with entries indicating primality of $i^2 + j^2$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the determinant of the $n \times n$ matrix $M$ defined by
$M(i,j) = 1$ if $i^2 + j^2$ is prime, and $0$ otherwise, where $1 \le i, j \le n$.

*References:*
- [A071524](https://oeis.org/A071524)

statements.name: OeisA71524.conjecture1
statements.doc:
Conjecture: $a(n) = 0$ for no $n > 28$.
- _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Aug 26 2013
statements.statement: theorem conjecture1 (n : ℕ) (hn : 28 < n) : a n ≠ 0

statements.name: OeisA71524.conjecture2
statements.doc:
Conjecture (Generalization): For every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, the determinant `generalDet m n` is
nonzero for all sufficiently large $n$.
- _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Aug 26-27 2013
statements.statement: theorem conjecture2 (m : ℕ) : ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N < n → generalDet m n ≠ 0

problems.title: Alternating sum of signs of powers of $3/2$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n) = -\sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{\lfloor (3/2)^k \rfloor}$.

*References:*
- [A071532](https://oeis.org/A071532)

statements.name: OeisA71532.conjecture1
statements.doc:
"Is $a(n)>0$?"

The answer is negative: $a(331523) = -1$. The restriction $n > 2$ excludes the initial
zero $a(2) = 0$.

The counterexample and formal proof were developed by Codex (GPT-6), prompted by
Samuel Schlesinger.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture1 : ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 2 < n → 0 < a n

statements.name: OeisA71532.conjecture2
statements.doc: For $n$ large enough, does $a(n) > \sqrt{n}$ always hold?
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2 :
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → (a n : ℝ) > Real.sqrt (n : ℝ)

statements.name: OeisA71532.conjecture3
statements.doc: Conjecture: asymptotically, $a(n) \sim C \log(n)^2$ for some constant $C > 0$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture3 :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ (fun n : ℕ ↦ (a n : ℝ)) ~[atTop] (fun n : ℕ ↦ C * Real.log (n : ℝ) ^ 2)

statements.name: OeisA71532.conjecture3_value
statements.doc: Conjecture: the constant $C$ in $a(n) \sim C \log(n)^2$ is approximately $1.4$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture3_value :
    |conjecture3_value.answer - 1.4| < 0.1 ∧
      (fun n : ℕ ↦ (a n : ℝ)) ~[atTop] (fun n : ℕ ↦ conjecture3_value.answer * Real.log (n : ℝ) ^ 2)

problems.title: Smallest factorial containing exactly $n$ 6's
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ gives the smallest $k$ such that the decimal expansion of $k!$
contains exactly $n$ occurrences of the digit '6', or $0$ if no such $k$ exists.

*References:*
- [A072200](https://oeis.org/A072200)

statements.name: OeisA72200.conjecture
statements.doc: It is conjectured that $a(24) = 0$ since no factorial less than $10000$ contained just 24 sixes.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : a 24 = 0

problems.title: Number of times $n$ occurs as a binary sub-pattern of $n^2$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the number of times the binary expansion of $n$ appears as a contiguous
sublist (infix) in the binary expansion of $n^2$.

*References:*
- [A076141](https://oeis.org/A076141)

statements.name: OeisA76141.conjecture
statements.doc: Is $a(n) \le 1$ for all $n$?
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) : a n ≤ 1

problems.title: Smallest $x$ such that $\sigma(x) \bmod x = n$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the smallest positive integer $x$ such that $\sigma_1(x) \bmod x = n$,
or $0$ if no such $x$ exists.

*References:*
- [A076495](https://oeis.org/A076495)

statements.name: OeisA76495.conjecture
statements.doc:
At present, the 0 entry for $n = 5$ is only a conjecture.
That is, it is conjectured that there is no positive integer $x$ such that
$\sigma_1(x) \bmod x = 5$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : a 5 = 0

problems.title: Trajectory of 103 under the Reverse and Add! operation in base 3
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the trajectory of $103$ under the Reverse and Add! operation carried out
in base $3$, written in base $10$.
$a(0) = 103$, and $a(n+1) = a(n) + \text{rev}_3(a(n))$.

*References:*
- [A077408](https://oeis.org/A077408)

statements.name: OeisA77408.conjecture
statements.doc:
$103$ is conjectured to be the smallest number such that the Reverse and Add! algorithm in base $3$
does not lead to a palindrome. Its trajectory is conjectured to never reach a palindrome.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 3 (a n)

problems.title: $a(1)=1, a(2)=1, a(n)=(2^{a(n-1)} + 1)/a(n-2)$
problems.doc:
The sequence is defined by $a(1) = 1, a(2) = 1$, and for $n \ge 3$,
$$a(n) = \frac{2^{a(n-1)} + 1}{a(n-2)}$$

*References:*
- [A078590](https://oeis.org/A078590)

statements.name: OeisA78590.conjecture
statements.doc:
Are all terms integers?

No. Exact divisibility first fails at $n = 7$; the corresponding rational term has reduced
denominator $19$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ, 3 ≤ n → a (n - 2) ∣ 2 ^ a (n - 1) + 1

problems.title: Smallest $m > 0$ such that $n \cdot 2^m + 1$ is prime
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the smallest positive integer $m$ such that $n \cdot 2^m + 1$ is prime,
or $0$ if no such $m$ exists.

*References:*
- [A078680](https://oeis.org/A078680)

statements.name: OeisA78680.conjecture
statements.doc:
There is a conjecture that the first zero is $n = 65536 = 2^{16}$ (which is equivalent to
the statement that $2^{2^k} + 1$ is composite for $k > 4$). - _T. D. Noe_, Feb 25 2011
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    a (2 ^ 16) = 0 ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n ∧ n < 2 ^ 16 → a n ≠ 0

problems.title: Least $k > 0$ such that $(k+1)(k+2)\cdots(k+n) + 1$ is prime
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the least positive integer $k$ such that $(k+1)(k+2)\cdots(k+n) + 1$ is
prime,
if such $k$ exists; otherwise $a(n) = 0$.

*References:*
- [A078729](https://oeis.org/A078729)

statements.name: OeisA78729.conjecture
statements.doc:
$(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)(k+4) + 1 = (k^2 + 5k + 5)^2$, which is never prime. Hence $a(4) = 0$.
Conjecture: $a(n) = 0$ if and only if $n = 4$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) : a n = 0 ↔ n = 4

problems.title: $a(n) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{2k}{k}^3$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n) = 1 + \binom{2}{1}^3 + \binom{4}{2}^3 + \cdots + \binom{2n}{n}^3$:
$$a(n) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{2k}{k}^3$$

*References:*
- [A079727](https://oeis.org/A079727)

statements.name: OeisA79727.conjecture1
statements.doc:
Conjecture 1 (Peter Bala, 2024):
If prime $p$ is in A003625 then $a(p^2) \equiv 8 + p^2 \pmod{p^3}$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture1 (p : ℕ) (hp : OeisA3625.A p) :
    a (p ^ 2) ≡ 8 + p ^ 2 [MOD p ^ 3]

statements.name: OeisA79727.conjecture2
statements.doc:
Conjecture 2 (Peter Bala, 2024):
If prime $p$ is in A003625 then $a(p(p-1)) \equiv p^2 \pmod{p^3}$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2 (p : ℕ) (hp : OeisA3625.A p) :
    a (p * (p - 1)) ≡ p ^ 2 [MOD p ^ 3]

statements.name: OeisA79727.conjecture3
statements.doc:
Conjecture 3 (Peter Bala, 2024):
If prime $p$ is in A003625 then $a((p^2-1)/2) \equiv p^2 \pmod{p^4}$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture3 (p : ℕ) (hp : OeisA3625.A p) :
    a ((p ^ 2 - 1) / 2) ≡ p ^ 2 [MOD p ^ 4]

statements.name: OeisA79727.conjecture4
statements.doc:
Conjecture 4 (Peter Bala, 2024):
If $n$ is a product of distinct primes from A003625 then $a((n-1)/2)$ is divisible by $n^2$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture4 (S : Finset ℕ) (hS : ∀ p ∈ S, OeisA3625.A p) :
    (∏ p ∈ S, p) ^ 2 ∣ a ((∏ p ∈ S, p - 1) / 2)

problems.title: Number of prime powers strictly between $n$-th prime and $(n+1)$-th prime
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the number of prime powers $k$ strictly between the $n$-th prime $p_n$
and the $(n+1)$-th prime $p_{n+1}$: $p_n < k < p_{n+1}$.

*References:*
- [A080101](https://oeis.org/A080101)

statements.name: OeisA80101.conjecture
statements.doc: It is conjectured that $a(n) \le 2$ for all $n$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) : a n ≤ 2

problems.title: Conjecture relating two characterizations of a set of integers.
problems.doc:
Informal Statement:
For an integer $k \ge 2$, the following are equivalent:

1. The greatest common divisor of the binomial coefficients
    $\binom{2k}{k}, \binom{3k}{k}, \dots, \binom{(k+1)k}{k} = 1$.

2. Writing prime factorization of $k$ as
    $k = \prod p_i^{e_i}$, and let
    $P = \max_i p_i^{e_i}$,
    one has $k / P > P$.

This conjecture asserts that the sequence defined by 1. is obtained by
taking 1 off each number in the sequence defined by 2.

*References:*
- [A80170](https://oeis.org/A80170)
- [A51283](https://oeis.org/A51283)

statements.name: OeisA80170.gcdCondition_iff_primePowerCondition
statements.doc:
Conjecture: The gcd condition is equivalent to the prime power condition.
This has been conjectured by Ralf Stephan.

Both the natural-language proof and its Lean 4 formalization were carried out
by the KLMM MechMath Agent Team; see the `formal_proof` attribute.

*References:*
- [Ralf Stephan, *Prove or Disprove. 100 Conjectures from the OEIS*, 2004, Conjecture 17 (arXiv:math/0409509)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409509)
- [Dakai Guo et al., *A Greatest Common Divisor Criterion of Certain Binomial Coefficients*, 2026 (arXiv:2606.22997)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22997)
statements.statement:
theorem gcdCondition_iff_primePowerCondition (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) :
    A k ↔ B (k + 1)

problems.title: Denominator of $\sum_{k=1}^n k^{\mu(k)}$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the denominator of $\sum_{k=1}^n k^{\mu(k)}$, where $\mu$ is the
Möbius function.

*References:*
- [A080326](https://oeis.org/A080326)

statements.name: OeisA80326.conjecture
statements.doc: Conjecture: $a(n) = \text{primorial}(n)$ for infinitely many $n$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : {n : ℕ | a n = primorial n}.Infinite

problems.title: Primes of the form 2^n + 2^i + 1
problems.doc:
There are infinite primes of the form $2^n + 2^i + 1$, with $0 < i < n$.
See Wagstaff (2001) where this conjecture is posed.

*References:*
- [A81091](https://oeis.org/A81091)
- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., [Prime Numbers with a fixed number of one bits or zero bits in their binary representation](http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.em/999188636), Exp. Math. vol. 10, issue 2 (2001) 267.

statements.name: OeisA81091.conjectureA81091
statements.doc:
**Conjecture (A81091)**: There are infinite primes of the form $2^n + 2^i + 1$,
with $0 < i < n$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjectureA81091 :
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | A p}

problems.title: Smallest palindrome with exactly $n$ divisors
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the smallest palindromic number with exactly $n$ divisors, or $0$
if no such number exists.

*References:*
- [A083753](https://oeis.org/A083753)

statements.name: OeisA83753.conjecture
statements.doc:
There are no palindromic numbers greater than 1 which are the fifth or higher power of a natural
number.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture (m k : ℕ) (hm : 1 < m) (hpal : IsDecimalPalindrome m) (hk : 5 ≤ k) :
    ¬ ∃ x : ℕ, m = x ^ k

problems.title: Smallest prime $p$ such that $p + n$ is an $n$-th power
problems.doc:
Smallest prime $p$ such that $p + n$ is an $n$-th power, or $0$ if no such number exists.
That is, the smallest prime of the form $k^n - n$.

*References:*
- [A084046](https://oeis.org/A084046)

statements.name: OeisA84046.conjecture
statements.doc:
Conjecture: if a(k) = 0 then k is an even square.

This is false for $k = 27$. Every candidate $x^{27} - 27$ factors as
$(x^9 - 3)(x^{18} + 3x^9 + 9)$, so $a(27) = 0$, but $27$ is not an even square.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : ¬ ∀ k : ℕ, a k = 0 → ∃ m : ℕ, k = (2 * m) ^ 2

problems.title: Smallest $r$ such that (concatenation of $n$, $r$ times) $\cdot 10 + 1$ is prime
problems.doc:
$a(n)$ is the smallest $r$ where (concatenation of $n$, $r$ times with itself) $\cdot 10 + 1$
is a prime, or $0$ if no such number exists.
The number resulting from concatenating $n$, $r$ times, is
$n \cdot \sum_{i=0}^{r-1} (10^d)^i$, where $d$ is the number of digits of $n$.

*References:*
- [A086766](https://oeis.org/A086766)

statements.name: OeisA86766.conjecture1
statements.doc:
What is the smallest integer $m > 1$ such that $a(10^m)$ is nonzero?
- _Farideh Firoozbakht_, Jan 07 2015
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture1 :
    conjecture1.answer =
      if h : ∃ m, 1 < m ∧ a (10 ^ m) ≠ 0 then
        some (sInf {m | 1 < m ∧ a (10 ^ m) ≠ 0})
      else
        none

statements.name: OeisA86766.conjecture2
statements.doc:
Conjecture: If $n$ is not of the form $10^m$ then $a(n)$ is nonzero.
- _Farideh Firoozbakht_, Jan 07 2015
statements.statement: theorem conjecture2 (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (h : ∀ m : ℕ, n ≠ 10 ^ m) : a n ≠ 0

statements.name: OeisA86766.conjecture3
statements.doc:
What is the smallest odd prime $p$ such that $(10^{p^2}-1)/(10^p-1)$ is a prime number
(and $a(10^{p-1})$ could be nonzero)?
- _Farideh Firoozbakht_, Jan 07 2015
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture3 :
    conjecture3.answer =
      if h : ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 2 < p ∧ ((10 ^ (p ^ 2) - 1) / (10 ^ p - 1)).Prime then
        some (sInf {p | p.Prime ∧ 2 < p ∧ ((10 ^ (p ^ 2) - 1) / (10 ^ p - 1)).Prime})
      else
        none

problems.title: Binary representation of primes that divide a number, in decimal
problems.doc:
The value $a(n)$ is given by
$$ a(n) = \sum_{p \mid n, p \text{ prime}} 2^{\pi(p) - 1} $$
where $\pi(p) = \mathrm{primeCounting}(p)$ gives the 1-based index of the prime $p$.

*References:*
- [A087207](https://oeis.org/A087207)

statements.name: OeisA87207.conjecture
statements.doc:
Starting at any $n$ and iterating the map $n \mapsto a(n)$, we will always reach $0$.
- _Antti Karttunen_, Jun 18,20 2017
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) : ∃ k : ℕ, (a^[k]) n = 0

problems.title: Expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$
problems.doc:
This sequence is the expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$ in powers of $x$.
It satisfies the linear recurrence relation $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,
with initial values $a(0)=1$ and $a(1)=1$.

*References:*
- [A087455](https://oeis.org/A087455)

statements.name: OeisA87455.conjecture
statements.doc:
It is an open question whether or not this sequence satisfies Benford's law
[Berger-Hill, 2017; Arno Berger, email, Jan 06 2017]. - N. J. A. Sloane, Feb 08 2017
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : SatisfiesBenford a

problems.title: Smallest prime formed by concatenation $n, n-1, \dots, n-k$
problems.doc:
$a(n)$ is the smallest prime which has the form of the concatenation
$n, n-1, n-2, \dots, n-k$ for some $k < n$, or $0$ if no such prime exists.

*References:*
- [A087571](https://oeis.org/A087571)

statements.name: OeisA87571.conjecture
statements.doc: Conjecture: There are infinitely many composite numbers $n$ such that $a(n)$ is nonzero.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (M : ℕ) : ∃ n > M, 1 < n ∧ ¬ n.Prime ∧ a n ≠ 0

problems.title: Conjectures associated with A087719
problems.doc:
Define $\varsigma(n)$ the smallest prime factor of $n$ (`Nat.minFac`). Let $a_n$ be the least
number such that the count of numbers $k \le a_n$ with $k > \varsigma(k)^n$ exceeds the count
of numbers with $k \le \varsigma(k)^n$.

The conjecture states that $a_n = 3^n + 3 \cdot 2^n + 6$ for $n \ge 1$.

*References:*
- [A087719](https://oeis.org/A087719)

statements.name: OeisA87719.a_exists
statements.doc: There exists m such that countExceeding n m > countNotExceeding n m.
statements.statement: theorem a_exists (n : ℕ) : ∃ m, countExceeding n m > countNotExceeding n m

statements.name: OeisA87719.a_formula
statements.doc: We have the following formula: $a(n) = 3^n + 3 * 2^n + 6$ for $n \geq 1$.
statements.statement: theorem a_formula {n : ℕ} (hn : n ≥ 1) : a n = 3 ^ n + 3 * 2 ^ n + 6

problems.title: $a(n) = n$ if $n$ is prime, otherwise $a(n) = 1$
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [A089026](https://oeis.org/A089026)

problems.title: Number of pairs of twin primes between $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$
problems.doc:
$a(n)$ is the number of pairs of twin primes between $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$.
This counts the number of primes $p$ such that $p$ and $p+2$ are both prime,
and the entire twin prime pair $(p, p+2)$ lies strictly between $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$.
That is, $n^2 < p$ and $p + 2 < (n+1)^2$.

*References:*
- [A091591](https://oeis.org/A091591)

statements.name: OeisA91591.conjecture
statements.doc:
It is conjectured that $a(n)>0$ for all $n>122$.
Proving this would also prove Legendre's conjecture that there is a prime
between $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$. - _T. D. Noe_, Feb 28 2007
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ∀ n : ℕ, n > 122 → a n > 0

problems.title: Primality and primitive root property from divisibility $n \mid (a(n-1) + 2^{n-2})$
problems.doc:
$a(n) = \frac{2^{n-1}}{n!} \prod_{k=1}^{n-1} (2^k-1)$.
The sequence $a(n)$ is composed of natural numbers, thus we define it
as a function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$.

*References:*
- [A091669](https://oeis.org/A091669)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.

statements.name: OeisA91669.prime_and_primitive_root_of_dvd
statements.doc:
Conjecture (for $n > 2$): if $n \mid a(n-1) + 2^{n-2}$, then $n$ is a prime with primitive root 2 (A001122). - _Amiram Eldar_ and _Thomas Ordowski_, Jan 19 2020

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
statements.statement:
theorem prime_and_primitive_root_of_dvd (n : ℕ) (hn : n > 2) : n ∣ (a (n - 1) + 2 ^ (n - 2)) →
    Nat.Prime n ∧ IsPrimitiveRoot (2 : ZMod n) (Nat.totient n)

problems.title: Tug of war score between prime gap increases and decreases
problems.doc:
Score at stage $n$ in "tug of war" between prime gap increases vs. prime gap decreases:
start with score $= 0$ at $n = 1$ and at stage $k > 1$, increase (resp. decrease) the score by $1$
if the $k$-th prime gap is greater (resp. less) than the previous prime gap.

*References:*
- [A092243](https://oeis.org/A092243)

statements.name: OeisA92243.conjecture1
statements.doc: Is the score $a(n) > 0$ for some $n > 250000$?
statements.statement: theorem conjecture1 : ∃ n > 250000, a n > 0

statements.name: OeisA92243.conjecture2
statements.doc: Is the score $a(n)$ bounded from below?
statements.statement: theorem conjecture2 : ∃ B : ℤ, ∀ n : ℕ, B ≤ a n

statements.name: OeisA92243.conjecture3
statements.doc: Is the score $a(n)$ bounded from above?
statements.statement: theorem conjecture3 : ∃ B : ℤ, ∀ n : ℕ, a n ≤ B

statements.name: OeisA92243.conjecture4
statements.doc: Is the score $a(n) > 0$ for infinitely many values of $n$?
statements.statement: theorem conjecture4 : Set.Infinite {n : ℕ | a n > 0}

statements.name: OeisA92243.conjecture5
statements.doc: Is the score $a(n) < 0$ for infinitely many values of $n$?
statements.statement: theorem conjecture5 : Set.Infinite {n : ℕ | a n < 0}

problems.title: Product of composite numbers in triangular intervals
problems.doc:
Product of all composite numbers between $n(n-1)/2+1$ and $n(n+1)/2$ (including boundaries),
where $n(n-1)/2 = \binom{n}{2}$ and $n(n+1)/2 = \binom{n+1}{2}$.

*References:*
- [A093456](https://oeis.org/A093456)

statements.name: OeisA93456.conjecture
statements.doc:
Conjecture: There are finitely many numbers such that $a(n)$ is not $\equiv 0 \pmod{a(n-1)}$.
(Also mentioned in A093455.) In fact there are infinitely many such numbers.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ¬ Set.Finite {n : ℕ | 1 < n ∧ ¬ (a (n - 1) ∣ a n)}

problems.title: $\gcd(\mathrm{numerator}(H_n), n!)$
problems.doc:
$a(n) = \gcd(\mathrm{A001008}(n), n!)$, where $\mathrm{A001008}(n)$ is the numerator of
the $n$-th harmonic number $H_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{i}$.

*References:*
- [A093818](https://oeis.org/A093818)

statements.name: OeisA93818.conjecture
statements.doc: Conjecture: Every odd prime occurs as a term in the sequence.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hp_odd : p ≠ 2) : ∃ n > 0, a n = p

problems.title: Recurrence $a(n) = (a(n-1) + a(n-2)) \pmod n$
problems.doc:
$a(0) = a(1) = 1$; $a(n) = (a(n-1) + a(n-2)) \pmod n$.

*References:*
- [A096535](https://oeis.org/A096535)

statements.name: OeisA96535.conjecture
statements.doc:
All numbers appear infinitely often, i.e., for every number $k \ge 0$ and every frequency $f > 0$
there is an index $i$ such that $a(i) = k$ is the $f$-th occurrence of $k$ in the sequence.
- _Klaus Brockhaus_, Aug 29 2006
statements.statement: theorem conjecture (k : ℕ) (N : ℕ) : ∃ i : ℕ, i > N ∧ a i = k

problems.title: Coefficients in a simultaneous approximation to two polylogarithms
problems.doc:
Coefficients in a simultaneous approximation to $\operatorname{Li}_2(-1)$ and
$\operatorname{Li}_3(-1)$, given by
$a(n)=\sum_{i,j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^2\binom{n}{j}^2\binom{n+i}{n}\binom{i+j}{i}$.

*References:*
- [A098275](https://oeis.org/A098275)
- [Li26] Wentao Li, [A proof of the OEIS A098275 conjecture](https://github.com/VictorLiwentao/lean-oeis-proofs/blob/0a23974e54b90afd1453ef02c27cf8f617bad940/proofs/new-proofs/A098275/PROOF.md), 2026.

statements.name: OeisA98275.conjecture_1
statements.doc:
Conjecture 1:
"Conjecture: $a(n)$ is divisible by $n+1$."
- F. Chapoton, Jan 28 2026.

Proved and formalized in Lean by Wentao Li, with AI assistance; see [Li26].
statements.statement: theorem conjecture_1 (n : ℕ) : n + 1 ∣ a n

problems.title: Expansion of g.f. $(1+x)(3+x)/(1+6x^2+x^4)$
problems.doc:
This sequence is defined by the linear recurrence relation
$a(n) = -6 a(n-2) - a(n-4)$ for $n \ge 4$,
with initial values $a(0)=3$, $a(1)=4$, $a(2)=-17$, $a(3)=-24$.

*References:*
- [A100434](https://oeis.org/A100434)

statements.name: OeisA100434.a_even
statements.doc: For all $n \ge 0$, we have $a(2n) = - c(2n+1)$.
statements.statement: theorem a_even (n : ℕ) : a (2 * n) = - c (2 * n + 1)

statements.name: OeisA100434.a_odd
statements.doc: For all $n \ge 0$, we have $a(2n+1) = d(2n+1)$.
statements.statement: theorem a_odd (n : ℕ) : a (2 * n + 1) = d (2 * n + 1)

statements.name: OeisA100434.conjecture1
statements.doc:
**Conjecture from Creighton Dement (A100434)**:
Let the auxiliary sequences c, d, e, f, g, b be defined as specified.
Then for all $n \ge 0$, $c(n) + d(n) = b(n)$.

**Proof outline**:
strong two-step induction on the paired recurrences. The even/odd cases are coupled
through closed identities between consecutive terms of the relevant pair of sequences
(here $c, d$), and the induction step is discharged by `rfl`-level unfolding of the definitions
plus linear arithmetic. (Numerically verified for $n < 600$ before formalization.)
statements.statement: theorem conjecture1 (n : ℕ) : c n + d n = b n

statements.name: OeisA100434.conjecture2
statements.doc:
**Conjecture from Creighton Dement (A100434)**:
Let the auxiliary sequences c, d, e, f, g, b be defined as specified.
Then for all $n \ge 0$, $e(n) + f(n) = b(n)$.

**Proof outline**:
strong two-step induction on the paired recurrences. The even/odd cases are coupled
through closed identities between consecutive terms of the relevant pair of sequences
(here $e, f$), and the induction step is discharged by `rfl`-level unfolding of the definitions
plus linear arithmetic. (Numerically verified for $n < 600$ before formalization.)
statements.statement: theorem conjecture2 (n : ℕ) : e n + f n = b n

statements.name: OeisA100434.conjecture3
statements.doc:
**Conjecture from Creighton Dement (A100434)**:
Let the auxiliary sequences c, d, e, f, g, b be defined as specified.
Then for all $n \ge 0$, $g(n) + a(n) = b(n)$.

**Proof outline**:
strong two-step induction on the paired recurrences. The even/odd cases are coupled
through closed identities between consecutive terms of the relevant pair of sequences
(here $g, a$), and the induction step is discharged by `rfl`-level unfolding of the definitions
plus linear arithmetic. (Numerically verified for $n < 600$ before formalization.)
statements.statement: theorem conjecture3 (n : ℕ) : g n + a n = b n

problems.title: Prime-th recurrence with reversal at each step
problems.doc:
$$a(n) = \operatorname{reversal}(p_{a(n-1)})$$
with $a(0)=1$, where $p_k$ is the $k$-th prime number.

*References:*
- [A100475](https://oeis.org/A100475)

statements.name: OeisA100475.conjecture_with_zero
statements.doc:
If zero is admitted as a starting value, then a start other than $1$ does go into a loop: the
sequence starting at zero is constant. This records the degenerate answer created by totalizing
the one-based prime recurrence at index zero.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture_with_zero :
    ∃ x : ℕ, x ≠ 1 ∧ IsUltimatelyPeriodic (aStartAt x)

statements.name: OeisA100475.conjecture
statements.doc:
Starting at a positive value other than $a(0) = 1$, does this sequence ever go into a loop?

The positivity hypothesis is required because the source recurrence uses the one-based prime index
`p₁ = 2`; the `x = 0` branch above is only an artifact of making `aStartAt` total on `ℕ`.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ∃ x : ℕ, 0 < x ∧ x ≠ 1 ∧ IsUltimatelyPeriodic (aStartAt x)

problems.title: Pentanacci $\pi$ sequence
problems.doc:
Start with $a(1)=a(2)=a(3)=a(4)=a(5)=1$ and
for $n>5$, $a(n) = \pi(\sum_{j=1}^5 a(n-j))$ where $\pi = A000720$.

statements.name: OeisA100478.conjecture
statements.doc:
Starting with other values of $a(1)$, $a(2)$, $a(3)$, $a(4)$, $a(5)$ what behaviors are possible?
Does the sequence always stick at a single integer after some point, or can it go into a loop,
or is there a third pattern?

KitaKen1 showed the sequence either becomes constant or goes into a loop,
see https://github.com/KitaKen1/oeis-a100478-eventual-periodicity/blob/642eed0ffee26415528ab8c48c5181826be04860/lean/OeisA100478FC.lean#L158-L168.

tadamcz showed the sequence always becomes constant, see
https://tadamcz.com/fc-review-results/aea251bb26/#/f/OEIS/100478.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture:
  ∀ v : Fin 5 → ℕ, (∀ i, 0 < v i) → ∃ c ∈ ({66, 67, 68, 70, 71, 72} : Finset ℕ),
  ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, aGeneral v n = c

problems.title: Conjectures associated with A102371
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is defined by the recurrence relation $a(1)=1$,
and for $n>1$, $a(n) = a(n-1) \operatorname{XOR} (a(n-1) + n)$.
The conjecture asks if $a(n) = 2^n - 1 - \operatorname{A105033}(n-1)$ for $n \ge 1$.

*References:*
- [A102371](https://oeis.org/A102371)

statements.name: OeisA102371.conjecture
statements.doc:
Do we have $a(n) = 2^n - 1 - \operatorname{A105033}(n-1)$ for $n \ge 1$?

Note: The OEIS comment suggests $n-1$ which means this applies at least for $n \ge 1$,
as we assume $\operatorname{A105033}(\mathbb{N})$ is defined on $\mathbb{N}$.
We include the case $n=1$ which relies on $A105033(0)$, which is 0.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → a n = 2^n - 1 - OeisA105033.a (n - 1)

problems.title: Floor of sum of $\{n/k\}$
problems.doc:
Given $n$, sum all division remainders $\{n/k\}$, with $k=1,\dots,n$.
The value $a(n)$ is given by the floor of that sum. Note that $\{x\}:=x-[x]$.
Conjecture: a(n) ~ (1-EulerGamma)n.

      (fun n : ℕ => (1 - Real.eulerMascheroniConstant) * (n : ℝ))

problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ satisfies the linear recurrence relation:
$$a(n) = 3a(n-1) - 4a(n-2) + 2a(n-3) - a(n-4)$$
with initial terms $a(0)=0, a(1)=1, a(2)=1, a(3)=0$.
The sequence takes values in $\mathbb{Z}$.

*References:*

Fibonacci transform satisfying $|a(n)| = F(n+1)$.

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
statements.statement: theorem a_abs_eq_fib (n : ℕ) : ∃ m : ℕ, Int.natAbs (a n) = Nat.fib m

problems.title: $a(n) = 3a(n-1) + a(n-2) - 3a(n-3)$
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [A103425](https://oeis.org/A103425)

statements.name: OeisA103425.conjecture
statements.doc:
The current sequence contains primes, including $3, 5, 41, 21523361$.
Is there an $(a, b, c)$ weighted tribonacci sequence with $a, b, c$ relatively prime
which is prime-free?

Yes: take $(a, b, c) = (1, 1, -1)$ and the constant sequence $x(n) = 4$.
The linked Lean proof is by Kenta Kitamura.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ∃ (a b c : ℤ) (x : ℕ → ℤ),
      Nat.gcd (Int.gcd a b) c.natAbs = 1 ∧
      IsWeightedTribonacci a b c x ∧
      ∀ n, ¬ (x n).natAbs.Prime

statements.name: OeisA103425.conjecture.variants.nonconstant
statements.doc:
Is there a non-constant $(a, b, c)$ weighted tribonacci sequence with $a, b, c$ relatively
prime which is prime-free?

Yes: take $(a, b, c) = (1, 1, -1)$ and $x(n) = 4(n + 1)$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture.variants.nonconstant :
    ∃ (a b c : ℤ) (x : ℕ → ℤ),
      Nat.gcd (Int.gcd a b) c.natAbs = 1 ∧
      IsWeightedTribonacci a b c x ∧
      (∃ m n, x m ≠ x n) ∧
      ∀ n, ¬ (x n).natAbs.Prime

statements.name: OeisA103425.conjecture.variants.nonconstant_distinct_coeffs
statements.doc:
Is there a non-constant $(a, b, c)$ weighted tribonacci sequence with $a, b, c$ relatively
prime and pairwise distinct which is prime-free?

Yes: take $(a, b, c) = (3, -3, 1)$ and $x(n) = (n + 2)^2$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture.variants.nonconstant_distinct_coeffs :
    ∃ (a b c : ℤ) (x : ℕ → ℤ),
      Nat.gcd (Int.gcd a b) c.natAbs = 1 ∧
      a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ b ≠ c ∧
      IsWeightedTribonacci a b c x ∧
      (∃ m n, x m ≠ x n) ∧
      ∀ n, ¬ (x n).natAbs.Prime

problems.title: Smallest power with base>1 and exponent $n$ without digit 0
problems.doc:
For statistical reasons it is conjectured that the sequence is finite.
Also it is conjectured that $a(40)$ does not exist (i.e. the sequence is empty for $n=40$).

*References:*
- [A103662](https://oeis.org/A103662)

statements.name: OeisA103662.conjecture
statements.doc:
For statistical reasons it is conjectured that the sequence is finite.
Finite means here that for some $n$, no power $b^n$ with base $b > 1$ has a zeroless decimal
representation, which in our definition results in $a(n) = 0$.

This holds for $n = 2500$
([source](https://tadamcz.com/fc-review-results/aea251bb26/#/f/OEIS/103662)).
Take any integer $b > 1$ and let $N = b^{2500}$. Since $b \ge 2$, we have
$N \ge 2^{2500} > 10^5$, so $N$ has at least six decimal digits. We split into four cases
depending on the divisibility of $b$ by $2$ and $5$:

- **If $10 \mid b$:** Then $10 \mid N$, so the units digit of $N$ is $0$.
- **If $b$ is odd and $5 \nmid b$:** Since $b$ is odd and the Carmichael function satisfies
  $\lambda(16) = 4 \mid 2500$, we have $N \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$. Since $5 \nmid b$ and
  $\varphi(5^5) = 2500$, Euler's totient theorem gives $N \equiv 1 \pmod{3125}$. By the Chinese
  Remainder Theorem, $N \equiv 1 \pmod{50000}$ (as $16 \cdot 3125 = 50000$), so the tens digit
  of $N$ is $0$.
- **If $b$ is odd and $5 \mid b$:** As above, $N \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$. Since $5 \mid b$ and
  $2500 \ge 4$, we also have $5^4 = 625 \mid N$, so $N \equiv 0 \pmod{625}$. Since
  $16 \cdot 625 = 10^4$ and $625 \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$, the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives
  $N \equiv 625 \pmod{10^4}$. Because $N > 10^4$, the last four digits of $N$ are $0625$, so its
  thousands digit is $0$.
- **If $b$ is even and $5 \nmid b$:** Since $2 \mid b$ and $2500 \ge 5$, we have
  $2^5 = 32 \mid N$, so $N \equiv 0 \pmod{32}$. Since $5 \nmid b$, Euler's theorem again gives
  $N \equiv 1 \pmod{3125}$. Because $32 \cdot 3125 = 10^5$ and
  $9376 = 293 \cdot 32 = 3 \cdot 3125 + 1$, the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives
  $N \equiv 9376 \pmod{10^5}$. Since $N > 10^5$, the last five digits of $N$ are $09376$, so its
  ten-thousands digit is $0$.

In every case, the decimal representation of $N$ contains the digit $0$, so $a(2500) = 0$.
statements.statement: theorem conjecture : ∃ n : ℕ, a n = 0

statements.name: OeisA103662.conjecture.variants.a_40
statements.doc:
$a(40)$, if it exists, is not known.

This claim is rooted in the finiteness conjecture. The most direct mathematical expression
of the open problem concerning $a(40)$ is the negation of the existence of a valid base.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture.variants.a_40 :
  ¬ ∃ (b : ℕ), IsValidZerolessPower 40 b

problems.title: $a(n) = [x^{2n}] \left(\frac{1 + x}{1 - x}\right)^n$
problems.doc:
The sequence is given by the combinatorial identity:
$a(n) = \sum_{k = 0}^n \binom{n}{k} \binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}$
with $a(0) = 1$.

*References:*
- [A103885](https://oeis.org/A103885)

statements.name: OeisA103885.conjecture
statements.doc:
The recurrence given below can be rewritten in the form
$$(2n+1)(2n+2)P(2,n)a(n+1) - (2n-1)(2n-2)P(2,-n)a(n-1) = Q(2,n^2)a(n),$$
where the polynomial $Q(2,n) = 4(55n^2 - 34n + 3)$ and the polynomial $P(2,n) = 5n^2 - 5n + 1$
satisfies the symmetry condition $P(2,n) = P(2,1-n)$ and has real zeros.
More generally, for fixed $m = 1,2,3, \ldots$, we conjecture that the sequence $b(n) := a(mn)$
satisfies a recurrence of the form
$$( \prod_{k = 1}^{2m} (2mn + k) )P(2m,n)b(n+1) + (-1)^m( \prod_{k = 1}^{2*m} (2mn - k) )
  P(2m,-n)b(n-1) = Q(2m,n^2)b(n),$$
where the polynomials $P(2m,n)$ and $Q(2m,n)$ have degree $2m$. Conjecturally, the polynomial
$P(2m,n) = P(2m,1-n)$ and has real zeros in the interval [0, 1].
The $4m$ zeros of the polynomial $Q(2m,n^2)$ seem to belong to the interval $[-1, 1]$ and
$4m - 2$ of these zeros appear to be approximated by the rational numbers
$\pm k/(3m)$, where $1 \le k \le 3m - 2$, $k$ not a multiple of $3$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) :
    ∃ (P Q : Polynomial ℝ),
      -- P and Q have degree 2m
      P.degree = (2 * m : ℕ) ∧ Q.degree = (2 * m : ℕ) ∧
      -- The recurrence relation holds for all n >= 1
      (∀ (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n),
        (prodFactorPlus m n * P.eval (n : ℝ)) * (aSubsequenceReal m (n + 1)) +

        ((-1 : ℝ) ^ m * prodFactorMinus m n * P.eval (-(n : ℝ))) * (aSubsequenceReal m (n - 1)) =

        (Q.eval ((n : ℝ)^2)) * (aSubsequenceReal m n)) ∧

      -- P symmetry: P(x) = P(1-x)
      (∀ x : ℝ, P.eval x = P.eval (1 - x)) ∧

      -- P has real zeros in [0, 1]: all complex zeros are real and in [0, 1]
      (∀ z : ℂ, (P.map (algebraMap ℝ ℂ)).eval z = 0 → z.im = 0 ∧ z.re ∈ (Set.Icc 0 1)) ∧

      -- Q zero properties: The zeros of Q(x^2) are real and in [-1, 1].
      (∀ z : ℂ, (Q.map (algebraMap ℝ ℂ)).eval (z^2) = 0 → z.im = 0 ∧ z.re ∈ (Set.Icc (-1) 1))

problems.title: Array read by upward antidiagonals
problems.doc:
Array read by upward antidiagonals: row $n$ ($n \ge 0$) contains the numbers
$m^2 - n^2$, $m \ge n+1$.

*References:*
- [A105020](https://oeis.org/A105020)

statements.name: OeisA105020.conjecture
statements.doc:
A "Goldbach Conjecture" for this sequence: when there are $n$ terms between consecutive odd
integers $2n+1$ and $2n+3$ for $n > 0$, at least one will be the product of 2 primes
(not necessarily distinct). Example: $n=3$ for consecutive odd integers $a(7) = 7$ and
$a(11) = 9$ and of the 3 sequence entries $a(8) = 12$, $a(9) = 15$ and $a(10) = 16$ between
them, one is the product of 2 primes $a(9) = 15=3*5$. - _Michael Hiebl_, Jul 15 2007
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
  ∀ (n i j : ℕ), 1 ≤ n →
    a i = 2 * n + 1 →
    a j = 2 * n + 3 →
    j = i + n + 1 →
    ∃ (k : ℕ),
      i < k ∧
      k < j ∧
      (a k).IsSemiprime

statements.name: OeisA105210.conjecture_disjoint_starting_values
statements.doc:
Cormier and Selfridge found 5 starting values for which the sequences appear to not merge.
The sequences were checked up to 10^8.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture_disjoint_starting_values :
    ∀ j k : ℕ,
      j ∈ ({1, 393, 412, 668, 932} : Set ℕ) →
      k ∈ ({1, 393, 412, 668, 932} : Set ℕ) →
      j ≠ k →
      sequenceSet j ∩ sequenceSet k = ∅

statements.name: OeisA105210.conjecture

This suggests that there may be infinitely many different (non-merging) sequences obtained
by choosing different starting values.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
  ∃ K : Set ℕ,
    Set.Infinite K ∧
    (∀ k ∈ K, 1 ≤ k) ∧
    (∀ j k : ℕ,
      j ∈ K → k ∈ K → j ≠ k →
      sequenceSet j ∩ sequenceSet k = ∅)

problems.title: Indicator sequence for 5 Fibonacci numbers with n digits
problems.doc:
$a(n) = 1$ if exactly 5 Fibonacci numbers exist with exactly $n$ digits, otherwise $0$.
For the partial sums $S(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n a(k)$, it is conjectured that
$\beta-2 < S(n)-\alpha n < \beta-1$, where $\alpha = \log(10)/\log(\phi) - 4$
and $\beta = \log(5)/(2\log(\phi)) - 1$.

*References:*

statements.name: OeisA105565.conjecture
statements.doc:
Conjecture: $\beta-2 < S(n)-\alpha n < \beta-1$.
The constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are as defined in the formula section.

Solved by OpenAI Codex, prompted by Adam Haig. A complete Lean 4 proof is
linked by the `formal_proof` attribute below.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    betaConst - 2 < s n - alphaConst * (n : Real) ∧
      s n - alphaConst * (n : Real) < betaConst - 1

statements.name: OeisA105751.prime_divides_some_term
statements.doc:
Numerical calculation suggests that a similar division holds in this case.
Type 1: primes p that do not divide any element of the sequence {$a(n)$}.
In this case, unlike in A105750, the set of type 1 primes is empty;
that is, every prime p divides some term of this sequence.

Note: The triangular number n*(n+1)/2 divides $a(n)$ (see A164652).
In particular, if $p$ is an odd prime then $p$ divides $a(p)$. For $p=2$, $2$ divides $a(4)=-40$.
statements.statement:
theorem prime_divides_some_term (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) :
    ∃ n : ℕ, a n ≠ 0 ∧ (p : ℤ) ∣ a n

statements.name: OeisA105751.conjecture
statements.doc:
Moll's conjecture 5.5 extends to this sequence and takes the form:
(i) the $2$-adic valuation $\nu_2(a(n)) \sim n/4$ as n -> oo.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    Tendsto (fun n ↦ (4 : ℚ) * (padicValInt 2 (a n) : ℚ) / (n : ℚ)) atTop (nhds 1)

statements.name: OeisA105751.conjecture.variants.moll_p_mod_4_eq_1
statements.doc:
Moll's conjecture 5.5 extends to this sequence and takes the form:
(ii) for the other primes of type $2$, the p-adic valuation
$\nu_p(a(n)) \sim n/(p - 1)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

(Type 2 primes consists of primes p == 1 (mod 4))
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture.variants.moll_p_mod_4_eq_1 {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h_mod : p % 4 = 1) :
    Tendsto (fun n ↦ ((p - 1 : ℚ) * (padicValInt p (a n) : ℚ)) / (n : ℚ)) atTop (nhds 1)

problems.title: Fibonacci-Collatz sequence
problems.doc:
Fibonacci-Collatz sequence: $a(1)=1, a(2)=2$; for $n > 2$, let $\mathrm{fib} = a(n-1) + a(n-2)$;
if $\mathrm{fib}$ is odd then $a(n) = 3 \cdot \mathrm{fib} + 1$ else $a(n) = \mathrm{fib}/2$.

*References:*
- [A105801](https://oeis.org/A105801)

statements.name: OeisA105801.conjecture
statements.doc:
Conjecture: for every $k > 0$ there is an index $m$ such that all the $a(n)$ with $n > m$
have the same residue $\bmod 3^k$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture :
    ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → ∃ m : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, m < n → a n ≡ a (m + 1) [MOD (3^k)]

$a(11) = 86 = 2 * 43$, $a(13) = 1366 = 2 * 683$, $a(14) = 5462 = 2 * 2731$,
$a(16) = 87382 = 2 * 43691$, $a(17) = 348503 = 37 * 9419$,
$a(27) = 358201316657 = 71 * 5045088967$.
(Note: The OEIS comment uses 1-based indexing, so their indices are shifted by +1 compared
to this formalization).

problems.title: $a(n) = \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{2n-i}{n+i}$
problems.doc:
Alternatively the sequence `a` can be defined as
$a(n) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n+k-1}{k} F(n-k+1)$, where $F(m)$ is the $m$-th Fibonacci number.
We formalize a conjecture about the number of words of length $n$ in a set $X$ being related
to this sequence.

- [A108081](https://oeis.org/A108081)

statements.name: OeisA108081.count_words_in_x_is_a_shifted
statements.doc:
"The number of words of length $n$ for $n \le 12$ is given by $a(n+1)$. Is this always true?"

Formalized as $|X_n| = a(n-1)$ for $n \ge 1$, because the sequence values $a(0)=1, a(1)=2, a(2)=7$
match the examples given for word lengths $n=1, 2, 3$ respectively.

Solved: a Lean 4 proof, derived from the Atlas proofs in
[facebookresearch/atlas-lean](https://github.com/facebookresearch/atlas-lean), is linked in
`formal_proof`.
statements.statement:
theorem count_words_in_x_is_a_shifted (n : ℕ) :
    n ≥ 1 → Set.ncard (xN n) = a (n - 1)

problems.title: $a(n) = 16n^2 + 1$
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [A108211](https://oeis.org/A108211)

statements.name: OeisA108211.conjecture
statements.doc:
Conjecture:
$$a(n) = \left\lfloor \frac{1}{\frac{1}{4n} - \log(2) +
  \frac{1}{n+1} + \frac{1}{n+2} + \dots + \frac{1}{2n}} \right\rfloor.$$

**Proof sketch** (certificate style; the kernel-checked development lives at the
`formal_proof` permalink below). Write $T(n) = \log 2 - (H(2n) - H(n))$ for the harmonic
tail defect. The proof sandwiches $T(n)$ between two explicit telescoping bounds — $h(n)$
from below and $h(n) + 60/(4n+1)^7$ from above, where $h$ telescopes a degree-7 rational
certificate. The two resulting inequalities reduce to polynomial coefficient-nonnegativity
facts discharged by elementary tactics, after which the reciprocal lands in
$[16n^2 + 1,\, 16n^2 + 2)$ and the floor evaluates exactly.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : n > 0) :
    (a n : ℝ) =
      (⌊ 1 / ((4 * n : ℝ)⁻¹ - log 2 + ∑ k ∈ (Finset.Icc (n + 1) (2 * n)), (k : ℝ)⁻¹) ⌋ : ℝ)

problems.title: Numerator of $\binom{6n-2}{2n} / \left(2 \binom{4n-1}{2n}\right)$
problems.doc:
The sequence $a(n)$ is the numerator of $\binom{6n-2}{2n} / \left(2 \binom{4n-1}{2n}\right)$.
The OEIS entry records the conjecture that this ratio equals $\text{A005156}(n) / \text{A005156}(n-1)$,
where $\text{A005156}(n)$ is the number of $(2n+1) \times (2n+1)$ vertically symmetric alternating
sign matrices (VSASMs). This follows from Robbins's VSASM product formula, proved by Kuperberg
(2002).

*References:*
- [A109074](https://oeis.org/A109074)
- [A005156](https://oeis.org/A005156)
- G. Kuperberg, "Symmetry classes of alternating-sign matrices under one roof,"
  [arXiv:math/0008184](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0008184), *Ann. of Math.* **156** (2002),
  835–866.

statements.name: OeisA109074.conjecture
statements.doc:
"It is conjectured that $\binom{6n-2}{2n} / \left(2 \binom{4n-1}{2n}\right) =
\text{A005156}(n+1)/\text{A005156}(n)$."

The OEIS comment indexes A005156 from $1$; for the $0$-indexed sequence `b` this states
`frac (n + 1) = b (n + 1) / b n`. This holds by the product formula
$$\text{A005156}(n) = \frac{1}{2^n} \prod_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(6k-2)!\,(2k-1)!}{(4k-1)!\,(4k-2)!}$$
conjectured by Robbins and proved by Kuperberg (2002).
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture (n : ℕ) :
    frac (n + 1) = (b (n + 1) : ℚ) / (b n : ℚ)

problems.doc:
The canonical prime factorization is $n = p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$.
The written form is $p_1^{\wedge} e_1 * p_2^{\wedge} e_2 * \cdots * p_k^{\wedge} e_k$,
where the $\wedge$ appears only if $e_i > 1$.
$a(n) = (\text{number of distinct prime factors}) - 1 +$
$(\text{number of distinct prime factors with exponent } > 1)$.

problems.title: Number of refactorable numbers (A033950) $\le 10^n$
problems.doc:
A number $k$ is refactorable if its number of divisors, $\tau(k)$, divides $k$.

*References:*
- [A111291](https://oeis.org/A111291)
- [Co99] Colton, S., *Refactorable numbers - a machine invention*. J. Integer Seq. 2 (1999),
  Article 99.1.2.
- [Ze02] Zelinsky, J., *Tau numbers: a partial proof of a conjecture and other results*.
  J. Integer Seq. 5 (2002), Article 02.2.8.
- [Sp85] Spiro, C., *How often is the number of divisors of n a divisor of n?*
  J. Number Theory 21 (1985), 81--100.

statements.name: OeisA111291.conjecture
statements.doc:
Simon Colton conjectures that the number of refactorable numbers less than $x$ is at least
$\frac{x}{2\log x}$. This is an asymptotic claim, so we state it for sufficiently large $x$.

In this form it is a theorem: Zelinsky [Ze02, Theorem 7] proved that for every $k$ the number of
refactorable numbers $\le n$ exceeds $k \pi(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and
$\pi(n) \sim n / \log n$. It also follows from Spiro's asymptotic [Sp85], by which the count is
$\frac{x}{\sqrt{\log x}} (\log \log x)^{-1 + o(1)}$. See `colton_conjecture` for the
pointwise conjecture that remains open.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture : ∀ᶠ x in Filter.atTop,
    (countRefactorable x : ℝ) ≥ x / (2 * Real.log x)

statements.name: OeisA111291.colton_conjecture
statements.doc:
Colton's conjecture [Co99] as stated by Zelinsky [Ze02]: for every $n$, the number of
refactorable numbers $\le n$ is at least half the number of primes $\le n$, i.e.
$\pi(n) \le 2\,T(n)$.

Zelinsky [Ze02] proved this for all sufficiently large $n$ (see `conjecture`), with an explicit
bound of $7.42 \cdot 10^{13}$ beyond which it holds; the remaining range is open.
statements.statement: theorem colton_conjecture : ∀ n : ℕ, Nat.primeCounting n ≤ 2 * countRefactorableNat n

statements.name: OeisA114831.conjecture3
statements.doc:
Conjecture based on OEIS A114831: What is this sequence, asymptotically?
If the limit exists, the ratio of consecutive terms must tend to $\sqrt{3}$:
$$ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a(n+1)}{a(n)} = \sqrt{3}. $$
That's because $a(n)$ is positive, monotonically increasing ($a(n) > a(n-1)$)
and $a(n+2) \geq a(n+1) + a(n)$.
So $a(n)$ grows exponentially, at least as fast as the Fibonnaci numbers.
Assuming $\frac{a(n+1)}{a(n)}$ tend to a limit L, solving for L in the definition of $a(n)$
gives $L=\sqrt{3}$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture3 :
    Tendsto (fun n ↦ (a (n + 1) : ℝ) / (a n : ℝ)) atTop (nhds (Real.sqrt 3))

problems.title: Ratio of product of GCDs to product of factorials of floor divisions
problems.doc:
$$a(n) = \frac{\prod_{j=1}^n \prod_{k=1}^n \gcd(j,k)}{\prod_{k=1}^n (\lfloor n/k \rfloor!)^k}$$

*References:*
- [A129365](https://oeis.org/A129365)

statements.name: OeisA129365.conjecture1
statements.doc:
Conjecture (1): $a(n)$ is always an integer (the denominator divides the numerator).

Proof summary:

Let $c(n) = \prod_{j=1}^n \prod_{k=1}^n (j,k)$ be the numerator.
Observe that
$$\textrm{ord}(c(n), p) = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p} \right\rfloor^2 + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^2} \right\rfloor^2 + ...$$
proven similar to Legendre's formula for $\textrm{ord}(n!, p)$.

Next let $d(n) = \prod_{k=1}^n (\lfloor n/k \rfloor!)^k$ be the denominator.
Observe that
$$\textrm{ord}(d(n), p) = \sum_{k=1}^n k\,\textrm{ord}(\lfloor n/k \rfloor, p) = \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{r \geq 1} k \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor n/p^r \rfloor}{k} \right\rfloor.$$

Combining the two gives:
$$\textrm{ord}(a(n), p) = \sum_{r \geq 1} \sum_{k=1}^n \left(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^r} \right\rfloor \textrm{mod } k\right).$$

Defining $b(m) = \sum_{k=1}^m m \textrm{ mod } k$, we obtain $\textrm{ord}(a(n), p) = \sum_{r \geq 1} b(\lfloor n/p^r \rfloor)$.

As $b(m) \geq 0$, $\textrm{ord}(a(n), p)$ is non-negative for any $p$, so $a(n)$ is an integer.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture1 (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) :
    ((Finset.Icc 1 n).prod fun k => (n / k).factorial ^ k) ∣
      ((Finset.Icc 1 n).prod fun j => (Finset.Icc 1 n).prod fun k => Nat.gcd j k)

statements.name: OeisA129365.conjecture2
statements.doc:
Conjecture (2): If $p$ is a prime, then $p \mid a(n)$ if and only if $p \le n/3$.

Proof summary:

We use the formula shown above:
$\textrm{ord}(a(n), p) = \sum_{r \geq 1} b(\lfloor n/p^r \rfloor)$ where
$b(m) = \sum_{k=1}^m m \textrm{ mod } k$.

If $p ∣ a(n)$ then $b(\lfloor n/p^r \rfloor) ≥ 1$ for some $r ≥ 1$. Since b(m) = 0$ for $m \leq 2$,
we must have $n / p^r \geq 3$. If the inequality holds for $r \geq 1$, it must be true for $r = 1$.
Hence $n \geq 3p$, proving the conjecture.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture2 (n p : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (hp : p.Prime) :
    (∃ m : ℕ, a n = m ∧ p ∣ m) ↔ p ≤ n / 3

statements.name: OeisA129365.conjecture3
statements.doc:
Conjecture (3): For each positive integer $n$, prime $p$, and $0 \le k < p$,
$\mathrm{ord}_p(a(np)) = \mathrm{ord}_p(a(np + k))$.

Proof summary:

This follows from the formula shown above:
$\textrm{ord}(a(n), p) = \sum_{r \geq 1} b(\lfloor n/p^r \rfloor)$ where
$b(m) = \sum_{k=1}^m m \textrm{ mod } k$.

Since $k < p$, we have $\lfloor (np + k)/p^r \rfloor = \lfloor np/p^r \rfloor$ for every $r \geq 1$,
proving the claim.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture3 (n p k : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (hp : p.Prime) (hk : k < p) :
    padicValRat p (a (n * p)) = padicValRat p (a (n * p + k))

statements.name: OeisA129365.conjecture4
statements.doc:
Conjecture (4): Let $b(n) = \mathrm{A004125}(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n (n \bmod k)$. Then
$\mathrm{ord}_p(a(np)) = \sum_{i \ge 0} b(\lfloor n/p^i \rfloor)$.

Proof summary:

This follows directly from the formula shown at the beginning:
$\textrm{ord}(a(n), p) = \sum_{r \geq 1} b(\lfloor n/p^r \rfloor)$ where
$b(m) = \sum_{k=1}^m m \textrm{ mod } k$.
statements.statement:
theorem conjecture4 (n p : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (hp : p.Prime) :
    padicValRat p (a (n * p)) = ∑' i : ℕ, (b (n / p ^ i) : ℤ)

and $k \ge 1$.

proof by Epoch Research.

statements.name: OeisA153330.conjecture3
statements.doc:
Conjecture 3 (Ya-Ping Lu, 2024):

(Note: in the OEIS comment, "x and y are integers" means $x$ and $y$ have the same sign,
