problems.title: Is a finite locally free group scheme killed by its order?
problems.doc:
A finite locally free group scheme of rank `n` is the group scheme analogue of a finite group of
order `n`. Lagrange's theorem gives `g ^ n = 1` in a finite group of order `n`, and Grothendieck
asked whether the `n`-th power map of such a group scheme is trivial. The answer is affirmative
over a reduced base and for commutative group schemes, and negative in general. Which exponents
kill every group scheme of a given rank is open.

A group scheme is represented here by its coordinate Hopf algebra `A` over the base ring `R`.
`A` is not assumed to be cocommutative, so the group scheme is not assumed to be commutative.
The base is a ring rather than a scheme: a finite locally free group scheme is affine over its
base, and being killed by `m` is local on the base, so nothing is lost.

*References:*
- [M. Demazure and A. Grothendieck, *Schémas en groupes* (SGA 3), re-edition by P. Gille and
  P. Polo](https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~patrick.polo/SGA3/). Exp. VIII, Rem. 7.3.1 poses the
  question; an editors' note records that the re-edition drops the commutativity assumption there.
  Exp. VIIA, Prop. 8.5 settles the case of a field and Cor. 8.5.2 the case of a reduced base.
- [R. Schoof, *Is a finite locally free group scheme killed by its
  order?*](https://reneschoof.github.io/schoof_oortAAG.pdf), a survey of the question and of the
  cases that are known, written before the counterexample
- [J. Tate and F. Oort, *Group schemes of prime order*](https://www.numdam.org/item/ASENS_1970_4_3_1_1_0/),
  p. 4 for Deligne's theorem and p. 5, which records the general question as open in 1970
- [Mathlib, *A finite free group scheme of rank four that is not killed by
  four*](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Counterexamples/GrothendieckPower.html),
  the counterexample

reference.text:
M. Demazure and A. Grothendieck, *Schémas en groupes* (SGA 3), re-edition by P. Gille and
  P. Polo

statements.name: FiniteLocallyFreeGroupSchemeExponent.killed_by_rank
statements.doc:
Grothendieck's question: is every finite locally free group scheme of rank $n$, over every
commutative ring, killed by $n$?

The answer is no. There is a commutative Hopf algebra of rank $4$ over a finite non-reduced ring
whose fourth power map is not trivial; its eighth power map is trivial. The formalised
counterexample lives in `Type`, so the statement quantifies over rings and algebras in `Type`.
statements.statement:
theorem killed_by_rank :
    ¬ ∀ n : ℕ+, IsUniversalKillingExponent.{0, 0} n n

statements.name: FiniteLocallyFreeGroupSchemeExponent.killed_by_rank.variants.field
statements.doc:
Over a field the answer is affirmative: a finite group scheme of rank $n$ over a field is killed
by $n$. This is [SGA 3], Exp. VIIA, Prop. 8.5.
statements.statement:
theorem killed_by_rank.variants.field (n : ℕ+) (k : Type*) [Field k] (A : Type*) [CommRing A]
    [HopfAlgebra k A] [Module.Finite k A] (hn : Module.finrank k A = (n : ℕ)) :
    IsKilledBy k A n

statements.name: FiniteLocallyFreeGroupSchemeExponent.killed_by_rank.variants.reduced_base
statements.doc:
Over a reduced base ring the answer is affirmative: every finite locally free group scheme of
rank $n$ over a reduced commutative ring is killed by $n$. This is [SGA 3], Exp. VIIA, Cor. 8.5.2,
deduced there from the case of a field.
statements.statement:
theorem killed_by_rank.variants.reduced_base (n : ℕ+) (R : Type*) [CommRing R] [IsReduced R]
    (A : Type*) [CommRing A] [HopfAlgebra R A] [Module.Finite R A] [Module.Projective R A]
    (hn : Module.rankAtStalk (R := R) A = fun _ ↦ (n : ℕ)) :
    IsKilledBy R A n

statements.name: FiniteLocallyFreeGroupSchemeExponent.killed_by_rank.variants.commutative
statements.doc:
Deligne's theorem: a finite locally free *commutative* group scheme of rank $n$ over any
commutative ring is killed by $n$. Commutativity of the group scheme is cocommutativity of its
coordinate Hopf algebra. See [SGA 3], Exp. VIIA, Rem. 8.5.3 and [TO70], p. 4.
statements.statement:
theorem killed_by_rank.variants.commutative (n : ℕ+) (R : Type*) [CommRing R] (A : Type*)
    [CommRing A] [HopfAlgebra R A] [Coalgebra.IsCocomm R A] [Module.Finite R A]
    [Module.Projective R A]
    (hn : Module.rankAtStalk (R := R) A = fun _ ↦ (n : ℕ)) :
    IsKilledBy R A n

statements.name: FiniteLocallyFreeGroupSchemeExponent.optimal_exponent
statements.doc:
Determine the function assigning to each positive integer $n$ the least positive integer $m$
such that every finite locally free group scheme of rank $n$, over every commutative ring, is
killed by $m$. The value is $0$ if there is no such $m$, since `sInf ∅ = 0` in `ℕ`. As in
`killed_by_rank`, the rings and algebras are in `Type`.

Grothendieck asked whether this least exponent is $n$ itself. It is not, already for $n = 4$.
If some positive exponent kills every group scheme of rank $n$, then these exponents are the
multiples of the least one, so minimality for $\le$ agrees with minimality for divisibility.
statements.statement:
theorem optimal_exponent :
    ∀ n, sInf ((↑) '' {m | IsUniversalKillingExponent.{0, 0} n m} : Set ℕ) = optimal_exponent.answer
      n

problems.title: Main conjecture on fusible numbers
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [Fusible numbers and Peano Arithmetic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.14342),
  by Jeff Erickson, Gabriel Nivasch, and Junyan Xu.
- [Fusible numbers and Peano Arithmetic](https://doi.org/10.46298/lmcs-18%283%3A6%292022),
  Logical Methods in Computer Science, Volume 18, Issue 3 (July 28, 2022).

statements.name: FusibleNumber.conj_7_1
statements.doc:
If `x` is a fusible number and `y` is its successor, then the interval `[x + 1, y + 1)` can be
divided into intervals `[ℓₙ, ℓₙ₊₁)`, such that the fusible numbers in `[ℓₙ, ℓₙ₊₁)` are obtained by
fusing the `n + 1`st successor of `x` with a fusible number.
This formalization differs from Conjecture 7.1 in the paper in four ways:
(1) it is obtained from Conjecture 7.1 by plugging in `n + 1` into `n`, which simplifies the expressions
  and removes the need to assume `n ≥ 1`;
(2) the `n + 1`st successor `s^(n+1)(x)` is replaced by the explicit value `x + (2 - 1 / 2 ^ n) * m`;
(3) instead of defining `y` to be the successor of `x`, we assert that there is no fusible number
  strictly between `x` and `y`;
(4) instead of using `∃ z, IsFusible z ∧ q = s^(n+1)(x) ~ z` we use the value of `z` determined by the equality,
  namely `z = 2 * q - 1 - s^(n+1)(x)`, and it is easy to see `z ∈ [x + 1 - m / 2 ^ n, x + 1)` as required.
statements.statement:
theorem conj_7_1 (x y q : ℚ) (n : ℕ) (fus_x : IsFusible x) (fus_y : IsFusible y) (lt : x < y)
    (nmem_Ioo : ∀ z, IsFusible z → z ∉ Set.Ioo x y) :
    let m := y - x
    let ℓ (n : ℕ) := y + 1 - m / 2 ^ n
    IsFusible q → q ∈ Set.Ico (ℓ n) (ℓ (n + 1)) → IsFusible (2 * q - 1 - x - (2 - 1 / 2 ^ n) * m)

problems.title: Gourevitch's series identity
problems.doc:
*References:*
 - [About a New Kind of Ramanujan-Type Series](https://doi.org/10.1080/10586458.2003.10504518) by *Jesús Guillera*
 - [G2003] Guillera, Jesús. "About a new kind of Ramanujan-type series." Experimental Mathematics 12.4 (2003): 507-510.
 - [A2025] Au, Kam Cheong. "Wilf-Zeilberger seeds and non-trivial hypergeometric identities." Journal of Symbolic Computation 130 (2025): 102421. [arXiv:2312.14051](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14051)

reference.text: About a New Kind of Ramanujan-Type Series

statements.name: Gourevitch.gourevitch_series_identity
statements.doc:
The Gourevitch series identity:
The following identity holds:
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1 + 14 n + 76 n^2 + 168 n^3}{2^{20 n}} \binom{2n}{n}^7 = \frac{32}{\pi^3}.$
This was originally conjectured in [G2003] by Guillera and proven in [A2025] by Au.
statements.statement:
theorem gourevitch_series_identity :
    ∑' n : ℕ, ((1 + 14 * n + 76 * n ^ 2 + 168 * n ^ 3) / (2 ^ (20 * n)) : ℝ)
      * Nat.centralBinom n ^ 7 = 32 / (Real.pi ^ 3)

problems.title: The Hall ratio conjecture (Harris 2019) — disproved
problems.doc:
*References:*
* [Ha19] Harris, D. G. (2019). "Some results on chromatic number as a function of triangle
  count." *SIAM J. Discrete Math.* 33, pp. 546--563.
* [DOW20] Dvořák, Z., Ossona de Mendez, P. and Wu, H. (2020). "1-subdivisions, the fractional
  chromatic number and the Hall ratio." *Combinatorica* 40, pp. 759--774.
  [arXiv:1812.07327](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07327)
* [BLMNPV22] Blumenthal, A., Lidický, B., Martin, R. R., Norin, S., Pfender, F. and Volec, J.
  (2022). "Counterexamples to a conjecture of Harris on Hall ratio." *SIAM J. Discrete Math.*
  36, pp. 1678--1686. [arXiv:1811.11116](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.11116)
* [SU97] Scheinerman, E. R. and Ullman, D. H. (1997). *Fractional Graph Theory.* Wiley.

statements.name: HallRatioConjecture.hall_ratio_conjecture
statements.doc:
**The Hall ratio conjecture (Harris 2019) — disproved.**

Harris conjectured that the fractional chromatic number is bounded by a constant multiple of the
Hall ratio: there is a constant $C$ with $\chi_f(G) \le C\,\rho(G)$ for every graph $G$. This
is **false**: Dvořák, Ossona de Mendez and Wu [DOW20] and, independently, Blumenthal, Lidický,
Martin, Norin, Pfender and Volec [BLMNPV22] constructed graphs with $\chi_f / \rho$
arbitrarily large.
statements.statement:
theorem hall_ratio_conjecture : ¬
    ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
      G.fractionalChromaticNumber ≤ C * hallRatio G

statements.name: HallRatioConjecture.hall_ratio_conjecture.variants.hallRatio_le_fractionalChromaticNumber
statements.doc:
**The Hall ratio is a lower bound for the fractional chromatic number.**

For every graph, $\rho(G) \le \chi_f(G)$ (see [SU97]); the conjecture asked for an inequality in
the other direction up to a constant.
statements.statement:
theorem hall_ratio_conjecture.variants.hallRatio_le_fractionalChromaticNumber
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    hallRatio G ≤ G.fractionalChromaticNumber

statements.name: HallRatioConjecture.hall_ratio_conjecture.variants.unbounded
statements.doc:
**Unbounded ratio (Dvořák–Ossona de Mendez–Wu 2020; Blumenthal et al. 2022).**

For every $C$ there is a graph with $\chi_f(G) > C\,\rho(G)$.

*References:* [DOW20], [BLMNPV22].
statements.statement:
theorem hall_ratio_conjecture.variants.unbounded (C : ℝ) :
    ∃ (V : Type) (_ : Fintype V) (_ : DecidableEq V) (G : SimpleGraph V),
      C * hallRatio G < G.fractionalChromaticNumber

problems.title: Hartshorne's conjecture on Vector Bundles
problems.doc:
*References:*
* [Har1974] R. Hartshorne, [Varieties of small codimension in projective space](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society-new-series/volume-80/issue-6/Varieties-of-small-codimension-in-projective-space/bams/1183535999.full).
* [MO2010] [Evidences on Hartshorne's conjecture? References?](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/13990/evidences-on-hartshornes-conjecture-references)

reference.text: Varieties of small codimension in projective space

statements.name: AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.harthshorne_conjecture
statements.doc:
There are no indecomposable vector bundles of rank 2 on $\mathbb{P}^n$ for $n \ge 7$.
This is Conjecture 6.3 in [Har1974].
statements.statement:
theorem harthshorne_conjecture (n : ℕ) (hn : 7 ≤ n)
    (𝓕 : VectorBundles ℙ(Fin (n + 1); Spec (.of ℂ)))
    (h𝓕 : 𝓕.rank = 2) :
    Nonempty (𝓕.Splitting (Fin 2))

problems.title: Conjectures around homogeneous topological spaces
problems.doc:
This file formalizes the notions of a homogeneous topological space and of (ω-)monolithic
topological spaces, and states some open problems about homogeneous and monolithic compact spaces.

*References:*
* [Ar2013] Arhangeliski, Alexandr. "Selected old open problems in general topology."
  Buletinul Academiei de Ştiinţe a Republicii Moldova. Matematica 73.2-3 (2013): 37-46.
  https://www.math.md/files/basm/y2013-n2-3/y2013-n2-3-(pp37-46).pdf.pdf
* [Ar1987] Arhangel'skii, A. V. "Topological homogeneity. Topological groups and their continuous
  images." Russian Mathematical Surveys 42.2 (1987): 83-131.
  https://doi.org/10.1070/RM1987v042n02ABEH001333

statements.name: Homogeneous.homogeneousSpace_exists_inj_tendsto
statements.doc:
Problem 13 in [Ar2013]:
Is it true that every infinite homogeneous compact hausdorff
space contains a non-trivial convergent sequence?
statements.statement:
theorem homogeneousSpace_exists_inj_tendsto :
    ∀ (X : Type) (_ : TopologicalSpace X), ¬ Finite X → T2Space X → CompactSpace X →
      HomogeneousSpace X → ∃ s : ℕ → X, s.Injective ∧ ∃ a : X, Tendsto s atTop (nhds a)

statements.name: Homogeneous.homogeneousSpace_exists_surjective
statements.doc:
Problem 14 in [Ar2013]:
Is it possible to represent an arbitrary compact hausdorff space as an image
of a homogeneous compact space under a continuous mapping?
statements.statement:
theorem homogeneousSpace_exists_surjective :
    ∀ (X : Type) (_ : TopologicalSpace X), T2Space X → CompactSpace X →
      ∃ (Y : Type) (_ : TopologicalSpace Y), T2Space Y ∧ CompactSpace Y ∧ HomogeneousSpace Y ∧
        ∃ f : Y → X, Continuous f ∧ f.Surjective

statements.name: Homogeneous.firstCountableTopology_of_countablyMonolithicSpace
statements.doc:
Problem 15 in [Ar2013]:
Is every homogeneous ω-monolithic compact hausdorff space first countable?
statements.statement:
theorem firstCountableTopology_of_countablyMonolithicSpace :
    ∀ (X : Type) (_ : TopologicalSpace X), T2Space X → CompactSpace X →
      HomogeneousSpace X → CountablyMonolithicSpace X → FirstCountableTopology X

statements.name: Homogeneous.countablyMonolithicSpace_card_lt
statements.doc:
Problem 16 in [Ar2013]:
Is the cardinality of every homogeneous ω-monolithic compact hausdorff space not greater than 𝔠?
statements.statement:
theorem countablyMonolithicSpace_card_lt :
    ∀ (X : Type) (_ : TopologicalSpace X), T2Space X → CompactSpace X →
      HomogeneousSpace X → CountablyMonolithicSpace X → #X ≤ 𝔠

statements.name: Homogeneous.monolithicSpace_exists_nhds_generated_countable
statements.doc:
Problem 17 in [Ar2013]:
Is it true that every nonempty monolithic compact hausdorff space contains a point with a
first countable neighborhood basis?

Note: `Nonempty X` is required since the conclusion asserts the existence of a point.
statements.statement:
theorem monolithicSpace_exists_nhds_generated_countable :
    ∀ (X : Type) (_ : TopologicalSpace X), T2Space X → CompactSpace X →
      Nonempty X → MonolithicSpace X → ∃ x : X, (𝓝 x).IsCountablyGenerated

problems.title: Kaplansky's problem on the values of the $u$-invariant
problems.doc:
The $u$-invariant $u(F)$ of a field $F$ is the largest dimension of an anisotropic quadratic form
over $F$, or $\infty$ if there is no largest one; that is, $u(F) = n$ exactly when
`IsGreatest (QuadraticForm.anisotropicDims F) n`. Following [Kaplansky1953] and
[MerkurjevParimala2025, §5.1], all fields are of characteristic not $2$.

Kaplansky introduced the invariant (his $C(F)$) in [Kaplansky1953, p. 201], proved that $u(F) \ne 3$
(his Theorem 2), observed that every power of $2$ occurs (his Theorem 3 gives
$u(F((t))) = 2u(F)$), and conjectured that $u(F)$ is a power of $2$ whenever it is finite
[Kaplansky1953, p. 202]. It is classical that $u(F) \notin \{3, 5, 7\}$
[Lam2005, Proposition XI.6.8], [EKM2008, Corollary 36.4]. Merkurjev disproved Kaplansky's
conjecture with a field of $u$-invariant $6$ [Merkurjev1989] and then showed that every positive
even integer is a $u$-invariant [Merkurjev1991]. Izhboldin constructed a field of $u$-invariant
$9$ [Izhboldin2001], and Vishik fields of $u$-invariant $2^r + 1$ for every $r \ge 3$
[Vishik2009]. A 2026 preprint of Karpenko constructs fields of $u$-invariant $n$ for every $n$
that is neither of the form $2^r - 1$ nor of the form $2^r - 3$ [Karpenko2026]; as of September
2026 it is not yet peer-reviewed.

The problem (`u_invariant_values`) is to determine which integers are $u$-invariants of fields.
The survey [MerkurjevParimala2025, §5.1] records the expectation that every odd integer $\ge 9$
is a $u$-invariant (`u_invariant_values.variants.odd`). Given the results above, the problem is
open exactly for the integers $2^r - 1$ and $2^r - 3$ with $r \ge 4$, the smallest of which are
$13$ and $15$.

*References:*
- [Kaplansky1953] I. Kaplansky, *Quadratic forms*, J. Math. Soc. Japan 5 (1953), 200–207,
  [doi:10.2969/jmsj/00520200](https://doi.org/10.2969/jmsj/00520200).
- [Lam2005] T. Y. Lam, *Introduction to quadratic forms over fields*, Grad. Stud. Math. 67,
  Amer. Math. Soc., 2005, [doi:10.1090/gsm/067](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/067).
- [EKM2008] R. Elman, N. Karpenko, A. Merkurjev, *The algebraic and geometric theory of quadratic
  forms*, Amer. Math. Soc. Colloq. Publ. 56, Amer. Math. Soc., 2008,
  [doi:10.1090/coll/056](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/056).
- [Merkurjev1989] A. S. Merkurjev, *Kaplansky's conjecture in the theory of quadratic forms*
  (Russian), Zap. Nauchn. Sem. LOMI 175 (1989), 75–89; English transl. J. Soviet Math. 57
  (1991), no. 6, 3489–3497, [doi:10.1007/BF01100118](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01100118).
- [Merkurjev1991] A. S. Merkurjev, *Simple algebras and quadratic forms* (Russian), Izv. Akad.
  Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 55 (1991), no. 1, 218–224; English transl. Math. USSR-Izv. 38 (1992),
  no. 1, 215–221,
  [doi:10.1070/IM1992v038n01ABEH002195](https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1992v038n01ABEH002195).
- [Izhboldin2001] O. T. Izhboldin, *Fields of $u$-invariant $9$*, Ann. of Math. (2) 154 (2001),
  no. 3, 529–587, [doi:10.2307/3062141](https://doi.org/10.2307/3062141).
- [Vishik2009] A. Vishik, *Fields of $u$-invariant $2^r + 1$*, pp. 661–685 in Algebra,
  arithmetic, and geometry: in honor of Yu. I. Manin, Vol. II, Progr. Math. 270, Birkhäuser,
  2009, [doi:10.1007/978-0-8176-4747-6_22](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4747-6_22).
- [Karpenko2026] N. A. Karpenko, *Fields of any $u$-invariant but a 2-power minus 1 or 3*,
  preprint, 5 August 2026,
  [author's web page](https://sites.ualberta.ca/~karpenko/publ/u1or3-02.pdf).
- [MerkurjevParimala2025] A. Merkurjev, R. Parimala, *Quadratic forms beyond arithmetic*, Notices
  Amer. Math. Soc. 72 (2025), no. 7, 711–718,
  [doi:10.1090/noti3192](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3192).

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values
statements.doc:
**The values of the $u$-invariant**, stated as in [MerkurjevParimala2025, §5.1]: which integers
are $u$-invariants of fields (of characteristic not $2$)? The question goes back to
[Kaplansky1953], who conjectured that only powers of $2$ occur
(`u_invariant_values.variants.kaplansky_conjecture`). Every positive even integer is a
$u$-invariant (`u_invariant_values.variants.even`), $3$, $5$ and $7$ are not
(`u_invariant_values.variants.not_three`, `u_invariant_values.variants.not_five`,
`u_invariant_values.variants.not_seven`), and it is expected that every odd integer $\ge 9$ is
(`u_invariant_values.variants.odd`). Granting the preprint [Karpenko2026]
(`u_invariant_values.variants.karpenko`), the answer is known for every $n$ except $n = 2^r - 1$
and $n = 2^r - 3$ with $r \ge 4$.
statements.statement:
theorem u_invariant_values :
    ∀ n, n ∈ u_invariant_values.answer ↔ IsUInvariant n

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.kaplansky_conjecture
statements.doc:
**Kaplansky's conjecture** [Kaplansky1953, p. 202]: the $u$-invariant of a field is a power of
$2$ whenever it is finite. Disproved by Merkurjev, who constructed a field of $u$-invariant $6$
[Merkurjev1989] (`u_invariant_values.variants.even`).
statements.statement:
theorem u_invariant_values.variants.kaplansky_conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ n, IsUInvariant n → ∃ k, n = 2 ^ k

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.not_three
statements.doc:
The $u$-invariant is never $3$ [Kaplansky1953, Theorem 2]; see also
[Lam2005, Proposition XI.6.8] and [EKM2008, Corollary 36.4].
statements.statement: theorem u_invariant_values.variants.not_three : ¬ IsUInvariant 3

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.not_five
statements.doc: The $u$-invariant is never $5$ [Lam2005, Proposition XI.6.8], [EKM2008, Corollary 36.4].
statements.statement: theorem u_invariant_values.variants.not_five : ¬ IsUInvariant 5

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.not_seven
statements.doc: The $u$-invariant is never $7$ [Lam2005, Proposition XI.6.8], [EKM2008, Corollary 36.4].
statements.statement: theorem u_invariant_values.variants.not_seven : ¬ IsUInvariant 7

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.two_pow
statements.doc:
Every power of $2$ is a $u$-invariant [Kaplansky1953, p. 202]: Theorem 3 of [Kaplansky1953]
gives $u(F((t))) = 2u(F)$, so $u(\mathbb{C}((t_1)) \cdots ((t_k))) = 2^k$; see also
[EKM2008, §38].
statements.statement: theorem u_invariant_values.variants.two_pow (k : ℕ) : IsUInvariant (2 ^ k)

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.even
statements.doc:
**Merkurjev's theorem** [Merkurjev1991], see also [EKM2008, Theorem 38.4]: every positive even
integer is a $u$-invariant. The case $6$, the first counterexample to Kaplansky's conjecture, is
[Merkurjev1989].
statements.statement:
theorem u_invariant_values.variants.even (n : ℕ) (hn : Even n) (hn₀ : n ≠ 0) :
    IsUInvariant n

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.nine
statements.doc:
**Izhboldin's theorem** [Izhboldin2001]: there is a field of $u$-invariant $9$,
the first example of an odd $u$-invariant greater than $1$.
statements.statement: theorem u_invariant_values.variants.nine : IsUInvariant 9

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.two_pow_add_one
statements.doc:
**Vishik's theorem** [Vishik2009, Corollary 5.2]: for every $r \ge 3$ there is a field of
$u$-invariant $2^r + 1$.
statements.statement:
theorem u_invariant_values.variants.two_pow_add_one (r : ℕ) (hr : 3 ≤ r) :
    IsUInvariant (2 ^ r + 1)

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.karpenko
statements.doc:
**Karpenko's theorem** [Karpenko2026, Theorem 1.1]: if neither $n + 1$ nor $n + 3$ is a power
of $2$, then there is a field of $u$-invariant $n$. This covers every positive integer except
$1$, $3$, $5$, $7$ and the integers $2^r - 1$, $2^r - 3$ with $r \ge 4$. As of September 2026
the result is a preprint and not yet peer-reviewed.
statements.statement:
theorem u_invariant_values.variants.karpenko (n : ℕ) (h₁ : ∀ r, 2 ^ r ≠ n + 1)
    (h₃ : ∀ r, 2 ^ r ≠ n + 3) : IsUInvariant n

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.eleven
statements.doc:
The special case $n = 11$ of `u_invariant_values.variants.karpenko` (neither $12$ nor $14$ is a
power of $2$), the first odd value not of the form $2^r + 1$ shown to be a $u$-invariant; it was
announced in the preprint *Fields of $u$-invariant 11* (21 April 2026) that [Karpenko2026]
absorbs.
statements.statement: theorem u_invariant_values.variants.eleven : IsUInvariant 11

statements.name: KaplanskyUInvariant.u_invariant_values.variants.odd
statements.doc:
The expectation recorded in [MerkurjevParimala2025, §5.1]: every odd integer $\ge 9$ is a
$u$-invariant. By `u_invariant_values.variants.karpenko` this is open exactly for the integers
$2^r - 1$ and $2^r - 3$ with $r \ge 4$.
statements.statement:
theorem u_invariant_values.variants.odd :
    ∀ n, Odd n → 9 ≤ n → IsUInvariant n

problems.title: Kotzig's Conjecture
problems.doc:
*Reference:* A. Kotzig, cited in A. Rosa, *On certain valuations of the vertices of a graph*,
Theory of Graphs (Internat. Sympos., Rome, 1966), Gordon and Breach, 1967, pp. 349–355.

Kotzig conjectured that for every $n$, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into copies of
any $n$-edge tree via cyclic shifts of a single embedding. This is strictly stronger than
Ringel's conjecture; see `Paper/RingelConjecture.lean`. The large-$n$ case is proved by
Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov; see `Arxiv/2001.02665/RingelConjecture.lean`.

statements.name: KotzigConjecture.kotzig_conjecture
statements.doc:
For any tree $T$ with $n$ edges, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into
$2n+1$ edge-disjoint copies of $T$ via cyclic shifts of a single embedding.

The $2n+1$ copies are $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{2n}$ where $f_i(v) = f_0(v) + i$ for all vertices
$v$ — each copy is obtained by adding $i \pmod{2n+1}$ to every vertex of the base copy.
This is strictly stronger than `RingelConjecture.ringel_conjecture`.
statements.statement:
theorem kotzig_conjecture {V : Type} [Finite V]
    (T : SimpleGraph V) (hT : T.IsTree)
    (n : ℕ) (hn : T.edgeSet.ncard = n) :
    ∃ f : Fin (2 * n + 1) → (V ↪ Fin (2 * n + 1)),
      (∀ i v, f i v = f 0 v + i) ∧
      Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (T.map (f i)).edgeSet (T.map (f j)).edgeSet) ∧
      ⨆ i, T.map (f i) = (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * n + 1)))

problems.title: Kurepa's conjecture
problems.doc: *Reference:* [On the left factorial function !N](https://oeis.org/A3422), by *Đuro Kurepa* Math. Balkanica 1, p. 147-153, 1971

statements.name: Kurepa.kurepa_conjecture
statements.doc:
## Kurepa's conjecture

For all $n$, $$!n\not\equiv 0 \mod n$$

This appears as B44 "Sums of factorials."
in [Unsolved Problems in Number Theory](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0)
by *Richard K. Guy*
statements.statement: theorem kurepa_conjecture (n : ℕ) (h_n : 2 < n) : (!n : ℕ) % n ≠ 0

statements.name: Kurepa.kurepa_conjecture.variants.prime
statements.doc: This statement can be reduced to the prime case only.
statements.statement:
theorem kurepa_conjecture.variants.prime (p : ℕ) (h_p : 2 < p) :
    p.Prime → (!p : ℕ) % p ≠ 0

statements.name: Kurepa.kurepa_conjecture.prime_reduction
statements.doc: Kurepa's conjecture for all integers greater than 2 is equivalent to the conjecture restricted to primes greater than 2.
statements.statement:
theorem kurepa_conjecture.prime_reduction : (∀ n, 2 < n → (!n : ℕ) % n ≠ 0)
    ↔ (∀ p, 2 < p → p.Prime → (!p : ℕ) % p ≠ 0)

statements.name: Kurepa.kurepa_conjecture.variants.gcd
statements.doc: An equivalent formulation in terms of the gcd of $n!$ and $!n$.
statements.statement: theorem kurepa_conjecture.variants.gcd (n : ℕ) : 2 < n → (n !).gcd (! n) = 2

statements.name: Kurepa.kurepa_conjecture.gcd_reduction
statements.doc: Kurepa's conjecture for all integers greater than 2 is equivalent to the statement that $\gcd(n!, !n) = 2$ for all integers greater than 2.
statements.statement:
theorem kurepa_conjecture.gcd_reduction : (∀ n, 2 < n → (!n : ℕ) % n ≠ 0)
    ↔ (∀ n, 2 < n → (n)!.gcd (!n) = 2)

problems.title: Conjectures about Latin Squares
problems.doc:
This file formalizes some conjectures and theorems around latin squares.

*References:*
* [Wa2011] Wanless, Ian. "Transversals in Latin Squares: A Survey."
  Surveys in Combinatorics 2011, R. Chapman, Ed. Cambridge University Press, 2011, pp. 403–437.
  https://users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/papers/transurveyBCC.pdf
* https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problems_in_Latin_squares

statements.name: LatinSquare.oddOrderLatinSquareTransversal
statements.doc:
Conjecture 3.2 in [Wa2011]:
Each Latin square of odd order has at least one transversal.
statements.statement:
theorem oddOrderLatinSquareTransversal :
    ∀ (n : ℕ), Odd n → ∀ (L : LatinSquare n), ∃ σ, IsTransversal L σ

statements.name: LatinSquare.oddOrderLeq9LatinSquareTransversal
statements.doc: The conjecture is known to be true for $n \leq 9$.
statements.statement:
theorem oddOrderLeq9LatinSquareTransversal :
    ∀ n ≤ 9, Odd n → ∀ (L : LatinSquare n), ∃ σ, IsTransversal L σ

statements.name: LatinSquare.latinSquareOrder11Transversal
statements.doc: The smallest odd number for which this conjecture is not known is 11.
statements.statement:
theorem latinSquareOrder11Transversal :
    ∀ (L : LatinSquare 11), ∃ σ, IsTransversal L σ

statements.name: LatinSquare.latinSquareNearTransversal
statements.doc:
Conjecture 5.1 in [Wa2011]:
Every latin square has a near-transversal
statements.statement:
theorem latinSquareNearTransversal :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (L : LatinSquare n), ∃ ρ σ, IsNearTransversal L ρ σ

statements.name: LatinSquare.z_even
statements.doc: The Cayley table of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for positive even $n$ has no transversals.
statements.statement: theorem z_even (n : ℕ) : z (2 * (n + 1)) = 0

statements.name: LatinSquare.numTransversalsZn
statements.doc:
Conjecture 6.7 in [Wa2011]:
There exist real constants $0 < c_1 < c_2 < 1$ such that
$$
c_1^n n! \leq z_n \leq c_2^n n!
$$
for all odd $n \geq 3$.
statements.statement:
theorem numTransversalsZn :
      ∃ᵉ (c₁ > (0 : ℝ)) (c₂ < (1 : ℝ)) (_ : c₁ < c₂),
      ∀ n ≥ 3, Odd n →
        (z n : ℝ) ∈ Set.Icc (c₁ ^ n * n.factorial) (c₂ ^ n * n.factorial)

statements.name: LatinSquare.growthRateZn
statements.doc:
Conjecture 6.9 in [Wa2011]:
$$
\lim_{\substack{n \to \infty \\ n \text{ odd}}} \frac{1}{n} \log(z_n / n!) = -1
$$
It is not even known if this limit exists. Note that $z_n = 0$ for even $n$ (see `z_even`), so the
limit must be restricted to odd $n$; here we parametrise odd $n$ as $2k + 1$.
statements.statement:
theorem growthRateZn :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun k => (1 : ℝ) / (2 * k + 1) *
      Real.log (z (2 * k + 1) / (2 * k + 1).factorial)) Filter.atTop
      (nhds (-1))

statements.name: LatinSquare.maxTransversalsBound
statements.doc:
Theorem 7.2 in [Wa2011]:
For all $n \geq 5$,
$$
15^{n/5} \leq T(n) \leq c^n \sqrt{n} \cdot n!
$$
where $c = \sqrt{\frac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{6}} \cdot e^{\sqrt{3}/6}$
statements.statement:
theorem maxTransversalsBound :
    let c := Real.sqrt ((3 - Real.sqrt 3) / 6) * Real.exp (Real.sqrt 3 / 6)
    ∀ n : ℕ, n ≥ 5 →
      (T n : ℝ) ∈ Set.Icc ((15 : ℝ) ^ ((n : ℝ) / 5)) (c ^ n * Real.sqrt n * n.factorial)

statements.name: LatinSquare.molsExistenceProblem
statements.doc:
MOLS existence problem: determine exactly which orders `n` admit a complete set of `n - 1`
mutually orthogonal latin squares.

Equivalently, this asks for which orders affine planes of order `n` exist. Complete sets are known
for prime-power orders; the smallest currently unresolved order is `12`.
statements.statement: theorem molsExistenceProblem : molsExistenceProblem.answer = {n : ℕ | HasCompleteMOLS n}

statements.name: LatinSquare.molsOrder12
statements.doc:
The smallest unresolved case of the MOLS existence problem: whether there are `11` mutually
orthogonal latin squares of order `12`.
statements.statement: theorem molsOrder12 : HasCompleteMOLS 12

problems.title: Latin Tableau Conjecture
problems.doc:
The Latin Tableau Conjecture states that the graph associated
to any (finite) Young diagram (i.e., whose vertices are the
cells of the diagram, with edges between cells in the same row
or column) is CDS-colorable, meaning that there exists a proper
coloring of the vertices of the graph such that for all k > 0, the
number of vertices with color < k equals the maximum size of
the union of k independent sets of the graph.

*References:*

* [The Latin Tableau Conjecture](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v32i2p48)

statements.name: LatinTableau.SimpleGraph.LatinTableauConjecture
statements.doc:
The Latin Tableau Conjecture: If G is the simple graph
of a Young diagram, then G is CDS-colorable.
statements.statement:
theorem LatinTableauConjecture (μ : YoungDiagram) :
     μ.toSimpleGraph.CDSColorable

problems.title: Lennon–Pittel conjecture on random stable matchings
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [On the Likely Number of Stable Marriages](https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=osu1194991095&disposition=inline)
  by *Craig Lennon*, PhD dissertation, The Ohio State University (2007).
- [On the Likely Number of Solutions for the Stable Marriage Problem](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548308009607)
  by *Craig Lennon and Boris Pittel*, *Combinatorics, Probability and Computing* 18 (2009),
  371–421.

Let $S_n$ be the number of stable matchings under uniformly random complete strict preferences.

reference.text: On the Likely Number of Stable Marriages

statements.name: LennonPittel.lennon_pittel_conjecture
statements.doc:
The [Lennon–Pittel conjecture](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548308009607) states that for every
positive nonincreasing sequence $\varepsilon_n \to 0$, the probability that the number $S_n$ of
stable matchings is at least $\varepsilon_n \mathbb{E}[S_n]$ tends to one.
statements.statement:
theorem lennon_pittel_conjecture
    (ε : ℕ → ℝ) (hε_pos : ∀ n, 0 < ε n) (hε_antitone : Antitone ε)
    (hε_tendsto : Tendsto ε atTop (𝓝 0)) :
    Tendsto
      (fun n ↦
        (StableMarriage.uniformProfile n).toMeasure
          {p | (StableMarriage.numStableMatchings p : ℝ) ≥
            ε n * StableMarriage.expectedNumStableMatchings n})
      atTop (𝓝 1)

problems.title: The Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture (1988)
problems.doc:
*References:*
* [MM88] Manickam, N. and Miklós, D. (1988). "On the number of nonnegative partial sums of a
  nonnegative sum." *Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai* 52, pp. 385--392.
* [MS88] Manickam, N. and Singhi, N. M. (1988). "First distribution invariants and EKR theorems."
  *J. Combin. Theory Ser. A* 48, pp. 91--103.
* [CSS14] Chowdhury, A., Sarkis, G. and Shahriari, S. (2014). "The Manickam–Miklós–Singhi
  conjectures for sets and vector spaces." *J. Combin. Theory Ser. A* 128, pp. 84--103.
  [arXiv:1309.2212](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.2212)
* [Po15] Pokrovskiy, A. (2015). "A linear bound on the Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture."
  *J. Combin. Theory Ser. A* 133, pp. 280--306. [arXiv:1308.2176](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.2176)

statements.name: ManickamMiklosSinghiConjecture.manickam_miklos_singhi_conjecture
statements.doc:
**The Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture (1988).**

If $n \ge 4k$ and $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are real numbers with $x_1 + \dots + x_n = 0$, then at least
$\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ of the $k$-element subsets $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ have
$\sum_{i \in S} x_i \ge 0$. (The bound is attained by $x = (n-1, -1, \dots, -1)$; the
condition $n \ge 4k$ cannot be weakened to $n \ge 3k + 1$ in general.)
statements.statement:
theorem manickam_miklos_singhi_conjecture :
    ∀ (n k : ℕ), 1 ≤ k → 4 * k ≤ n → ∀ x : Fin n → ℝ, ∑ i, x i = 0 →
      (n - 1).choose (k - 1) ≤ nonnegSubsetCount n k x

statements.name: ManickamMiklosSinghiConjecture.manickam_miklos_singhi_conjecture.variants.pokrovskiy
statements.doc:
**Pokrovskiy (2015): the conjecture holds for $n \ge C k$ with an absolute constant $C$.**

Pokrovskiy proved this with $C = 10^{46}$, the first bound linear in $k$.

*Reference:* [Po15].
statements.statement:
theorem manickam_miklos_singhi_conjecture.variants.pokrovskiy :
    ∃ C : ℕ, ∀ (n k : ℕ), 1 ≤ k → C * k ≤ n → ∀ x : Fin n → ℝ, ∑ i, x i = 0 →
      (n - 1).choose (k - 1) ≤ nonnegSubsetCount n k x

statements.name: ManickamMiklosSinghiConjecture.manickam_miklos_singhi_conjecture.variants.quadratic
statements.doc:
**Chowdhury–Sarkis–Shahriari (2014): the conjecture holds for $n \ge 8k^2$.**

*Reference:* [CSS14].
statements.statement:
theorem manickam_miklos_singhi_conjecture.variants.quadratic (n k : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k)
    (hn : 8 * k ^ 2 ≤ n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (hx : ∑ i, x i = 0) :
    (n - 1).choose (k - 1) ≤ nonnegSubsetCount n k x

problems.title: Monochromatic quantum graphs (inherited vertex colorings)
problems.doc:
This file studies the existence of *monochromatic quantum graphs*: edge-coloured, edge-weighted
complete graphs whose perfect matchings induce vertex colourings, with the property that

- every **non-monochromatic** inherited vertex colouring has total weight `0`, while
- each of the `D` **monochromatic** colourings has total weight `1`.

In the quantum-optics motivation, such a construction corresponds to generating high-dimensional
multipartite GHZ-type states using probabilistic pair sources and linear optics (without additional
resources), where interference patterns can be expressed as weighted sums over perfect matchings.

## Main questions (informal)

- For `N = 4` and `D ≥ 4`, does there exist such a graph/weighting?
- For even `N ≥ 6` and `D ≥ 3`, does there exist such a graph/weighting?

## Formalisation sketch

A quantum graph with `N` vertices and `D` colours can be encoded by a weight function
`W : EdgeN N D α → α` (for a coefficient domain `α`).

For each assignment of vertex indices `ι : V N → Fin D`, we define a perfect-matching sum
`pmSumN N D W ι` (a sum over perfect matchings, where each matching contributes the product of the
corresponding edge weights determined by `ι`). The equation system `EqSystemN N D W` requires

`pmSumN N D W ι = 1` iff `ι` is constant (all entries equal), and `0` otherwise.

The open conjectures in this file ask for non-existence/existence of such `W` over various
coefficient domains (e.g. `ℂ`, `ℝ`, `ℤ`, and restricted integer weights).

## References

* [Krenn2017] M. Krenn, X. Gu, A. Zeilinger,
  "Quantum Experiments and Graphs: Multiparty States as Coherent Superpositions of Perfect Matchings",
  *Physical Review Letters* 119(24), 240403 (2017).

* [MO2018] [Vertex coloring inherited from perfect matchings (motivated by quantum physics)](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/311325),
  MathOverflow question 311325.

* [Gu2019] X. Gu, M. Erhard, A. Zeilinger, M. Krenn,
  "Quantum experiments and graphs II: Quantum interference, computation, and state generation",
  *PNAS* 116(10), 4147–4155 (2019).

* [Krenn2019] [Questions on the Structure of Perfect Matchings inspired by Quantum Physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06023)
  by *M. Krenn, X. Gu, U. Soltész*,
  Proc. 2nd Croatian Combinatorial Days, 57–70 (2019).

* [Chandran2022] [Edge-coloured graphs with only monochromatic perfect matchings and their connection to quantum physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05562)
  by *N. Chandran, S. Gajjala* (2022).

* [Chandran2024] [Krenn–Gu conjecture for sparse graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00303)
  by *N. Chandran, S. Gajjala, S. Illickan, M. Krenn*, MFCS 2024.

* [Ki26] [A solver-free Lean 4 proof of the sharp bound $D \le N - 2$ for monochromatic quantum
  graph equation systems over integral domains](https://github.com/KitaKen1/monochromatic-quantum-graph-sharp-bound-lean/tree/6c5340384479dbb36129b2e0084449be2458cce2),
  commit `6c534038`.

* [Ki26b] [A solver-free Lean 4 proof that the monochromatic quantum graph equation system has no
  solution for $N = 10$ and $D = 8$ over integral domains](https://github.com/KitaKen1/monochromatic-quantum-graph-n10-d8-lean/tree/a9309005c7a27a2615f8e7eebef7a1db017809ab),
  commit `a9309005`.

problems.title: Energy-critical NLS in three dimensions.
problems.doc:
This file states an a priori estimate for the energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $ℝ^3$.
By 'soft' arguments, this bound implies global well-posedness in the energy space, scattering,
asymptotic completeness, and uniform regularity (all of which are less elementary to state).
This is remarked on p. 770 and p. 793 in the referenced article which first proved the a priori bound.

The main theorem is:
- `NLS_apriori`: a bound on the space-time $L^10$ norm in terms of the initial energy for local
  smooth solutions to the NLS equation.

## References
* [Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka, Tao](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.767),
  Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008) proves the a priori estimate, and thereby, global well-posedness.

statements.name: NLSCritical.NLS_apriori
statements.doc: The $L^10_{t,x}$ a priori estimate for local schwartz solutions.
statements.statement:
theorem NLS_apriori :
    ∃ f : ℝ → ℝ, ∀ l > 0, ∀ s : LocalSchwartzSolution l,
    L10_local l s.u ≤ f (energy (s.u 0))

problems.title: The 1-2-3 conjecture (Karoński–Łuczak–Thomason 2004; proved by Keusch 2024)
problems.doc:
*References:*
* [KLT04] Karoński, M., Łuczak, T. and Thomason, A. (2004). "Edge weights and vertex colours."
  *J. Combin. Theory Ser. B* 91, pp. 151--157.
* [ABDMRT07] Addario-Berry, L., Dalal, K., McDiarmid, C., Reed, B. A. and Thomason, A.
  (2007). "Vertex-colouring edge-weightings." *Combinatorica* 27, pp. 1--12.
* [KKP10] Kalkowski, M., Karoński, M. and Pfender, F. (2010). "Vertex-coloring edge-weightings:
  towards the 1-2-3-conjecture." *J. Combin. Theory Ser. B* 100, pp. 347--349.
* [Ke24] Keusch, R. (2024). "A solution to the 1-2-3 conjecture."
  *J. Combin. Theory Ser. B* 166, pp. 183--202.
  [arXiv:2303.02611](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02611)

statements.name: OneTwoThreeConjecture.one_two_three_conjecture
statements.doc:
**The 1-2-3 conjecture (Karoński–Łuczak–Thomason 2004), proved by Keusch (2024).**

Every finite simple graph with no isolated edge admits an edge weighting with weights in
$\{1, 2, 3\}$ such that adjacent vertices have different weighted degrees.
statements.statement:
theorem one_two_three_conjecture :
    ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      NoIsolatedEdge G →
      ∃ w : Sym2 V → ℕ, (∀ e ∈ G.edgeFinset, 1 ≤ w e ∧ w e ≤ 3) ∧
        IsVertexColouringWeighting G w

statements.name: OneTwoThreeConjecture.one_two_three_conjecture.variants.one_to_five
statements.doc:
**Kalkowski–Karoński–Pfender (2010): weights in $\{1, \dots, 5\}$ suffice.**

*Reference:* [KKP10].
statements.statement:
theorem one_two_three_conjecture.variants.one_to_five
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : NoIsolatedEdge G) :
    ∃ w : Sym2 V → ℕ, (∀ e ∈ G.edgeFinset, 1 ≤ w e ∧ w e ≤ 5) ∧
      IsVertexColouringWeighting G w

statements.name: OneTwoThreeConjecture.one_two_three_conjecture.variants.one_to_thirty
statements.doc:
**Addario-Berry–Dalal–McDiarmid–Reed–Thomason (2007): weights in $\{1, \dots, 30\}$ suffice.**

*Reference:* [ABDMRT07]; see also the introduction of [KKP10].
statements.statement:
theorem one_two_three_conjecture.variants.one_to_thirty
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hG : NoIsolatedEdge G) :
    ∃ w : Sym2 V → ℕ, (∀ e ∈ G.edgeFinset, 1 ≤ w e ∧ w e ≤ 30) ∧
      IsVertexColouringWeighting G w

statements.name: OneTwoThreeConjecture.one_two_three_conjecture.variants.isolated_edge_necessary
statements.doc:
**The hypothesis "no isolated edge" is necessary.**

A single edge `K₂` has no vertex-colouring edge weighting at all: both endpoints receive the
weight of the unique edge as their weighted degree.
statements.statement:
theorem one_two_three_conjecture.variants.isolated_edge_necessary :
    ¬ ∃ w : Sym2 (Fin 2) → ℕ, IsVertexColouringWeighting (completeGraph (Fin 2)) w

statements.name: OneTwoThreeConjecture.one_two_three_conjecture.variants.two_weights_insufficient
statements.doc:
**Weights $\{1, 2\}$ do not suffice: the triangle.**

In `K₃` the three vertex sums are `a + b`, `a + c`, `b + c` for the three edge weights
`a, b, c`, and they are pairwise distinct only if `a, b, c` are, which is impossible with
two available weights. Hence the constant `3` in the conjecture cannot be lowered to `2`.
statements.statement:
theorem one_two_three_conjecture.variants.two_weights_insufficient :
    ¬ ∃ w : Sym2 (Fin 3) → ℕ, (∀ e ∈ (completeGraph (Fin 3)).edgeFinset, 1 ≤ w e ∧ w e ≤ 2) ∧
      IsVertexColouringWeighting (completeGraph (Fin 3)) w

problems.title: Parities of partition numbers
problems.doc:
There are several conjectures on parities of partition numbers. The most famous conjecture is the
Parkin-Shanks conjecture, which states that the natural density of `n` where the partition number
`p(n)` is even (resp. odd) exists and equals `1/2`.

There are several related (weaker) results toward the conjecture. Kolberg showed that `p(n)` takes
each parity infinitely often. Subbarao conjectured that every arithmetic progression `r (mod t)`
contains infinitely many `n` with `p(n)` even and infinitely many `n` with `p(n)` odd; the even
case was proved by Ono and the odd case by Radu. Quantitative lower bounds for the number of
`n ≤ X` with `p(n)` even (resp. odd) have also been studied. The best known bounds are
`≫ √X log log X` for even values (Bellaïche–Nicolas) and `≫ √X` for odd values (Zheng, in an
appendix to Ono–Swaminathan). Ono–Swaminathan also proved that both parities occur infinitely often
along the quadratic progressions `(D m² + 1) / 24`, and Ono conjectured the same for every nonconstant
integer-valued polynomial that is eventually positive.

*References:*
* [On the distribution of parity in the partition function](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2003251),
  T. R. Parkin, D. Shanks, Math. Comp. 21 (1967), 466–480.
* [Note on the parity of the partition function](https://doi.org/10.7146/math.scand.a-10584),
  O. Kolberg, Math. Scand. 7 (1959), 377–378.
* Some remarks on the partition function, M. V. Subbarao, Amer. Math. Monthly 73 (1966), 851–854.
* [Parity of the partition function in arithmetic progressions](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1996.472.1),
  K. Ono, J. Reine Angew. Math. 472 (1996), 1–16.
* [Distribution of parity of the partition function in arithmetic progressions](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-3577(99)80014-7),
  S. Ahlgren, Indag. Math. (N.S.) 10 (1999), 173–181.
* [Parity of the partition function](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aim.2010.02.023), K. Ono,
  Adv. Math. 225 (2010), 349–366.
* [A proof of Subbarao's conjecture](https://doi.org/10.1515/CRELLE.2011.165), C.-S. Radu,
  J. Reine Angew. Math. 672 (2012), 161–175.
* [Parité des coefficients de formes modulaires](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11139-014-9645-9),
  J. Bellaïche, J.-L. Nicolas, Ramanujan J. 40 (2016), 1–44.
* [Nonzero coefficients of half-integral weight modular forms mod ℓ](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.07440),
  J. Bellaïche, B. Green, K. Soundararajan, Res. Math. Sci. 5 (2018), Paper No. 6.
* [Parity of the partition function in quadratic progressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09553)
  (with an appendix by Q.-Y. Zheng), K. Ono, A. Swaminathan, arXiv:2509.09553.
* [Cox] D. A. Cox, Primes of the Form $x^2 + ny^2$, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2013.

reference.text: On the distribution of parity in the partition function

statements.name: PartitionParity.kolberg
statements.doc: `p(n)` is even for infinitely many `n` and odd for infinitely many `n`. (Kolberg)
statements.statement:
theorem kolberg :
    {n : ℕ | Even (partitionNumber n)}.Infinite ∧ {n : ℕ | Odd (partitionNumber n)}.Infinite

statements.name: PartitionParity.parkin_shanks
statements.doc:
The natural density of `n` where the partition number `p(n)` is even (resp. odd) exists and
equals `1/2`.
statements.statement:
theorem parkin_shanks :
    {n : ℕ | Even (partitionNumber n)}.HasDensity (1 / 2) ∧
    {n : ℕ | Odd (partitionNumber n)}.HasDensity (1 / 2)

statements.name: PartitionParity.subbarao.even
statements.doc:
Every arithmetic progression contains infinitely many `n` where `p(n)` is even.
Conjectured by Subbarao and proved by Ono.
statements.statement:
theorem subbarao.even : ∀ r t, 0 < t →
    {n : ℕ | n ≡ r [MOD t] ∧ Even (partitionNumber n)}.Infinite

statements.name: PartitionParity.subbarao.odd
statements.doc:
Every arithmetic progression contains infinitely many `n` where `p(n)` is odd.
Conjectured by Subbarao; Ono proved it for every progression containing at least one `n` with
`p(n)` odd, and Radu showed that every progression contains such an `n`.
statements.statement:
theorem subbarao.odd : ∀ r t, 0 < t →
    {n : ℕ | n ≡ r [MOD t] ∧ Odd (partitionNumber n)}.Infinite

statements.name: PartitionParity.ahlgren.even
statements.doc:
For every arithmetic progression `r (mod t)`, the number of `n ≤ X` with `n ≡ r (mod t)` and
`p(n)` even is `≫ √X`. (Ahlgren)
statements.statement:
theorem ahlgren.even : ∀ r t, 0 < t →
    (fun X : ℝ ↦ √X) =O[atTop]
      fun X : ℝ ↦ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ X ∧ n ≡ r [MOD t] ∧ Even (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.ahlgren.odd
statements.doc:
For every arithmetic progression `r (mod t)`, the number of `n ≤ X` with `n ≡ r (mod t)` and
`p(n)` odd is `≫ √X / log X`. Ahlgren proved this for every progression containing at least one
`n` with `p(n)` odd; by Radu's theorem every progression does.
statements.statement:
theorem ahlgren.odd : ∀ r t, 0 < t →
    (fun X : ℝ ↦ √X / X.log) =O[atTop]
      fun X : ℝ ↦ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ X ∧ n ≡ r [MOD t] ∧ Odd (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.bellaiche_nicolas.even
statements.doc: The number of `n ≤ X` with `p(n)` even is `≫ √X log log X`. (Bellaïche–Nicolas)
statements.statement:
theorem bellaiche_nicolas.even :
    (fun X : ℝ ↦ √X * X.log.log) =O[atTop]
      fun X : ℝ ↦ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ X ∧ Even (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.bellaiche_nicolas.even_explicit
statements.doc:
The number of `n ≤ x` with `p(n)` even is at least `0.069 √x log log x` for every `x > 1`.
(Bellaïche–Nicolas)
statements.statement:
theorem bellaiche_nicolas.even_explicit : ∀ x : ℝ, 1 < x →
    0.069 * √x * x.log.log ≤ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ x ∧ Even (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.bellaiche_nicolas.odd_explicit
statements.doc:
The number of `n ≤ x` with `p(n)` odd is at least `0.037 √x / (log x)^(7/8)` for every `x ≥ 2`.
(Bellaïche–Nicolas)
statements.statement:
theorem bellaiche_nicolas.odd_explicit : ∀ x : ℝ, 2 ≤ x →
    0.037 * √x / (x.log) ^ (7 / 8 : ℝ) ≤ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ x ∧ Odd (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.bellaiche_green_soundararajan.odd
statements.doc:
The number of `n ≤ X` with `p(n)` odd is `≫ √X / log log X`.
(Bellaïche–Green–Soundararajan)
statements.statement:
theorem bellaiche_green_soundararajan.odd :
    (fun X : ℝ ↦ √X / X.log.log) =O[atTop]
      fun X : ℝ ↦ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ X ∧ Odd (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.ono_swaminathan.quadratic
statements.doc:
For square-free `D > 1` with `D ≡ 23 (mod 24)`, both parities occur infinitely often among
`p((D m² + 1) / 24)` as `m` ranges over the positive integers coprime to `6`. Note that
`24 ∣ D m² + 1` for such `m`. Conjectured by Ono and proved by Ono–Swaminathan.
statements.statement:
theorem ono_swaminathan.quadratic : ∀ D : ℕ, 1 < D → Squarefree D → D % 24 = 23 →
    {m : ℕ | m.Coprime 6 ∧ Even (partitionNumber ((D * m ^ 2 + 1) / 24))}.Infinite ∧
    {m : ℕ | m.Coprime 6 ∧ Odd (partitionNumber ((D * m ^ 2 + 1) / 24))}.Infinite

statements.name: PartitionParity.ono_swaminathan.odd_bound
statements.doc:
The odd half of Theorem 1 of Ono–Swaminathan, with its effective bound: for square-free `D > 1`
with `D ≡ 23 (mod 24)` there is an `m` coprime to `6` with `m ≤ 12 h(-D) + 2` such that
`p((D m² + 1) / 24)` is odd, where `h(-D)` is the class number of `ℚ(√-D)`. Here `ℚ(√-D)` is
`AdjoinRoot (X ^ 2 + D)`, a number field since `X ^ 2 + D` is irreducible over `ℚ` for `D > 0`.
statements.statement:
theorem ono_swaminathan.odd_bound (D : ℕ) (hD : 1 < D) (hsq : Squarefree D) (h23 : D % 24 = 23) :
    haveI : Fact (Irreducible (X ^ 2 + C (D : ℚ))) :=
      ⟨irreducible_X_sq_add_C_of_pos (Nat.cast_pos.2 (by lia))⟩
    ∃ m : ℕ, m.Coprime 6 ∧
      m ≤ 12 * NumberField.classNumber (AdjoinRoot (X ^ 2 + C (D : ℚ))) + 2 ∧
      Odd (partitionNumber ((D * m ^ 2 + 1) / 24))

statements.name: PartitionParity.classNumber_eq_ncard_reducedForms
statements.doc:
For square-free `D ≡ 3 (mod 4)`, the discriminant `-D` is fundamental and the class number of
`ℚ(√-D)` equals the number of reduced primitive positive-definite binary quadratic forms of
discriminant `-D` [Cox, Theorem 2.8].
This identification is used in Zheng's appendix to Ono–Swaminathan.
statements.statement:
theorem classNumber_eq_ncard_reducedForms (D : ℕ) (hsq : Squarefree D) (h3 : D % 4 = 3) :
    haveI : Fact (Irreducible (X ^ 2 + C (D : ℚ))) :=
      ⟨irreducible_X_sq_add_C_of_pos (Nat.cast_pos.2 (by lia))⟩
    NumberField.classNumber (AdjoinRoot (X ^ 2 + C (D : ℚ))) =
      {⟨a, b, c⟩ : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ | IsReducedForm D a b c}.ncard

statements.name: PartitionParity.zheng.liminf
statements.doc:
Zheng's explicit lower bound: `liminf_{X → ∞} N_odd(X) / √X ≥ 243 / (64 √6 π⁵)`, where
`N_odd(X)` is the number of `n ≤ X` with `p(n)` odd [Ono-Swaminathan, Appendix A, Corollary 2].
statements.statement:
theorem zheng.liminf :
    ((243 / (64 * √6 * π ^ 5) : ℝ) : EReal) ≤
      liminf (fun X : ℝ ↦
        ((({n : ℕ | n ≤ X ∧ Odd (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ) / √X : ℝ) : EReal)) atTop

statements.name: PartitionParity.zheng.odd
statements.doc: The number of `n ≤ X` with `p(n)` odd is `≫ √X`.
statements.statement:
theorem zheng.odd :
    (fun X : ℝ ↦ √X) =O[atTop]
      fun X : ℝ ↦ ({n : ℕ | n ≤ X ∧ Odd (partitionNumber n)}.ncard : ℝ)

statements.name: PartitionParity.ono.polynomial
statements.doc:
Ono's conjecture, as stated in Section 1 of Ono–Swaminathan: if `g` is a nonconstant
integer-valued polynomial that is eventually positive, then `p(g(n))` is even for infinitely many
`n` and odd for infinitely many `n`.
statements.statement:
theorem ono.polynomial (g : ℚ[X]) (hg : 0 < g.natDegree)
    (hint : ∀ n : ℕ, ∃ k : ℤ, g.eval (n : ℚ) = k)
    (hpos : ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, 0 < g.eval (n : ℚ)) :
    {n : ℕ | Even (partitionNumber ⌊g.eval (n : ℚ)⌋₊)}.Infinite ∧
    {n : ℕ | Odd (partitionNumber ⌊g.eval (n : ℚ)⌋₊)}.Infinite

problems.title: Pfister's problem on the Pythagoras number of $\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)$
problems.doc:
The Pythagoras number $p(K)$ of a field $K$ is the least $p$ such that every sum of squares in
$K$ is a sum of $p$ squares, i.e. the least element of `pythagorasBounds K`.

Artin's solution of Hilbert's 17th problem shows that a positive semidefinite rational function
in $\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ is a sum of squares, and Pfister showed that $2^n$ squares
suffice ([Pfister1967, Theorem 1]; for the field, Corollary 1 of Theorem 2 in [Pfister1971]).
Since sums of squares are positive semidefinite, $p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)) \le 2^n$
[Pfister1995, p. 95].

Problem 1 of [Pfister1971, §4] asks for the true value of $p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n))$.
The question is often posed as: is $p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)) = 2^n$, i.e. is Pfister's
bound optimal? See e.g. [Benoist2017, Question 0.2].

Problem 1 itself quotes the lower bound $n + 1 \le p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n))$ from Cassels'
theorem [Cassels1964]. For $n \ge 2$ the best known bounds are
$n + 2 \le p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)) \le 2^n$ [Pfister1995, p. 97], where the lower bound
follows from the Cassels–Ellison–Pfister theorem [CEP1971]. The bounds agree for $n = 2$, so the
value is known for $n \le 2$ and open for every $n \ge 3$. The survey
[MerkurjevParimala2025, §5.2] records the question as open even for $\mathbb{R}(X_1, X_2, X_3)$
(Question 5.7).

*References:*
- [Pfister1971] A. Pfister, *Sums of squares in real function fields*, pp. 297–300 in Actes du
  Congrès International des Mathématiciens, Tome 1 (Nice, 1970), Gauthier-Villars, 1971,
  [IMU scan](https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1970.1/ICM1970.1.ocr.pdf).
- [Pfister1967] A. Pfister, *Zur Darstellung definiter Funktionen als Summe von Quadraten*,
  Invent. Math. 4 (1967), 229–237, [doi:10.1007/BF01425382](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01425382).
- [Cassels1964] J. W. S. Cassels, *On the representation of rational functions as sums of squares*,
  Acta Arith. 9 (1964), 79–82, [doi:10.4064/aa-9-1-79-82](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-9-1-79-82).
- [Pfister1995] A. Pfister, *Quadratic forms with applications to algebraic geometry and
  topology*, London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Ser. 217, Cambridge University Press, 1995.
- [CEP1971] J. W. S. Cassels, W. J. Ellison, A. Pfister, *On sums of squares and on elliptic
  curves over function fields*, J. Number Theory 3 (1971), 125–149,
  [doi:10.1016/0022-314X(71)90030-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-314X(71)90030-8).
- [Benoist2017] O. Benoist, *On Hilbert's 17th problem in low degree*, Algebra Number Theory 11
  (2017), 929–959, [doi:10.2140/ant.2017.11.929](https://doi.org/10.2140/ant.2017.11.929),
  [arXiv:1602.07330](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07330).
- [MerkurjevParimala2025] A. Merkurjev, R. Parimala, *Quadratic forms beyond arithmetic*, Notices
  Amer. Math. Soc. 72 (2025), no. 7, 711–718,
  [doi:10.1090/noti3192](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti3192).

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem
statements.doc:
**Pfister's problem** (Problem 1 of [Pfister1971, §4]): what is the true value of
$p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n))$, as a function of $n$? It is $1$, $2$, $4$ for $n = 0, 1, 2$
(`pfister_problem.variants.zero`, `pfister_problem.variants.one`, `pfister_problem.variants.two`)
and open for every $n \ge 3$, where only the bounds
$n + 2 \le p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)) \le 2^n$ are known.
statements.statement:
theorem pfister_problem :
    ∀ n, IsLeast (pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin n) ℝ)) (pfister_problem.answer n)

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.eq_two_pow
statements.doc:
Pfister's problem in its common yes/no form (e.g. Question 0.2 of [Benoist2017]): is
$p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)) = 2^n$ for every $n$, i.e. is Pfister's bound optimal? This
holds for $n \le 2$ and is open for every $n \ge 3$.
statements.statement:
theorem pfister_problem.variants.eq_two_pow :
    ∀ n : ℕ, IsLeast (pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin n) ℝ)) (2 ^ n)

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.upper_bound
statements.doc:
**Pfister's theorem**: every sum of squares in $\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ is a sum of $2^n$
squares [Pfister1995, p. 95]; this is Corollary 1 of Theorem 2 in [Pfister1971]. For positive
semidefinite polynomials it is [Pfister1967, Theorem 1], the quantitative refinement of Artin's
theorem `Hilbert17.hilbert_17th_problem` in `FormalConjectures/HilbertProblems/17.lean`.
statements.statement:
theorem pfister_problem.variants.upper_bound (n : ℕ) :
    2 ^ n ∈ pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin n) ℝ)

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.cassels
statements.doc:
**Cassels' theorem** [Cassels1964], as quoted in Problem 1 of [Pfister1971, §4]:
$1 + X_1^2 + \dots + X_n^2$ is not a sum of $n$ squares in $\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)$.
statements.statement:
theorem pfister_problem.variants.cassels (n : ℕ) :
    ¬IsSumSqOfLength n (algebraMap (MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ) (MvRatFunc (Fin n) ℝ)
      (1 + ∑ i, MvPolynomial.X i * MvPolynomial.X i))

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.add_one_le
statements.doc:
The lower bound $n + 1 \le p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n))$ quoted in Problem 1 of
[Pfister1971, §4]: $1 + X_1^2 + \dots + X_n^2$ is a sum of $n + 1$ squares but, by Cassels'
theorem `pfister_problem.variants.cassels`, not of $n$ squares. It is superseded by
`pfister_problem.variants.lower_bound` for $n \ge 2$.
statements.statement:
theorem pfister_problem.variants.add_one_le (n : ℕ) {p : ℕ}
    (hp : p ∈ pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin n) ℝ)) : n + 1 ≤ p

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.lower_bound
statements.doc:
The lower bound $n + 2 \le p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n))$ for $n \ge 2$ [Pfister1995, p. 97],
a consequence of the Cassels–Ellison–Pfister theorem [CEP1971]. The hypothesis $n \ge 2$ is
needed: $p(\mathbb{R}(X)) = 2 < 3$.
statements.statement:
theorem pfister_problem.variants.lower_bound (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) {p : ℕ}
    (hp : p ∈ pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin n) ℝ)) : n + 2 ≤ p

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.zero
statements.doc:
$p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, \dots, X_n)) = 1$ for $n = 0$, i.e. $p(\mathbb{R}) = 1$: here the bounds $n + 1$
and $2^n$ of `pfister_problem.variants.add_one_le` and `pfister_problem.variants.upper_bound`
agree. Compare `isLeast_pythagorasBounds_real`, the same value for `ℝ` itself.
statements.statement: theorem pfister_problem.variants.zero : IsLeast (pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin 0) ℝ)) 1

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.one
statements.doc:
$p(\mathbb{R}(X)) = 2$ [Pfister1995, p. 96]: Pfister's bound gives $p \le 2$, and Cassels'
theorem `pfister_problem.variants.cassels` gives $p \ge 2$ through
`pfister_problem.variants.add_one_le`, since $1 + X^2$ is a sum of two squares that is not a
square in $\mathbb{R}(X)$.
statements.statement: theorem pfister_problem.variants.one : IsLeast (pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin 1) ℝ)) 2

statements.name: PfisterPythagorasNumber.pfister_problem.variants.two
statements.doc:
$p(\mathbb{R}(X_1, X_2)) = 4$ [CEP1971], as recorded in [Pfister1971, §4] and [Pfister1995, p. 96]:
the bounds $n + 2$ and $2^n$ agree when $n = 2$.
statements.statement: theorem pfister_problem.variants.two : IsLeast (pythagorasBounds (MvRatFunc (Fin 2) ℝ)) 4

problems.title: Prime Tuples Conjecture
problems.doc:
*Reference:* [FLC07] Friedlander, J. B. and Luca, F. and Stoiciu, M., On the irrationality of a
divisor function series. Integers (2007).

statements.name: PrimeTuplesConjecture.prime_tuples_conjecture
statements.doc:
For any `k ≥ 2`, let `a₁,...,aₖ` and `b₁,...,bₖ` be integers with `aᵢ > 0`. Suppose that for
every prime `p` there exists an integer `n` such that `p ∤ ∏ i, (aᵢ n + bᵢ)`. Then there exist
infinitely many `n` such that `aᵢ n + bᵢ` is prime for all `i`.

problems.title: Pudlák's conjectures on incompleteness in the finite domain
problems.doc:
*References:*
* [CR79] Cook, S. A. and Reckhow, R. A. (1979). "The relative efficiency of propositional proof
  systems." *J. Symbolic Logic* 44, pp. 36--50.
* [HH88] Hartmanis, J. and Hemachandra, L. A. (1988). "Complexity classes without machines: on
  complete languages for UP." *Theoret. Comput. Sci.* 58, pp. 129--142.
* [KP89] Krajíček, J. and Pudlák, P. (1989). "Propositional proof systems, the consistency of
  first order theories and the complexity of computations." *J. Symbolic Logic* 54,
  pp. 1063--1079.
* [MP91] Megiddo, N. and Papadimitriou, C. H. (1991). "On total functions, existence theorems
  and computational complexity." *Theoret. Comput. Sci.* 81, pp. 317--324.
* [Pa94] Papadimitriou, C. H. (1994). "On the complexity of the parity argument and other
  inefficient proofs of existence." *J. Comput. System Sci.* 48, pp. 498--532.
* [KMT03] Köbler, J., Messner, J., and Torán, J. (2003). "Optimal proof systems imply complete
  sets for promise classes." *Inform. and Comput.* 184, pp. 71--92.
* [Pu17] Pudlák, P. (2017). "Incompleteness in the finite domain." *Bull. Symbolic Logic* 23,
  pp. 405--441. [arXiv:1601.01487](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01487)
* [Kh22] Khaniki, E. (2022). "New relations and separations of conjectures about incompleteness
  in the finite domain." *J. Symbolic Logic* 87, pp. 912--937.
  [arXiv:1904.01362](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01362)

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.sat_no_p_optimal_proof_system
statements.doc:
**SAT has no p-optimal proof system** (Pudlák's conjecture `SAT` [Pu17]).

No proof system for `SAT` p-simulates every other proof system for `SAT`. Since the existence of
a p-optimal proof system depends only on the polynomial-time many-one degree of the language
[KMT03], the conjecture is stated here for an arbitrary NP-complete language. Equivalently
[Pu17], for every consistent polynomial-time axiomatized theory `T ⊇ S¹₂` there is a proof
system for `SAT` whose soundness `T` cannot prove.
statements.statement:
theorem sat_no_p_optimal_proof_system (L : DecisionProblem) (hL : IsCompleteFor NP L) :
    ¬∃ P : List Bool → List Bool, IsPOptimalProofSystem L P

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.tfnp_no_complete_problem
statements.doc:
**TFNP has no complete problem** (Megiddo–Papadimitriou [MP91]; Pudlák's conjecture `TFNP`
[Pu17]).

No total NP search problem is complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions of search
problems. Equivalently [Pu17], for every consistent polynomial-time axiomatized theory
`T ⊇ S¹₂` some total NP search problem is not polynomially reducible to any total NP
search problem provably total in `T`.
statements.statement: theorem tfnp_no_complete_problem : ¬∃ T : TFNPProblem, T.IsComplete

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.up_no_complete_language
statements.doc:
**UP has no complete language** (Hartmanis–Hemachandra [HH88]; Pudlák's conjecture `UP`
[Pu17]).

No language accepted by an unambiguous polynomial-time verifier is complete for `UP` under
polynomial-time many-one reductions.
statements.statement: theorem up_no_complete_language : ¬∃ L : DecisionProblem, IsCompleteFor UP L

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.np_inter_conp_no_complete_language
statements.doc:
**NP ∩ coNP has no complete language** (Pudlák's conjecture `NP ∩ coNP` [Pu17]).

No language in `NP ∩ coNP` is complete for that class under polynomial-time many-one
reductions.
statements.statement:
theorem np_inter_conp_no_complete_language :
    ¬∃ L : DecisionProblem, IsCompleteFor (NP ∩ coNP) L

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.tfnp_no_complete_problem.variants.exists_of_NP_eq_coNP
statements.doc:
**If `NP = coNP` then TFNP has a complete problem** [MP91, Pu17].

Under `NP = coNP` the search problem "given a CNF, find a satisfying assignment or a short
proof of unsatisfiability" is total and complete.
statements.statement:
theorem tfnp_no_complete_problem.variants.exists_of_NP_eq_coNP (h : NP = coNP) :
    ∃ T : TFNPProblem, T.IsComplete

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.tfnp_no_complete_problem.variants.NP_ne_coNP
statements.doc: **The conjecture implies `NP ≠ coNP`** [Pu17].
statements.statement:
theorem tfnp_no_complete_problem.variants.NP_ne_coNP
    (h : ¬∃ T : TFNPProblem, T.IsComplete) : NP ≠ coNP

statements.name: PudlakFiniteDomain.sat_no_p_optimal_proof_system.variants.exists_of_P_eq_NP
statements.doc:
**If `P = NP` then every NP-complete language has a p-optimal proof system.**

The map sending `π` to itself when `π ∈ L` and to a fixed element of `L` otherwise is then
polynomial-time, and every proof system `Q` for `L` is p-simulated by it via `Q` itself.
statements.statement:
theorem sat_no_p_optimal_proof_system.variants.exists_of_P_eq_NP (h : P = NP)
    (L : DecisionProblem) (hL : IsCompleteFor NP L) (hne : ∃ y, L y = true) :
    ∃ P : List Bool → List Bool, IsPOptimalProofSystem L P

problems.title: Reed's omega, delta, and chi conjecture
problems.doc:
*References*:
- [B. Reed,  ω Δ and χ, J. Graph Theory 27 (1998) 177-212.](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0118(199804)27:4%3C177::AID-JGT1%3E3.0.CO;2-K)
- [openproblemgarden](http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/reeds_omega_delta_and_chi_conjecture)
- [mathoverflow/37923](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/37923) asked by user [Andrew D. King](https://mathoverflow.net/users/4580/andrew-d-king)

reference.text: B. Reed,  ω Δ and χ, J. Graph Theory 27 (1998) 177-212.

statements.name: ReedOmegaDeltaChi.reed_omega_delta_chi_conjecture
statements.doc:
For a graph $G$, we define $\Delta(G)$ to be the maximum degree, $\omega(G)$ to be the size of the
largest clique subgraph, and $\chi(G)$ to be the chromatic number. Reed's omega, delta, and chi
conjecture states that $$\chi(G) \leq \lceil \frac{1}{2}(\omega(G) + \Delta(G) + 1) \rceil.$$
statements.statement:
theorem reed_omega_delta_chi_conjecture :
  ∀ {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V),
    let χ := G.chromaticNumber
    let ω := G.ecliqueNum
    let Δ := G.emaxDegree
    2 * χ ≤ ω + Δ + 2

statements.name: ReedOmegaDeltaChi.reed_omega_delta_chi_conjecture_for_finite_graphs
statements.doc:
For a finite graph $G$, we define $\Delta(G)$ to be the maximum degree, $\omega(G)$ to be the
size of the largest clique subgraph, and $\chi(G)$ to be the chromatic number. Reed's omega,
delta, and chi conjecture states that $$\chi(G) \leq \lceil \frac{1}{2}(\omega(G) + \Delta(G) + 1) \rceil.$$
statements.statement:
theorem reed_omega_delta_chi_conjecture_for_finite_graphs :
  ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
    let χ := G.chromaticNumber
    let ω := G.cliqueNum
    let Δ := G.maxDegree
    2 * χ ≤ ω + Δ + 2

statements.name: ReedOmegaDeltaChi.reed_conjecture_Δ_6_ω_2
statements.doc: The simplest open case is when $\Delta(G) = 6$ and $\omega(G) = 2$.
statements.statement:
theorem reed_conjecture_Δ_6_ω_2 :
  ∀ {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V), G.emaxDegree = 6 ∧ G.cliqueNum = 2 → G.chromaticNumber ≤ 5

problems.title: Equivalents to the Riemann Hypothesis
problems.doc:
This file contains formal statements that are known to be equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis,
following the survey [Co26], §4. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis itself is in
`FormalConjectures.Millennium.RiemannHypothesis`.

*References:*
* [Co26] A. Connes, [The Riemann Hypothesis: Past, Present and a Letter Through
  Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04022), 2026.

reference.text:
The Riemann Hypothesis: Past, Present and a Letter Through
  Time

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.robin_criterion
statements.doc:
**Robin's Criterion**. The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to
$$
  \sigma(n) < e ^ {\gamma} n\log\log n
$$
for all $n > 5040$, where $\gamma$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant and $\sigma(n)$ is
the sum of divisors.
statements.statement:
theorem robin_criterion :
    RiemannHypothesis ↔ ∀ n > 5040, σ 1 n < (exp eulerMascheroniConstant) * n * log (log n)

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.robin_criterion_rhs
statements.doc: The statement that Robin's criterion holds.
statements.statement:
theorem robin_criterion_rhs {n : ℕ} (hn : n > 5040) :
    σ 1 n < exp eulerMascheroniConstant * n * log (log n)

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.lagarias_criterion
statements.doc:
**Lagarias' Criterion**. A refinement of Robin's criterion: the Riemann Hypothesis
is equivalent to
$$
  \sigma(n) < H_n + e^{H_n}\log H_n
$$
for all $n \geq 2$, where $H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \cdots + 1/n$ is the $n$th harmonic number.

Note that [Co26] states this for all $n \geq 1$, but at $n = 1$ both sides equal $1$; Lagarias'
original formulation is the non-strict inequality for all $n \geq 1$, with equality only at
$n = 1$.
statements.statement:
theorem lagarias_criterion : RiemannHypothesis ↔
    ∀ n > 1, σ 1 n < harmonic n + exp (harmonic n) * log (harmonic n)

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.lagarias_criterion_rhs
statements.doc: The statement that Lagarias' criterion holds.
statements.statement:
theorem lagarias_criterion_rhs {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 < n) :
    σ 1 n < harmonic n + exp (harmonic n) * log (harmonic n)

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.li_criterion
statements.doc:
**Li's Criterion**. The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to the positivity of
$$
  \lambda_n := \sum_{\rho}\left(1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{\rho}\right)^n\right)
$$
for each $n > 0$.
statements.statement: theorem li_criterion : RiemannHypothesis ↔ ∀ n > 0, 0 < lambda n

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.li_criterion_rhs
statements.doc: The statement that Li's criterion holds.
statements.statement: theorem li_criterion_rhs {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) : 0 < lambda n

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.beurling_nyman_criterion
RiemannHypothesis.beurling_nyman_criterion_rhs
statements.doc: The statement that the Beurling-Nyman criterion holds.

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.weil_positivity_criterion
statements.doc:
**Weil's Positivity Criterion**. The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to the non-positivity of
Weil factor sums on the convolution of test functions. In [Co26] this is expressed as
$$
  \sum_v W_v(g\star g^*) \leq 0
$$
for all compactly-supported smooth functions $g : \mathbb{R}_+^{\times} \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
the Mellin transform of $g$ vanishes at $\pm i / 2$, where $g^*(x) := \bar{g}(x^{-1})$ and $W_v$
are the multiplicative Weil factors defined in [Co26]. We formalise this as the corresponding
additive statement (via $x = e^u$), since convolution in mathlib is additive, and restrict to
real-valued test functions $g$, which suffices for the equivalence.
statements.statement:
theorem weil_positivity_criterion :
    RiemannHypothesis ↔ ∀ g : C_c(ℝ, ℝ), ContDiff ℝ ∞ g → IsTestFunction g →
      weilArchimedean (g ⋆ fun x ↦ g (-x)) +
        ∑' p : Nat.Primes, weilNonArchimedean p (g ⋆ fun x ↦ g (-x)) ≤ 0

statements.name: RiemannHypothesis.weil_positivity_criterion_rhs
statements.doc: The statement that the Weil criterion holds.
statements.statement:
theorem weil_positivity_criterion_rhs {g : C_c(ℝ, ℝ)} (hg : ContDiff ℝ ∞ g)
    (h : IsTestFunction g) :
    weilArchimedean (g ⋆ fun x ↦ g (-x)) +
      ∑' p : Nat.Primes, weilNonArchimedean p (g ⋆ fun x ↦ g (-x)) ≤ 0

problems.title: Moments of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line
problems.doc:
The moments $\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T |\zeta(1/2 + it)|^{2k}\,dt$ are conjectured to be asymptotic
to $c_k (\log T)^{k^2}$ for some constants $c_k$. This is a theorem for $k = 1$
(Hardy–Littlewood, $c_1 = 1$) and $k = 2$ (Ingham, $c_2 = 1/(2\pi^2)$), and these are the only
proven cases. Conrey–Ghosh and Conrey–Gonek conjectured $c_3 = 42 a_3 / 9!$ and
$c_4 = 24024 a_4 / 16!$, with $a_k$ the arithmetic factor
$a_k = \prod_p (1 - 1/p)^{k^2} \sum_{m \ge 0} \binom{m+k-1}{m}^2 p^{-m}$;
Keating–Snaith conjectured $c_k = a_k f_k$ with $f_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} j!/(j+k)!$ from random
matrix theory, recovering $g_k = (k^2)!\,f_k = 1, 2, 42, 24024$.

The statements and constants below are taken from §3.4.5 of [Co26].

*References:*
- [Co26] A. Connes, *The Riemann Hypothesis: Past, Present and a Letter Through Time*,
  [arXiv:2602.04022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04022), §3.4.5.
- [In26] A. E. Ingham, *Mean-value theorems in the theory of the Riemann zeta-function*,
  Proc. London Math. Soc. 27 (1926), 273–300.
- [CG98] J. B. Conrey, A. Ghosh, *A conjecture for the sixth power moment of the Riemann
  zeta-function*, Internat. Math. Res. Notices 1998, no. 15, 775–780.
- [CGo01] J. B. Conrey, S. Gonek, *High moments of the Riemann zeta-function*, Duke Math. J.
  107 (2001), no. 3, 577–604.
- [KS00] J. P. Keating, N. C. Snaith, *Random matrix theory and $\zeta(1/2+it)$*, Commun. Math.
  Phys. 214 (2000), no. 1, 57–89.

statements.name: RiemannZetaMoments.moment_isEquiv
statements.doc:
The asymptotic behaviour of the $k$th moment of the Riemann zeta function
is conjectured to be
$$
  \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T |\zeta(1/2 + it)|^{2k}dt \sim c_k \log(T)^{k^2},
$$
for some constant $c_k$.
statements.statement:
theorem moment_isEquiv (k : ℕ) : ∃ c > (0 : ℝ),
    moment k ~[atTop] fun T ↦ c * T.log ^ (k ^ 2)

statements.name: RiemannZetaMoments.moment_isEquiv₁
statements.doc:
The asymptotic behaviour of the first moment of the Riemann zeta function was proved by
Hardy and Littlewood, where $c_1 = 1$ [Co26, §3.4.5].
statements.statement: theorem moment_isEquiv₁ : moment 1 ~[atTop] fun T ↦ T.log

statements.name: RiemannZetaMoments.moment_isEquiv₂
statements.doc:
The asymptotic behaviour of the second moment of the Riemann zeta function was proved by
Ingham [In26], where $c_2 = 1/(2\pi^2)$.
statements.statement: theorem moment_isEquiv₂ : moment 2 ~[atTop] fun T ↦ (1 / (2 * π ^ 2)) * T.log ^ 4

statements.name: RiemannZetaMoments.moment_isEquiv₃
statements.doc:
The constant in the asymptotic formula for the 3rd zeta moment is conjectured
to be $42a_3/9!$ [CG98].
statements.statement: theorem moment_isEquiv₃ : moment 3 ~[atTop] fun T ↦ 42 * arithmeticFactor 3 / 9 ! * T.log ^ 9

statements.name: RiemannZetaMoments.moment_isEquiv₄
statements.doc:
The constant in the asymptotic formula for the 4th zeta moment is conjectured to
be $24024a_4/16!$ [CGo01].
statements.statement:
theorem moment_isEquiv₄ :
    moment 4 ~[atTop] fun T ↦ 24024 * arithmeticFactor 4 / 16 ! * T.log ^ 16

statements.name: RiemannZetaMoments.moment_isEquivₖ
statements.doc:
The Keating–Snaith conjecture [KS00] for the $k$th moment of the Riemann zeta function,
provides the value of $c_k$ in the asymptotic formula [Co26, §3.4.5].
statements.statement:
theorem moment_isEquivₖ (k : ℕ) : moment k ~[atTop]
    fun T ↦ (arithmeticFactor k * ∏ j ∈ Finset.range k, (j ! : ℝ) / (j + k) !) *
      T.log ^ (k ^ 2)

problems.title: Simple zeros of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line
problems.doc:
*References:*
- [Cl26] Claude (Anthropic), *More than two thirds of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are
  simple and on the critical line*, August 2026.
  [pdf](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/95c246936988e43127bc6b2ceb7077c1dad2d68e.pdf),
  [Lean formalisation](https://github.com/anthropics/zeta-23-lean).
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis#Zeros_on_the_critical_line)

For a nontrivial zero `ρ = β + iγ` of `ζ` (or of a Dirichlet `L`-function) with multiplicity
`m_ρ`, and `0 ≤ T₁ < T₂`, write
- `N(T₁, T₂) = ∑_{T₁ < γ ≤ T₂} m_ρ` for the zeros counted with multiplicity,
- `N_d(T₁, T₂) = #{ρ : T₁ < γ ≤ T₂}` for the distinct zeros, and
- `Ns(T₁, T₂) = #{ρ : T₁ < γ ≤ T₂, β = 1/2, m_ρ = 1}` for the simple zeros on the critical line.

[Cl26, Theorem A] proves unconditionally that `Ns(T, 2T) ≥ (2/3 - o(1)) N(T, 2T)` and
`N_d(T, 2T) ≥ (5/6 - o(1)) N(T, 2T)`, improving to `2 - c_MT⁻¹ = 0.6725…` and
`(3 - c_MT⁻¹) / 2 = 0.8362…` with the Montgomery–Taylor window, where
`c_MT⁻¹ = 1/2 + cot(1/√2)/√2`; [Cl26, Theorem B] is the same for `L(s, χ)`, `χ` primitive.

statements.name: riemannZeta.simple_prop_two_thirds
statements.doc:
At least two thirds of the nontrivial zeros of `ζ`, counted with
multiplicity, are simple and on the critical line [Cl26, Theorem A (i)].
statements.statement:
theorem simple_prop_two_thirds : ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ T > 0, (2 / 3 - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤ Ns riemannZeta T (2 * T)

statements.name: riemannZeta.distinct_prop_five_sixths
statements.doc:
At least five sixths of the nontrivial zeros of `ζ`, counted with
multiplicity, are distinct [Cl26, Theorem A (ii)].
statements.statement:
theorem distinct_prop_five_sixths : ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ T > 0, (5 / 6 - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤ Nd riemannZeta T (2 * T)

statements.name: riemannZeta.simple_prop_montgomeryTaylor
statements.doc:
The proportion of simple zeros of `ζ` on the critical line is at least
`2 - c_MT⁻¹ = 0.6725…`. [Cl26, Theorem A]
statements.statement:
theorem simple_prop_montgomeryTaylor : ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ T > 0, (2 - montgomeryTaylorConst⁻¹ - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤
      Ns riemannZeta T (2 * T)

statements.name: riemannZeta.distinct_prop_montgomeryTaylor
statements.doc:
The proportion of distinct zeros of `ζ` is at least `(3 - c_MT⁻¹) / 2 = 0.8362…`,
[Cl26, Theorem A].
statements.statement:
theorem distinct_prop_montgomeryTaylor : ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ T > 0, ((3 - montgomeryTaylorConst⁻¹) / 2 - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤
      Nd riemannZeta T (2 * T)

statements.name: riemannZeta.simple_prop_lt
statements.doc:
Is the proportion of simple zeros of `ζ` on the critical line unconditionally larger than
the Montgomery–Taylor bound `2 - c_MT⁻¹ = 0.6725…`? [Cl26, §7.2] puts the ceiling of its
method at about `0.682`.
statements.statement:
theorem simple_prop_lt : ∃ c > 2 - montgomeryTaylorConst⁻¹, ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ,
    o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
      ∀ T > 0, (c - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤ Ns riemannZeta T (2 * T)

statements.name: riemannZeta.simple_prop_one_hundred
statements.doc: Almost all nontrivial zeros of `ζ` are simple and on the critical line.
statements.statement:
theorem simple_prop_one_hundred : ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ T > 0, (1 - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤ Ns riemannZeta T (2 * T)

statements.name: riemannZeta.distinct_prop_lt
statements.doc:
Is the proportion of distinct zeros of `ζ` unconditionally larger than the Montgomery–Taylor
bound `(3 - c_MT⁻¹) / 2 = 0.8362…`?
statements.statement:

    o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ T > 0, (c - o T) * N riemannZeta T (2 * T) ≤ Nd riemannZeta T (2 * T)

problems.title: Ringel's Conjecture
problems.doc:
*Reference:* G. Ringel, *Problem 25*, in *Theory of Graphs and its Applications*
(Proc. Sympos. Smolenice, 1963), Academia, Prague, 1964.
